Ferguson stresses that this anointing makes the judges types of the Messiah, the Anointed One on whom the Spirit would rest without measure (Isa. 11:2; John 3:34). Every judge's Spirit-empowerment is a partial, temporary foreshadowing of Pentecost and of Christ, who at his baptism received the Spirit descending like a dove and went out in the power of the Spirit to deliver his people from a darker oppression than Mesopotamia's. Othniel is the first faint sketch of the Spirit-anointed Savior. (cf. Isa. 11:2; Luke 4:18)

verseByVerse.quote: So the land had rest forty years. Then Othniel the son of Kenaz died.
verseByVerse.commentary: The cycle closes with its fifth and sixth stages compressed into a single verse: 'So the land had rest forty years. Then Othniel the son of Kenaz died.' Forty years of rest — a full generation of peace, the fruit of Spirit-empowered deliverance. This is what God's salvation produces: not merely escape from the enemy but rest, shalom, the land at peace under God's blessing. It is the very thing Hebrews calls the believer's goal, a rest that remains for the people of God (Heb. 4:9). But the verse does not end on rest. 'Then Othniel... died.' There it is again — the deadly little word that ends every judge's tenure and triggers every relapse. Davis notes that the ideal judge is no exception to mortality; even Othniel, the model deliverer, the man on whom the Spirit rested, finally lies down in the grave, and his rest dies with him. The best of human saviors cannot outlast death, and so his salvation cannot outlast it either. The forty years of rest were real but borrowed, ending the moment the deliverer's heart stopped. How this aches for the Savior of whom it is said, 'Death no longer has dominion over him' (Rom. 6:9) — the Judge whose rest does not die when he does, because he does not stay dead. (cf. Heb. 4:9; Rom. 6:9)

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel relapses; God strengthens Eglon king of Moab against them for eighteen years. God raises Ehud, a left-handed Benjaminite, who assassinates the obese Eglon with a concealed dagger and leads Israel to crush Moab, securing eighty years of rest.
verseByVerse.theology: God delights to deliver through the unlikely and the weak. The despised tribe and the left-handed man become God's instruments, shaming human pride in strength.
verseByVerse.examples: God's instruments are often those the world overlooks. He still works through the unexpected to humble the proud and free the oppressed.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD strengthened Eglon the king of Moab against Israel... And the people of Israel served Eglon the king of Moab eighteen years.
verseByVerse.commentary: The wheel turns again: 'the people of Israel again did what was evil.' That word 'again' is the engine of the whole book; the relapse follows Othniel's death exactly as chapter 2 predicted. This time God 'strengthened Eglon the king of Moab against Israel.' The verb is arresting — God himself empowers the oppressor. Eglon's strength against Israel is not Eglon's achievement but God's gift of discipline; the LORD is sovereign even over the rod that beats his people. Moab joins with Ammon and Amalek, takes the City of Palms (Jericho), and Israel serves Eglon eighteen years — more than twice the bondage under Cushan, exactly as the spiral predicts deeper oppression with each cycle. There is bitter irony in the choice of Moab as oppressor. Moab was Israel's relative, descended from Lot, and Israel had been forbidden to harm them in the wilderness. Now this lesser kindred nation lords it over the covenant people. Begg notes how sin reduces us: the heirs of the promise, redeemed from Egypt with a mighty hand, now grovel before a petty Moabite king grown fat on their tribute. This is what idolatry always does — it shrinks the free children of God into the slaves of small and unworthy masters. (cf. Deut. 2:9; Rom. 6:16)

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people of Israel cried out to the LORD, and the LORD raised up for them a deliverer, Ehud, the son of Gera, the Benjaminite, a left-handed man. And Ehud made for himself a sword with two edges... and he bound it on his right thigh under his clothes.
verseByVerse.commentary: Israel cries out, and God raises up Ehud — and the narrator immediately flags the detail that will make the whole story work: he was 'a left-handed man.' The irony is delicious and surely intentional. Ehud is a Benjaminite, and Benjamin means 'son of the right hand,' yet this son of the right hand is left-handed (literally 'bound, restricted in the right hand'). What might look like a disability becomes the instrument of deliverance. Ehud forges a short, double-edged sword and straps it on his right thigh under his cloak — the one place a guard frisking a right-handed assassin would never check, since a right-handed man draws from the left. God's deliverer hides his weapon in plain sight, exploiting the very left-handedness the world might have dismissed. Davis loves this: God's salvation comes through what others overlook, through the 'limitation' that turns out to be the perfect equipment. Paul's principle is already at work — God chooses the weak things, the despised things, to shame the strong (1 Cor. 1:27). The left-handed man from the smallest tribe, carrying a homemade blade, is exactly the sort of unlikely savior God delights to use, so that the glory goes to God and not to human advantage. (cf. 1 Cor. 1:27; Judg. 20:16)

verseByVerse.quote: And Ehud said, "I have a secret message for you, O king." ...And Ehud reached with his left hand, took the sword from his right thigh, and thrust it into his belly. And the hilt also went in after the blade, and the fat closed over the blade, for he did not pull the sword out of his belly; and the dung came out.
verseByVerse.commentary: The narrative now revels in gruesome, almost comic detail. Ehud, having delivered the tribute, returns alone and gains a private audience with the obese king by promising 'a secret message for you, O king.' Eglon, intrigued, dismisses his attendants and rises from his cool roof chamber. Then Ehud says, 'I have a message from God for you' — and the 'message from God' is the blade. He draws with his left hand from his right thigh and drives the dagger so deep into the king's vast belly that 'the hilt also went in after the blade, and the fat closed over the blade.' The narrator does not spare us the indignity: 'and the dung came out.' This is earthy, satirical storytelling, and the satire has theology in it. Eglon (whose name may pun on 'fatted calf') has grown fat on Israel's tribute, gorging himself on the oppression of God's people — and now the bloated tyrant is butchered like the animal he resembles. Davis observes that the Bible can be deliberately, scandalously funny when it humbles the proud; heaven laughs at the petty kings who set themselves against the LORD (Ps. 2:4). The fat that symbolized Eglon's exploitation becomes his shroud, swallowing the blade that judges him. The oppressor's own corpulence becomes the agent of his disgrace. (cf. Ps. 2:4; 1 Sam. 2:7)

verseByVerse.quote: Then Ehud went out into the porch and closed the doors of the roof chamber behind him and locked them. ...the servants... waited till they were embarrassed. But when he still did not open the doors of the roof chamber, they took the key and opened them, and there lay their lord dead on the floor.
verseByVerse.commentary: The comedy continues at the servants' expense. Ehud calmly exits, closes and locks the doors of the roof chamber behind him, and escapes. The servants return and, finding the doors locked, assume the king is 'relieving himself in the closet of the cool chamber' — a euphemism the narrator clearly enjoys. So they wait. And wait. They wait 'till they were embarrassed,' standing helplessly outside while their murdered master lies dead within and the assassin slips farther away with every minute. Only at last do they fetch the key and discover the corpse. The whole scene is staged to make the enemy look ridiculous: a king dead and unguarded, servants paralyzed by misplaced delicacy, an assassin escaping unhurried. Davis notes the theological undertone beneath the farce — when God moves to deliver his people, the mightiest enemy becomes absurdly, helplessly inept. The Moabite court, which had lorded eighteen years over Israel, cannot even discover that its own king is dead. Pharaoh's chariots, Eglon's guards, every oppressor of God's people finally stands exposed as powerless before the purposes of heaven. The delay that embarrasses the servants is the providence that protects the deliverer; God times even the confusion of his enemies for the rescue of his own. (cf. Exod. 14:24–25; Prov. 21:30)

verseByVerse.quote: ...he sounded the trumpet in the hill country of Ephraim. Then the people of Israel went down with him from the hill country... And they killed at that time about 10,000 of the Moabites... So Moab was subdued that day under the hand of Israel. And the land had rest for eighty years.
verseByVerse.commentary: The assassination was only the beginning; Ehud now leads the deliverance. He sounds the trumpet in Ephraim, rallies Israel, and they seize the fords of the Jordan, cutting off Moab's retreat. Ten thousand Moabites fall — 'all strong, able-bodied men' — and 'Moab was subdued that day under the hand of Israel.' The result is the longest rest in the book: 'the land had rest for eighty years.' Twice the length of Othniel's peace. The headless oppressor is crushed, and Israel enjoys two full generations of quiet. Yet the reader, schooled by chapter 2, already feels the shadow over the eighty years. However long the rest, it is still temporary; another 'again' waits at the end of it. Ehud, the unlikely left-handed deliverer, has done his work well — better, in fact, than most who follow — and secured a remarkable peace. But Ehud too will die, and the peace will die with him. Davis draws the contrast that the whole book is building: each judge wins a rest that ends; only the true Deliverer wins the rest that remains. The eighty years are a long sabbath, a generous mercy, but they are a foretaste, not the fulfillment. They point past Ehud to the greater Son of the right hand, seated now at the right hand of God, whose finished deliverance secures an eternal rest no death can interrupt. (cf. Heb. 4:9–10; Ps. 110:1)

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In a single verse, Shamgar son of Anath strikes down six hundred Philistines with an oxgoad and also saves Israel.
verseByVerse.theology: God can deliver his people through the humblest instrument — a farmer's tool in a willing hand.
verseByVerse.examples: No one is too obscure and no instrument too ordinary for God to use for his people's deliverance.

verseByVerse.quote: After him was Shamgar the son of Anath, who killed 600 of the Philistines with an oxgoad, and he also saved Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter closes with the briefest judge of all — a single verse. 'Shamgar the son of Anath... killed 600 of the Philistines with an oxgoad, and he also saved Israel.' We are told almost nothing: no cycle formula, no years of rest, just a name, a weapon, and a body count. But what a weapon. An oxgoad was a long wooden pole tipped with a metal point, used to prod cattle and clean a plowshare — a farmer's everyday implement, not a soldier's sword. With this homely tool Shamgar cuts down six hundred of the dreaded, iron-equipped Philistines. The detail completes chapter 3's gallery of improbable saviors: a younger brother, a left-handed man, and now a farmer with a cattle-prod. Davis sees in Shamgar a miniature of the book's whole theology of grace — God needs no impressive resources to save his people; a willing hand and an ordinary stick will do. This is the same God who would arm a shepherd boy with five smooth stones against Goliath, who would feed five thousand with a boy's lunch, who would save the world through the foolish, weak instrument of a Roman cross. The oxgoad in Shamgar's hand whispers that deliverance never depended on the deliverer's equipment but on the God who wields him. Whatever ordinary thing is in your hand, the LORD can make it the instrument of his salvation. (cf. 1 Sam. 17:50; 1 Cor. 1:27–29)

3.theology:
Othniel the Ideal Judge. The first cycle is told in textbook form: sin, servitude, supplication, salvation, rest. Othniel, on whom 'the Spirit of the LORD' rested, is the standard against which every later judge will be measured — and a type of the Spirit-anointed Christ who delivers his people perfectly.

God's Delight in the Unlikely. A left-handed man from the smallest tribe, a farmer with an oxgoad — God deliberately chooses what the world overlooks to shame the strong (1 Cor. 1:27). The God who saved through Ehud's hidden dagger and Shamgar's cattle-prod would save the world through a crucified carpenter.

The Humbling of the Proud Oppressor. The satirical death of fat Eglon, and the comic helplessness of his servants, show that the mightiest enemy of God's people stands powerless when God moves to save. He who sits in the heavens laughs at the kings who set themselves against him (Ps. 2:4).
3.examples:
Then: Israel intermarried with idolaters and served their gods, fell under Cushan and then Eglon, and was rescued by a Spirit-empowered ideal judge, an unlikely left-handed assassin, and a farmer with an oxgoad — each deliverance real, each rest temporary, each judge mortal.

Now: Guard the relationships that shape your worship, for what we yoke ourselves to molds what we adore. And take heart: God still delights to use the overlooked, the 'disqualified,' the ordinary tool in a willing hand. You are not too weak or too obscure for God to wield. Offer him your oxgoad, and watch what he does with it.

4.title: Deborah and Barak
4.text: <sup>1</sup>And the people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD after Ehud died.<sup>2</sup>And the LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor. The commander of his army was Sisera, who lived in Harosheth-hagoyim.<sup>3</sup>Then the people of Israel cried out to the LORD for help, for he had 900 chariots of iron and he oppressed the people of Israel cruelly for twenty years.<sup>4</sup>Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time.<sup>5</sup>She used to sit under the palm of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim, and the people of Israel came up to her for judgment.<sup>6</sup>She sent and summoned Barak the son of Abinoam from Kedesh-naphtali and said to him, "Has not the LORD, the God of Israel, commanded you, 'Go, gather your men at Mount Tabor, taking 10,000 from the people of Naphtali and the people of Zebulun.<sup>7</sup>And I will draw out Sisera, the general of Jabin's army, to meet you by the river Kishon with his chariots and his troops, and I will give him into your hand'?"<sup>8</sup>Barak said to her, "If you will go with me, I will go, but if you will not go with me, I will not go."<sup>9</sup>And she said, "I will surely go with you. Nevertheless, the road on which you are going will not lead to your glory, for the LORD will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman." Then Deborah arose and went with Barak to Kedesh.<sup>10</sup>And Barak called out Zebulun and Naphtali to Kedesh. And 10,000 men went up at his heels, and Deborah went up with him.<sup>11</sup>Now Heber the Kenite had separated from the Kenites, the descendants of Hobab the father-in-law of Moses, and had pitched his tent as far away as the oak in Zaanannim, which is near Kedesh.<sup>12</sup>When Sisera was told that Barak the son of Abinoam had gone up to Mount Tabor,<sup>13</sup>Sisera called out all his chariots, 900 chariots of iron, and all the men who were with him, from Harosheth-hagoyim to the river Kishon.<sup>14</sup>And Deborah said to Barak, "Up! For this is the day in which the LORD has given Sisera into your hand. Does not the LORD go out before you?" So Barak went down from Mount Tabor with 10,000 men following him.<sup>15</sup>And the LORD routed Sisera and all his chariots and all his army before Barak by the edge of the sword. And Sisera got down from his chariot and fled away on foot.<sup>16</sup>And Barak pursued the chariots and the army to Harosheth-hagoyim, and all the army of Sisera fell by the edge of the sword; not a man was left.<sup>17</sup>But Sisera fled away on foot to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, for there was peace between Jabin the king of Hazor and the house of Heber the Kenite.<sup>18</sup>And Jael came out to meet Sisera and said to him, "Turn aside, my lord; turn aside to me; do not be afraid." So he turned aside to her into the tent, and she covered him with a rug.<sup>19</sup>And he said to her, "Please give me a little water to drink, for I am thirsty." So she opened a skin of milk and gave him a drink and covered him.<sup>20</sup>And he said to her, "Stand at the opening of the tent, and if any man comes and asks you, 'Is anyone here?' say, 'No.'"<sup>21</sup>But Jael the wife of Heber took a tent peg, and took a hammer in her hand. Then she went softly to him and drove the peg into his temple until it went down into the ground while he was lying fast asleep from weariness. So he died.<sup>22</sup>And behold, as Barak was pursuing Sisera, Jael went out to meet him and said to him, "Come, and I will show you the man whom you are seeking." So he went in to her tent, and there lay Sisera dead, with the tent peg in his temple.<sup>23</sup>So on that day God subdued Jabin the king of Canaan before the people of Israel.<sup>24</sup>And the hand of the people of Israel pressed harder and harder against Jabin the king of Canaan, until they destroyed Jabin king of Canaan.
4.overview:
The fourth cycle introduces the most remarkable leadership pairing in the book: Deborah, prophetess and judge, and Barak, the reluctant general. After Ehud's death Israel relapses, and God sells them to Jabin king of Canaan, whose commander Sisera oppresses them brutally for twenty years with nine hundred chariots of iron — the very iron chariots that had cowed Judah in chapter 1. The seeds of compromise have grown into a forest of oppression.

Deborah stands out as a singular figure — a woman judging Israel, dispensing God's word under her palm tree, and summoning Barak with a direct command from the LORD to march against Sisera. Barak's response is the hinge of the chapter: 'If you will go with me, I will go, but if you will not go with me, I will not go.' His faith is real but halting, conditional, leaning on the visible presence of the prophetess rather than the bare word of God. Deborah agrees to go but pronounces the consequence: the glory of the victory will go not to Barak but to a woman.

The battle is the LORD's. He routs Sisera's army — the next chapter reveals he used a flooding torrent to bog down the iron chariots — and Sisera flees on foot to the tent of Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite. There, in one of Scripture's most startling scenes, Jael lulls the exhausted commander with milk and a blanket, then drives a tent peg through his temple as he sleeps. The mighty Sisera, terror of Israel, dies at the hand of a woman with a household tool.

The theology is unmistakable. God deliberately arranges the victory so that no man can boast — a woman judges, a woman delivers, a woman strikes the fatal blow. The same God who chose the weak to shame the strong would one day overthrow the serpent through the seed of a woman. Barak makes the faith hall of fame in Hebrews 11, yet his hesitation reminds us that God will share his glory with no one, and will accomplish his salvation even through, and sometimes around, the faltering faith of his servants.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Oppression Under Jabin and Sisera
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel relapses after Ehud's death; God sells them to Jabin king of Canaan, whose commander Sisera oppresses them cruelly for twenty years with 900 iron chariots.
verseByVerse.theology: The iron chariots Judah feared in chapter 1 now oppress Israel — compromise tolerated becomes bondage endured. God remains sovereign over the oppressor.
verseByVerse.examples: The enemy we refuse to face in faith will one day face us in force. Twenty years of cruel oppression drive Israel at last to cry out.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD after Ehud died. And the LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan... The commander of his army was Sisera... He had 900 chariots of iron and he oppressed the people of Israel cruelly for twenty years.
verseByVerse.commentary: The cycle turns once more, and the trigger is stated plainly: Israel did evil again 'after Ehud died.' The deliverer's death undoes the deliverance, exactly as chapter 2 foretold. God sells them to Jabin king of Canaan, and the real menace is his commander Sisera, who fields 'nine hundred chariots of iron' and oppresses Israel 'cruelly for twenty years.' Note those iron chariots. In chapter 1, the iron chariots of the plain were the excuse for Judah's failure to drive out the enemy ('he could not drive them out... because they had chariots of iron,' 1:19). The very weapon Israel declined to face in faith has now multiplied into an army of nine hundred and become the instrument of their twenty-year torment. Davis draws the lesson with force: the compromise we tolerate today becomes the tyranny that crushes us tomorrow. The Canaanite left undriven-out grows into Sisera. And the oppression is 'cruel' and long — twenty years, the longest yet, the spiral deepening. Yet 'the LORD sold them'; even Sisera's chariots roll only by divine permission, as a rod of discipline. The God who governs the oppressor will also, in his time, drown those chariots in a torrent. The enemy we fear and will not fight in faith always grows stronger in the delay. (cf. Judg. 1:19; Josh. 17:16)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–5 — Deborah the Prophetess and Judge
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Deborah, a prophetess, is judging Israel from beneath her palm tree, and the people come up to her for judgment.
verseByVerse.theology: God raises up a woman as prophet and judge in a day when the men have failed — his sovereign freedom to use whom he wills for his glory.
verseByVerse.examples: When godly men shrink back, God will still accomplish his purposes, often through those the culture least expects.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time. She used to sit under the palm of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim, and the people of Israel came up to her for judgment.
verseByVerse.commentary: Deborah is introduced with a triple distinction: a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, and a judge of Israel. She is the only judge in the book also explicitly called a prophet, the one who speaks God's word, and the only one shown actually judging in the judicial sense — sitting under her palm, settling disputes, dispensing the word of the LORD to a people who 'came up to her for judgment.' She is a stable, settled presence of God's truth in a chaotic age. Davis and Ferguson both observe the quiet rebuke embedded in her prominence: in a period when the men of Israel are spiritually passive — when Barak will need a woman to stiffen his spine — God raises up a woman to lead. This is not God overturning his created order but God's sovereign freedom shaming a generation of faltering men. As Deborah herself will sing, the leaders failed until she 'arose as a mother in Israel' (5:7). There is great encouragement here for the obscure and the unlikely. When the expected leaders shrink back, God is never without a servant; he will raise up whom he pleases, anoint whom he chooses, and accomplish his deliverance through the very people the world overlooks. The throne of grace is never empty for lack of a courageous man; God can summon a faithful woman. (cf. Judg. 5:7; 1 Cor. 1:27)

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Deborah summons Barak with a direct command from the LORD: gather ten thousand men at Mount Tabor, and God will draw out Sisera and give him into Barak's hand.
verseByVerse.theology: The command comes with the promise attached — God's call always carries God's guarantee of success.
verseByVerse.examples: God's commands are never bare orders; they come wrapped in his promises. Obedience rests on the certainty of his word.

verseByVerse.quote: She sent and summoned Barak... and said to him, "Has not the LORD, the God of Israel, commanded you, 'Go, gather your men at Mount Tabor... And I will draw out Sisera... to meet you by the river Kishon with his chariots and his troops, and I will give him into your hand'?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Deborah summons Barak and delivers a word that is pure gospel logic: command fused with promise. 'Has not the LORD... commanded you, Go, gather your men at Mount Tabor... And I will draw out Sisera... and I will give him into your hand?' Notice the structure. The command — go and gather — is bracketed by the divine guarantee — I will draw out, I will give into your hand. God does not merely order Barak into danger; he promises the outcome before the battle begins. The victory is announced as already decided in heaven, just as it was for Judah in chapter 1 ('I have given the land into his hand'). Barak is asked only to act on a promise God has already secured. Davis stresses that this is the shape of all true obedience: God's imperatives always come riding on God's assurances. He never commands without promising to enable; he never sends without pledging to go before. The strategy even sounds like folly — infantry on Mount Tabor against nine hundred iron chariots in the plain — but the word 'I will give him into your hand' transforms folly into faith. The Christian fights every battle on the same terms: not for victory but from it, leaning the whole weight of obedience on the bare, sufficient word of God. (cf. Josh. 1:9; 2 Cor. 1:20)

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Barak agrees to go only if Deborah goes with him. She consents but warns that the glory will go to a woman, for the LORD will sell Sisera into a woman's hand.
verseByVerse.theology: God honors even weak faith but will not allow human glory to eclipse his own. The reluctant believer is still used, yet forfeits the honor that bold faith would have won.
verseByVerse.examples: Conditional, hesitant obedience still counts as obedience, but it costs us. God shares his glory with no one.

verseByVerse.quote: Barak said to her, "If you will go with me, I will go, but if you will not go with me, I will not go." And she said, "I will surely go with you. Nevertheless, the road on which you are going will not lead to your glory, for the LORD will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman."
verseByVerse.commentary: Here is the chapter's spiritual hinge. Barak has heard the command and the promise of God himself, yet he hesitates: 'If you will go with me, I will go, but if you will not go with me, I will not go.' His faith is genuine — he does not refuse outright — but it is conditional, leaning on the visible presence of the prophetess rather than the invisible word of the LORD. He wants a guarantee he can see beside him on the battlefield. Interpreters differ on how harshly to judge Barak; after all, Hebrews 11:32 will honor him among the heroes of faith. Yet Deborah's reply names the cost: 'the road on which you are going will not lead to your glory, for the LORD will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman.' Ferguson notes the sobering principle: weak faith is still saving faith, and God still uses the hesitant servant — but hesitation forfeits honor that boldness would have gained. Barak will win the battle, but the climactic glory of killing Sisera will go to Jael. God will not let his deliverance hang on a man who must see before he will trust, and he will not share the credit with halfhearted faith. The lesson is tender and searching at once: Christ welcomes our smallest mustard seed of trust, yet calls us to a fuller faith that takes him at his word without demanding to see. (cf. Heb. 11:32; John 20:29)

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Barak musters ten thousand at Tabor; Heber the Kenite's separation is noted; Sisera, informed of Barak's movement, gathers all his chariots and troops at the river Kishon.
verseByVerse.theology: God orchestrates the convergence of forces, drawing the enemy precisely where he intends to destroy him.
verseByVerse.examples: Behind the maneuvering of armies and the choices of men, God is quietly arranging the stage for his deliverance.

verseByVerse.quote: And Barak called out Zebulun and Naphtali to Kedesh. And 10,000 men went up at his heels... When Sisera was told that Barak the son of Abinoam had gone up to Mount Tabor, Sisera called out all his chariots, 900 chariots of iron, and all the men who were with him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The forces converge. Barak musters ten thousand men from Zebulun and Naphtali — lightly armed tribesmen with no chariots, taking the high ground of Tabor. A parenthetical note (v. 11) tells us that Heber the Kenite had separated from his kin and pitched his tent near Kedesh, a seemingly minor detail that will prove decisive when Sisera flees to Jael's tent. The narrator plants the clue quietly, and only later do we see God's providence in it. Sisera, informed of Barak's movement, gathers 'all his chariots, nine hundred chariots of iron, and all the men who were with him' to the river Kishon. From a military standpoint Israel is outmatched; infantry on a hill faces an armored host in a plain built for chariots. But Davis points to the deeper drama: Sisera thinks he is hunting Barak, when in truth God is drawing Sisera into a trap. Verse 7 had said the LORD would 'draw out Sisera... to the river Kishon,' and here he comes, marching confidently to the very ground God has chosen for his destruction. Behind the troop movements and the stratagems of generals, an unseen hand is arranging every piece. The enemy's confidence is itself part of the snare. God positions even the placement of a Kenite tent and the route of an enemy army to accomplish the deliverance of his people. (cf. Judg. 4:7; Prov. 16:9)

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Deborah gives the signal; the LORD routs Sisera and all his chariots before Barak. Sisera flees on foot while Barak destroys the entire army.
verseByVerse.theology: The victory is explicitly the LORD's: 'the LORD routed Sisera.' God himself fights for his people, neutralizing the iron chariots.
verseByVerse.examples: When God says 'the day has come,' faith advances. The enemy that terrified for twenty years collapses in a moment before the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: And Deborah said to Barak, "Up! For this is the day in which the LORD has given Sisera into your hand. Does not the LORD go out before you?" ...And the LORD routed Sisera and all his chariots and all his army before Barak by the edge of the sword. And Sisera got down from his chariot and fled away on foot.
verseByVerse.commentary: Deborah gives the command to charge: 'Up! For this is the day in which the LORD has given Sisera into your hand. Does not the LORD go out before you?' Her question is the engine of the whole assault. Barak is not asked to defeat Sisera; he is asked to follow a LORD who has already gone out before him to do it. And so it proves: 'the LORD routed Sisera and all his chariots and all his army before Barak.' The verb is decisive — the LORD routed them. Barak and his ten thousand wield the sword, but the victory is God's act. The next chapter will reveal the means: the Kishon flooded, the plain turned to mud, and the nine hundred iron chariots — Israel's twenty-year terror — became nine hundred useless, mired traps (5:21). The very thing Judah called an insurmountable obstacle, God turned into the enemy's grave. Sisera, the great commander, is reduced to abandoning his chariot and fleeing on foot like the lowest of men. Davis savors the reversal: the symbol of Canaanite might becomes the symbol of Canaanite humiliation. This is how God fights for his people. The obstacle that paralyzed our faith becomes, in his hand, the instrument of our deliverance. The day God says 'Up!' is the day the unconquerable enemy collapses. (cf. Judg. 5:21; 2 Chron. 20:17)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–22 — Jael and the Tent Peg
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sisera flees to the tent of Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite, who lulls him with milk and a blanket, then drives a tent peg through his temple as he sleeps. Barak arrives to find his enemy already dead.
verseByVerse.theology: Deborah's prophecy is fulfilled: Sisera falls 'into the hand of a woman.' God grants the climactic glory to the unlikeliest of agents, so no man can boast.
verseByVerse.examples: God overthrows the mighty through the despised and the domestic. The tent peg in a woman's hand topples the terror of nations.

verseByVerse.quote: But Sisera fled away on foot to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite... And Jael came out to meet Sisera and said to him, "Turn aside, my lord; turn aside to me; do not be afraid." ...He said to her, "Please give me a little water to drink..." So she opened a skin of milk and gave him a drink and covered him.
verseByVerse.commentary: Sisera flees to what he thinks is safety — the tent of Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite, whose clan was at peace with Jabin. Jael plays the gracious hostess to perfection. 'Turn aside, my lord; turn aside to me; do not be afraid,' she says, the very words to disarm a fugitive. He asks for water; she gives him milk — richer, warmer, sleep-inducing — and covers him with a rug. Every gesture breathes hospitality and safety, the ancient sacred bond between host and guest, and Sisera relaxes into it utterly, posting her as his sentry: 'if anyone comes and asks, say, No.' He has fled the battlefield where the LORD routed him into a tent where the LORD has prepared his end. Davis notes the dramatic irony thick over the scene: the exhausted general, who imagines he has found refuge, has in fact walked into the fulfillment of Deborah's prophecy. The milk and the blanket are the lulling of a doomed man. Sisera trusts the appearance of safety and overlooks the woman before him as no threat at all — and his blindness is his ruin. The mighty are often undone precisely where they feel most secure, and God's instruments are often the people the powerful never think to fear. (cf. Judg. 4:9; 1 Thess. 5:3)

verseByVerse.quote: But Jael the wife of Heber took a tent peg, and took a hammer in her hand. Then she went softly to him and drove the peg into his temple until it went down into the ground while he was lying fast asleep from weariness. So he died. And behold, as Barak pursued Sisera, Jael went out to meet him and said, "Come, and I will show you the man whom you are seeking."
verseByVerse.commentary: The deed is swift and shocking. While Sisera lies 'fast asleep from weariness,' Jael takes a tent peg and a hammer — the ordinary tools of a Bedouin woman who pitched the family tents — and 'drove the peg into his temple until it went down into the ground.' The terror of Israel, commander of nine hundred chariots, dies pinned to the earth by a woman with a household implement. Then comes the final, exquisite irony: Barak arrives in pursuit, and Jael steps out to meet him — 'Come, and I will show you the man whom you are seeking.' Barak, the general, finds his great enemy already dead, slain by a woman, exactly as Deborah foretold. The glory he might have had is gone, gathered up by Jael's tent peg. Davis sees here the book's theology of grace driven to its sharpest point: God arranged this deliverance so that no man could claim it. A woman judged; a woman commanded; a woman struck the killing blow. The pattern reaches back to Genesis 3:15, where the serpent's head would be crushed by the seed of the woman, and forward to the gospel, where God overthrows every proud power through the weak and despised things of the world. The tent peg in Jael's hand preaches that salvation belongs to the LORD, who shares his glory with no man. (cf. Gen. 3:15; 1 Cor. 1:27–29)

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God subdues Jabin king of Canaan before Israel, whose hand presses harder and harder until Jabin is destroyed.
verseByVerse.theology: God's deliverance is complete; the oppressor is not merely checked but destroyed. The victory belongs wholly to God.
verseByVerse.examples: What God begins to do for his people, he finishes. The enemy that oppressed for twenty years is utterly broken.

verseByVerse.quote: So on that day God subdued Jabin the king of Canaan before the people of Israel. And the hand of the people of Israel pressed harder and harder against Jabin the king of Canaan, until they destroyed Jabin king of Canaan.
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter ends with a summary that gives all the credit to its true author: 'On that day God subdued Jabin the king of Canaan before the people of Israel.' Not Barak subdued, not Israel subdued — God subdued. The whole campaign, from Deborah's summons to Jael's tent peg, is gathered up under the agency of God. And the deliverance is thorough: Israel's hand 'pressed harder and harder against Jabin... until they destroyed' him. This is not the partial, compromising conquest of chapter 1, where tribe after tribe 'did not drive out' the enemy. Here the oppressor is pursued to total destruction. When God fights for his people through even hesitant servants and unlikely instruments, the result is complete. Davis notes the contrast with the book's opening failures: faith, even Barak's conditional faith, finishes the job that unbelief left undone. The twenty-year torment ends not in a managed truce but in the enemy's ruin. There is gospel assurance here. The God who saves does not leave the work half done; he presses the victory to its end. The same Christ who began a good work in his people will bring it to completion (Phil. 1:6), pressing harder and harder against the sin that oppresses them until every enemy is destroyed and the last of them, death itself, is swallowed up in victory. (cf. Phil. 1:6; 1 Cor. 15:25–26)

4.theology:
The LORD Fights for His People. 'The LORD routed Sisera' (v. 15); 'God subdued Jabin' (v. 23). The victory is explicitly God's act. He turned the iron chariots that terrified Israel for twenty years into mired traps, proving that no obstacle is insurmountable to the God who goes out before his people.

God Shares His Glory with No One. Because Barak demanded to see the prophetess beside him before he would trust the word of the LORD, the climactic glory went to a woman. A woman judged, a woman commanded, and a woman struck the fatal blow — so that no man could boast (1 Cor. 1:29).

Weak Faith Truly Used. Barak's faith was real but conditional, yet God still used him and even enrolled him in the faith hall of fame (Heb. 11:32). God honors the mustard seed while calling us to fuller, bolder trust in his bare word.
4.examples:
Then: The iron chariots Judah feared had grown into Sisera's twenty-year tyranny, until God raised up Deborah and the reluctant Barak, routed the chariots in a flooded plain, and gave the great enemy into the hand of a woman with a tent peg.

Now: The enemy you will not face in faith grows stronger in the delay. Yet no obstacle, however armored, can stand when God goes out before you. Bring him your trembling, conditional faith — he will use it — but press on toward the bolder trust that takes him at his word without demanding to see, and let him have all the glory.

5.title: The Song of Deborah
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Then sang Deborah and Barak the son of Abinoam on that day:<sup>2</sup>"That the leaders took the lead in Israel, that the people offered themselves willingly, bless the LORD!<sup>3</sup>"Hear, O kings; give ear, O princes; to the LORD I will sing; I will make melody to the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>4</sup>"LORD, when you went out from Seir, when you marched from the region of Edom, the earth trembled and the heavens dropped, yes, the clouds dropped water.<sup>5</sup>The mountains quaked before the LORD, even Sinai before the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>6</sup>"In the days of Shamgar, son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the highways were abandoned, and travelers kept to the byways.<sup>7</sup>The villagers ceased in Israel; they ceased to be until I arose; I, Deborah, arose as a mother in Israel.<sup>8</sup>When new gods were chosen, then war was in the gates. Was shield or spear to be seen among forty thousand in Israel?<sup>9</sup>My heart goes out to the commanders of Israel who offered themselves willingly among the people. Bless the LORD.<sup>10</sup>"Tell of it, you who ride on white donkeys, you who sit on rich carpets and you who walk by the way.<sup>11</sup>To the sound of musicians at the watering places, there they repeat the righteous triumphs of the LORD, the righteous triumphs of his villagers in Israel. "Then down to the gates marched the people of the LORD.<sup>12</sup>"Awake, awake, Deborah! Awake, awake, break out in a song! Arise, Barak, lead away your captives, O son of Abinoam.<sup>13</sup>Then down marched the remnant of the noble; the people of the LORD marched down for me against the mighty.<sup>14</sup>From Ephraim their root they marched down into the valley, following you, Benjamin, with your kinsmen; from Machir marched down the commanders, and from Zebulun those who bear the lieutenant's staff;<sup>15</sup>the princes of Issachar came with Deborah, and Issachar faithful to Barak; into the valley they rushed at his heels. Among the clans of Reuben there were great searchings of heart.<sup>16</sup>Why did you sit still among the sheepfolds, to hear the whistling for the flocks? Among the clans of Reuben there were great searchings of heart.<sup>17</sup>Gilead stayed beyond the Jordan; and Dan, why did he stay with the ships? Asher sat still at the coast of the sea, staying by his landings.<sup>18</sup>Zebulun is a people who risked their lives to the death; Naphtali, too, on the heights of the field.<sup>19</sup>"The kings came, they fought; then fought the kings of Canaan, at Taanach, by the waters of Megiddo; they got no spoils of silver.<sup>20</sup>From heaven the stars fought, from their courses they fought against Sisera.<sup>21</sup>The torrent Kishon swept them away, the ancient torrent, the torrent Kishon. March on, my soul, with might!<sup>22</sup>"Then loud beat the horses' hoofs with the galloping, galloping of his steeds.<sup>23</sup>"Curse Meroz, says the angel of the LORD, curse its inhabitants thoroughly, because they did not come to the help of the LORD, to the help of the LORD against the mighty.<sup>24</sup>"Most blessed of women be Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, of tent-dwelling women most blessed.<sup>25</sup>He asked for water and she gave him milk; she brought him curds in a noble's bowl.<sup>26</sup>She sent her hand to the tent peg and her right hand to the workmen's mallet; she struck Sisera; she crushed his head; she shattered and pierced his temple.<sup>27</sup>Between her feet he sank, he fell, he lay still; between her feet he sank, he fell; where he sank, there he fell—dead.<sup>28</sup>"Out of the window she peered, the mother of Sisera wailed through the lattice: 'Why is his chariot so long in coming? Why tarry the hoofbeats of his chariots?'<sup>29</sup>Her wisest princesses answer, indeed, she answers herself,<sup>30</sup>'Have they not found and divided the spoil?— A womb or two for every man; spoil of dyed materials for Sisera, spoil of dyed materials embroidered, two pieces of dyed work embroidered for the neck as spoil?'<sup>31</sup>"So may all your enemies perish, O LORD! But your friends be like the sun as he rises in his might." And the land had rest for forty years.
5.overview:
Chapter 5 is the poetic celebration of the victory narrated in chapter 4 — the Song of Deborah and Barak, one of the oldest poems in the Bible, a triumph hymn sung on the day of deliverance. Where chapter 4 gave the prose account, chapter 5 gives the praise, and the difference matters: God's people are not merely to be rescued but to respond to rescue with worship.

The song opens by blessing the LORD for willing leaders and a willing people, recalls Yahweh's mighty advance from Sinai, paints the desolation of the oppression, and celebrates the rising of Deborah, 'a mother in Israel.' It then rolls through a roll call of the tribes, praising those who came to the fight and rebuking those who stayed home — Reuben dithering among the sheepfolds, Meroz cursed for not coming to the help of the LORD.

At the song's heart blazes the most stunning image in the book: 'From heaven the stars fought... The torrent Kishon swept them away.' The battle was won not by Israel's sword but by heaven itself. Then the song exults over Jael's deed and, in a final scene of dramatic irony, imagines Sisera's mother peering through the lattice for a son who will never come home.

It ends with a prayer that doubles as the book's deepest longing: 'So may all your enemies perish, O LORD! But your friends be like the sun as he rises in his might.' This is doxology after deliverance, anticipating the song of Moses and the Lamb (Rev. 15), the eternal anthem of the redeemed who praise the God who fought from heaven and saved them by his own arm.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Praise for Willing Leaders and the God of Sinai
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The song bursts into praise for leaders who led and people who volunteered, recalls the LORD's earth-shaking advance from Sinai, and laments the misery of the oppression before celebrating Deborah's rise.
verseByVerse.theology: True deliverance produces worship. The God who fought Sisera is the cosmic Warrior of Sinai; grace received must become grace recounted.
verseByVerse.examples: Service to God is glad self-offering, not grudging duty. Deliverance demands testimony — we must tell of his righteous triumphs.

verseByVerse.quote: Then sang Deborah and Barak on that day: "That the leaders took the lead in Israel, that the people offered themselves willingly, bless the LORD! Hear, O kings; give ear, O princes; to the LORD I will sing; I will make melody to the LORD, the God of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary: The song erupts in praise before it tells the story. The first cause for blessing the LORD is willing service: 'the leaders took the lead... the people offered themselves willingly.' After chapter 4, where Barak hesitated and the tribes had to be summoned, the song celebrates the grace that finally moved hearts to volunteer. Davis notes that willingness brackets the whole song (vv. 2, 9); the deliverance came when God's people stopped being conscripts and became volunteers, offering themselves freely. This is the heartbeat of all true service — not grudging duty but glad self-offering, the spirit Paul praises in the Macedonians who 'gave themselves first to the Lord' (2 Cor. 8:5). And the song is unashamedly God-directed: 'to the LORD I will sing.' Deborah summons even the pagan kings and princes to listen as she makes melody to Yahweh. The proper response to deliverance is not self-congratulation but worship that names God as the deliverer and invites the watching world to hear. Begg observes that the redeemed life is essentially a song — a heart so moved by rescue that it cannot keep silent. The victory of chapter 4 becomes the worship of chapter 5, as every salvation should. (cf. 2 Cor. 8:5; Ps. 30:11–12)

verseByVerse.quote: "LORD, when you went out from Seir, when you marched from the region of Edom, the earth trembled and the heavens dropped, yes, the clouds dropped water. The mountains quaked before the LORD, even Sinai before the LORD, the God of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary: The song sweeps back to Sinai. Before recounting the recent victory, Deborah frames it against the great theophany of Israel's founding: 'LORD, when you went out from Seir... the earth trembled and the heavens dropped... The mountains quaked before the LORD, even Sinai.' The God who fought Sisera is the cosmic Warrior of the Exodus, before whom creation itself convulses. Davis points out the brilliance of this poetic move: the deliverance from Canaan is set as one episode in the long story of the God who marches out to save his people, the same God whose approach shook the mountains at Sinai. To understand any small rescue rightly, we must set it against the great Rescuer who commands the storm and the quaking earth. Notice too the imagery of dropping clouds and water — already the song hints at the means of victory, the storm and flood that would mire Sisera's chariots (v. 21). The God of weather and earthquake, of Sinai's smoke and the Kishon's flood, is one God, always the Warrior for his covenant people. This is the same Lord who would later calm a storm with a word, proving that all creation serves its Maker. When we feel small before our enemies, the cure is to remember the God before whom Sinai itself trembled. (cf. Exod. 19:18; Hab. 3:3–6)

verseByVerse.quote: "In the days of Shamgar... the highways were abandoned, and travelers kept to the byways. The villagers ceased in Israel; they ceased to be until I arose; I, Deborah, arose as a mother in Israel. When new gods were chosen, then war was in the gates."
verseByVerse.commentary: The song now paints the misery of the oppression with stark realism. 'The highways were abandoned, and travelers kept to the byways. The villagers ceased.' Life under Sisera had shrunk to fear; commerce stopped, main roads emptied because they were unsafe, rural communities collapsed. This is what tyranny does — it shrivels ordinary life into terror. And the song names the root cause: 'When new gods were chosen, then war was in the gates.' The idolatry of chapter 4 is exposed as the spring of all the suffering. Choose new gods, and you choose the bondage that follows. Then the bright reversal: 'until I arose, Deborah, arose as a mother in Israel.' She names herself not a warrior but a mother — the nurturing, protecting, God-given presence raised up when the men had failed. Davis cherishes this image: a mother in Israel, fierce in defense of her endangered children, standing in the breach where leaders had fled. The song is honest about the depth of the affliction so that the praise for deliverance might be equally deep. Sin had emptied the roads and silenced the villages; grace, through a willing mother in Israel, would fill them again. (cf. Lev. 26:22; Isa. 33:8)

verseByVerse.quote: "My heart goes out to the commanders of Israel who offered themselves willingly among the people. Bless the LORD. ...to the sound of musicians at the watering places, there they repeat the righteous triumphs of the LORD... Then down to the gates marched the people of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary: Deborah's heart swells toward the willing commanders, returning again to the theme of glad volunteering: 'who offered themselves willingly among the people. Bless the LORD.' Then she calls all classes to join the praise — those who ride white donkeys (the well-off), those who sit on rich carpets, and those who walk the road (the common folk). High and low alike are summoned to 'tell of it' and to 'repeat the righteous triumphs of the LORD.' That phrase — 'the righteous triumphs of the LORD' — is the song's interpretation of the whole event. The victory was not Israel's triumph but the LORD's, and not merely a triumph but a righteous one, the just God vindicating his oppressed people and overthrowing the oppressor. Ferguson observes that worship and witness are inseparable here: even at the watering places, in the ordinary rhythms of daily life, the people are to recount what God has done. Grace received must become grace recounted; the deeds of God are not to be hoarded in the heart but told at the wells, in the gates, to the rising generation. This is the cure for the tragedy of 2:10 — the generation that 'did not know the LORD' arose because the works of God were not told. The song commands the telling, so the next generation might know. (cf. Ps. 145:4; Deut. 6:7)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–18 — The Roll Call of the Tribes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The song grades the tribes by their response: praising those who marched (Ephraim, Benjamin, Machir, Zebulun, Issachar, and above all Zebulun and Naphtali who risked their lives) and rebuking those who stayed home (Reuben, Gilead, Dan, Asher).
verseByVerse.theology: Participation in the work of God is a test of the heart. There is blessedness for those who hazard everything for the cause and rebuke for the comfortable who weigh the cost and choose ease.
verseByVerse.examples: When the trumpet sounds for God's work, deliberation that never moves the feet is cowardice dressed as piety. God remembers who showed up.

verseByVerse.quote: "Awake, awake, Deborah! Awake, awake, break out in a song! Arise, Barak, lead away your captives... Out of Ephraim... from you Benjamin... from Machir marched down the commanders, and from Zebulun those who bear the lieutenant's staff; the princes of Issachar came with Deborah."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Awake, awake, Deborah!' The song rouses itself to its central task — the muster roll of the tribes — and begins with those to be honored. Ephraim, Benjamin, Machir (representing Manasseh), Zebulun, and Issachar are named as the faithful who marched to the battle. Issachar especially 'came with Deborah,' faithful to the prophet-judge's summons, and 'into the valley they rushed at his heels' — eager, not dragged. This is no mere historical list; it is a theology of participation in the work of God. Davis observes that the song deliberately grades the tribes by their response to the call, and the grading searches every reader. The faithful tribes did not all share equal danger or equal glory, but they shared the decisive thing: they came. They answered the summons of the LORD through his prophet and threw themselves into the valley where the battle raged. There is a blessedness reserved for those who simply show up when God calls, who do not let distance or danger or the difficulty of the terrain keep them from the field. The kingdom of God advances through such willing feet — not the gifted few only, but the many who rush at the heels of God's purpose when the trumpet sounds. (cf. Judg. 5:2; Neh. 4:6)

verseByVerse.quote: "...Among the clans of Reuben there were great searchings of heart. Why did you sit still among the sheepfolds, to hear the whistling for the flocks? ...Gilead stayed beyond the Jordan; and Dan, why did he stay with the ships? Asher sat still at the coast of the sea..."
verseByVerse.commentary: Now the song turns to the absentees, and its rebukes sting. Reuben merely deliberated — and twice the song mocks his 'great searchings of heart,' the endless agonized discussion that never issued in action. 'Why did you sit still among the sheepfolds, to hear the whistling for the flocks?' Reuben weighed the matter earnestly, no doubt, but in the end stayed home with the sheep. Gilead 'stayed beyond the Jordan'; Dan lingered with his ships; Asher 'sat still at the coast of the sea.' Each had a reason — flocks, distance, commerce — and each reason was an excuse. Davis notes that the most damning portraits in the song are not of open rebels but of the comfortable and the calculating, those who weighed the risk and chose their own ease over the cause of God. The phrase 'great searchings of heart' is devastating precisely because it sounds so spiritual; Reuben agonized conscientiously and did nothing. Begg presses the point: there is a moment when deliberation becomes disobedience, when the searching of heart that never moves the feet is simply cowardice in pious dress. When the kingdom calls, which tribe are we? The one that rushed into the valley, or the one that sat among the sheepfolds with great searchings of heart? God remembers who came. (cf. Luke 9:62; James 1:22)

verseByVerse.quote: "Zebulun is a people who risked their lives to the death; Naphtali, too, on the heights of the field."
verseByVerse.commentary: Against the backdrop of the absentees, the song lifts up its highest praise. 'Zebulun is a people who risked their lives to the death; Naphtali, too, on the heights of the field.' These two tribes — the very ones Barak first mustered (4:6, 10) — did not count the cost; they hazarded everything, scorning death itself for the cause of the LORD on the exposed heights where the chariots could reach them. The song lingers lovingly on their courage. Davis observes that this verse is the summit of the muster roll, the antithesis of Reuben's searchings of heart: where Reuben calculated and stayed, Zebulun and Naphtali calculated and went, willing to die. There is a blessedness reserved for those who throw themselves wholly into God's battles, who love not their lives even unto death (Rev. 12:11). This is the spirit of every martyr and every faithful servant who has counted the cost and found the cause worth dying for. It is the spirit of Christ himself, who 'risked his life to the death' — indeed gave it — on the heights of Calvary for his people. And it is the spirit he calls his followers to share: 'whoever loses his life for my sake will find it' (Matt. 16:25). The song crowns not the safe but the self-spending, those who poured themselves out on the heights of the field. (cf. Rev. 12:11; Matt. 16:25)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–23 — From Heaven the Stars Fought
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The song reaches its theological summit: the kings of Canaan won no spoil because heaven itself fought — the stars in their courses and the flooding Kishon swept Sisera's chariots away. Meroz is cursed for refusing to help the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology: The battle is the LORD's, fought from heaven by the cosmic Warrior who commands the stars and the storm. There is no neutrality in God's war; to stand aside is treason.
verseByVerse.examples: The obstacle that paralyzes our faith becomes, in God's hand, the enemy's grave. Whoever is not with him is against him.

verseByVerse.quote: "The kings came, they fought... but they got no spoils of silver. From heaven the stars fought, from their courses they fought against Sisera. The torrent Kishon swept them away, the ancient torrent, the torrent Kishon. March on, my soul, with might!"
verseByVerse.commentary: Now the song reaches its theological summit. The kings of Canaan came for plunder 'but they got no spoils of silver' — they marched out to enrich themselves and went home with nothing, if they went home at all. And the reason is the most breathtaking line in the book: 'From heaven the stars fought, from their courses they fought against Sisera. The torrent Kishon swept them away.' Here at last we learn how the LORD 'routed Sisera' in chapter 4. It was not Israelite tactics or steel; heaven itself entered the battle. The stars in their courses, the very order of creation, fought against the enemy of God's people; the storm broke, the Kishon flooded, the plain turned to a quagmire, and the nine hundred iron chariots — Israel's twenty-year terror — sank uselessly into the mud and were swept away by the swollen torrent. The weapon that made Israel despair became the instrument of Canaan's destruction, undone by water and weather marshaled by God. Davis exults that this is the song's whole point: the battle is the LORD's, fought from heaven, won by the cosmic Warrior who commands the stars and the storm. Israel's role was to show up; God's role was to win. The obstacle that paralyzed faith in chapter 1 became, in God's hand, the enemy's grave. 'March on, my soul, with might!' (cf. Ps. 18:9–15; 2 Chron. 20:15)

verseByVerse.quote: "Then loud beat the horses' hoofs with the galloping, galloping of his steeds. 'Curse Meroz,' says the angel of the LORD, 'curse its inhabitants thoroughly, because they did not come to the help of the LORD, to the help of the LORD against the mighty.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The galloping hooves of fleeing horses give way to the song's most severe word: the curse of Meroz. 'Curse Meroz, says the angel of the LORD, curse its inhabitants thoroughly, because they did not come to the help of the LORD, to the help of the LORD against the mighty.' Meroz, evidently an Israelite community near the battlefield, is not merely overlooked like Reuben but explicitly and thoroughly cursed — and cursed by the angel of the LORD himself, the same divine figure who confronted Israel at Bochim. The severity is startling and instructive. To stand neutral when the LORD is at war, to refuse 'the help of the LORD against the mighty,' is not safe middle ground; it is treason. The repeated phrase — 'to the help of the LORD' — underlines that the battle was God's cause, and to sit it out was to side, by default, with his enemies. Davis draws the unflinching lesson: there is no neutrality in the conflict between the kingdom of God and the powers of darkness. Christ said it plainly: 'Whoever is not with me is against me' (Matt. 12:30). Meroz thought it could quietly avoid the war and keep its hands clean. The angel of the LORD calls down a curse on such cowardice. The lukewarm, the fence-sitting, the carefully neutral — these draw heaven's sharpest rebuke. (cf. Matt. 12:30; Rev. 3:15–16)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–30 — The Blessing of Jael and Sisera's Mother
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The song crowns Jael 'most blessed of women' for her deed, retelling the killing in pounding poetry. Then it shifts to Sisera's mother at the lattice, waiting for a son who will never return.
verseByVerse.theology: God blesses those who strike for him and exults in the overthrow of the oppressor. Yet the scene of the waiting mother lets us feel the human cost, the bitter harvest of a house built on oppression.
verseByVerse.examples: Sin always ends with someone watching at a window for a son who does not come home. The triumph of justice is cause for joy, not the suffering itself.

verseByVerse.quote: "Most blessed of women be Jael... He asked for water and she gave him milk... Her hand reached for the tent peg... she struck Sisera; she crushed his head... Between her feet he sank, he fell, he lay still; between her feet he sank, he fell; where he sank, there he fell — dead."
verseByVerse.commentary: The song crowns Jael in language that deliberately answers the curse on Meroz: 'Most blessed of women be Jael... of tent-dwelling women most blessed.' Meroz is cursed for staying out of the fight; Jael is blessed for striking the decisive blow. The poetry retells the deed with grim, deliberate relish — the milk served in a lordly bowl, the hand reaching for the tent peg, the workmen's mallet, the shattered skull. Then the pounding repetition: 'Between her feet he sank, he fell, he lay still; between her feet he sank, he fell; where he sank, there he fell — dead.' The lines hammer like the mallet itself, driving home the totality of the reversal. The mighty Sisera, terror of nations and commander of nine hundred chariots, falls dead at the feet of a tent-dwelling woman. Davis notes that the song does not sanitize the violence; it exults that God's enemy is destroyed and God's people are freed. This is not bloodlust but the joy of justice — the same Spirit-inspired rejoicing that heaven will voice over the fall of Babylon (Rev. 18:20). The deed echoes Genesis 3:15: the serpent's head crushed by the seed of the woman. Jael's blessedness is the blessedness of all who, in their place and with their humble tools, strike a blow for the kingdom of God. (cf. Gen. 3:15; Rev. 18:20)

verseByVerse.quote: "Out of the window she peered, the mother of Sisera wailed through the lattice: 'Why is his chariot so long in coming? Why tarry the hoofbeats of his chariots?' ...'Have they not found and divided the spoil? — A womb or two for every man...'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Now comes one of the most poignant and chilling scenes in all of Scripture. The camera shifts away from the battlefield to a window in Canaan, to the mother of Sisera, who peers through the lattice, waiting: 'Why is his chariot so long in coming? Why tarry the hoofbeats of his chariots?' Her wise ladies, and she herself, invent comforting explanations: surely they are delayed by dividing the plunder — 'a womb or two for every man,' a brutal reference to captive women treated as spoil, and dyed garments for Sisera's neck. The dramatic irony is devastating. We the readers know that the son will never come, that the chariots lie mired in the Kishon, that Sisera is dead between Jael's feet. The mother's hopeful waiting is the waiting of the bereaved who does not yet know her grief. Ferguson observes that Scripture here resists turning the enemy into a mere abstraction; even the oppressor had a mother who loved him and watched for him. Yet the casual cruelty of her imagined comforts — captive women as plunder — reminds us of the brutality of the regime that fell. The window of Sisera's mother is the price of oppression, the bitter harvest of a house built on the exploitation of God's people. Sin always ends with someone watching at a window for a son who does not return. (cf. Gal. 6:7; Prov. 1:31)

verseByVerse.ref: v. 31 — So May All Your Enemies Perish
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The song closes with a prayer for the perishing of all God's enemies and the rising glory of his friends, like the sun in its might — followed by forty years of rest.
verseByVerse.theology: The prayer aligns the heart with God's purposes, longing for the final triumph of justice. God's friends are destined to rise like the sun in ever-increasing glory.
verseByVerse.examples: To pray 'may your enemies perish' is to long for the end of all evil. The destiny of God's people is not to fade but to rise like the dawn.

verseByVerse.quote: "So may all your enemies perish, O LORD! But your friends be like the sun as he rises in his might." And the land had rest for forty years.
verseByVerse.commentary: The song closes with a prayer that gathers up its whole meaning and reaches beyond the day of victory to the end of all things: 'So may all your enemies perish, O LORD! But your friends be like the sun as he rises in his might.' This is not petty vindictiveness; it is the longing of the redeemed for the final triumph of God over all evil. Davis notes that the prayer aligns the singer's heart with God's heart — desiring what God desires, the perishing of his enemies and the flourishing of his friends. To pray it is to pray, in the end, the prayer of Revelation: that the kingdoms of this world become the kingdom of our Lord, that every rebel power be thrown down. And the other half shines with promise: God's friends will 'be like the sun as he rises in his might' — no fading, no twilight, but ever-increasing glory. Jesus echoes the very image: 'the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father' (Matt. 13:43). Then the prose returns with the sobering refrain: 'the land had rest for forty years.' A generation of peace, bought by God's victory and celebrated in song — but forty years, and then the wheel will turn. The song that ends in the rising sun is followed by a rest that will set, pointing past Deborah to the song of Moses and the Lamb, the everlasting anthem of those whose Deliverer does not die. (cf. Rev. 15:3; Matt. 13:43)

5.theology:
The Cosmic Warrior. 'From heaven the stars fought... the torrent Kishon swept them away' (vv. 20–21). The song reveals that the battle was won by God himself, who marshaled the storm, the flood, and the stars against his enemies. Salvation belongs to the LORD, the Warrior of Sinai who fights for his people.

Worship as the Response to Deliverance. God's people are not merely rescued but called to sing. The song models doxology after deliverance — recounting God's righteous triumphs, blessing his name, and aligning the heart with his purposes. Grace received must become praise expressed and testimony shared with the next generation.

No Neutrality in God's War. The blessing of Zebulun and Jael against the curse of Meroz and the rebuke of Reuben teaches that there is no safe middle ground. To refuse 'the help of the LORD against the mighty' is not caution but treason. Whoever is not with him is against him.
5.examples:
Then: Israel celebrated a victory won from heaven, praising the tribes that risked their lives, cursing Meroz that stayed home and blessing Jael who struck the blow, and ending with a prayer for the perishing of God's enemies and the rising glory of his friends.

Now: When God delivers you, do not merely move on — sing, testify, recount his righteous triumphs. When the trumpet sounds for the work of the kingdom, do not be Reuben lost in 'great searchings of heart'; be Zebulun who risks his life on the heights. And remember that the battle is the Lord's: he still fights from heaven for those who shine, in him, like the sun rising in its might.

6.title: The Call of Gideon
6.text: <sup>1</sup>The people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD gave them into the hand of Midian seven years.<sup>2</sup>And the hand of Midian overpowered Israel, and because of Midian the people of Israel made for themselves the dens that are in the mountains and the caves and the strongholds.<sup>3</sup>For whenever the Israelites planted crops, the Midianites and the Amalekites and the people of the East would come up against them.<sup>4</sup>They would encamp against them and devour the produce of the land, as far as Gaza, and leave no sustenance in Israel and no sheep or ox or donkey.<sup>5</sup>For they would come up with their livestock and their tents; they would come like locusts in number—both they and their camels could not be counted—so that they laid waste the land as they came in.<sup>6</sup>And Israel was brought very low because of Midian. And the people of Israel cried out for help to the LORD.<sup>7</sup>When the people of Israel cried out to the LORD on account of the Midianites,<sup>8</sup>the LORD sent a prophet to the people of Israel. And he said to them, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: I led you up from Egypt and brought you out of the house of slavery.<sup>9</sup>And I delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of all who oppressed you, and drove them out before you and gave you their land.<sup>10</sup>And I said to you, 'I am the LORD your God; you shall not fear the gods of the Amorites in whose land you dwell.' But you have not obeyed my voice."<sup>11</sup>Now the angel of the LORD came and sat under the terebinth at Ophrah, which belonged to Joash the Abiezrite, while his son Gideon was beating out wheat in the winepress to hide it from the Midianites.<sup>12</sup>And the angel of the LORD appeared to him and said to him, "The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor."<sup>13</sup>And Gideon said to him, "Please, my lord, if the LORD is with us, why then has all this happened to us? And where are all his wonderful deeds that our fathers recounted to us, saying, 'Did not the LORD bring us up from Egypt?' But now the LORD has forsaken us and given us into the hand of Midian."<sup>14</sup>And the LORD turned to him and said, "Go in this might of yours and save Israel from the hand of Midian; do not I send you?"<sup>15</sup>And he said to him, "Please, Lord, how can I save Israel? Behold, my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house."<sup>16</sup>And the LORD said to him, "But I will be with you, and you shall strike the Midianites as one man."<sup>17</sup>And he said to him, "If now I have found favor in your eyes, then show me a sign that it is you who speak with me.<sup>18</sup>Please do not depart from here until I come to you and bring out my present and set it before you." And he said, "I will stay till you return."<sup>19</sup>So Gideon went into his house and prepared a young goat and unleavened cakes from an ephah of flour. The meat he put in a basket, and the broth he put in a pot, and brought them to him under the terebinth and presented them.<sup>20</sup>And the angel of God said to him, "Take the meat and the unleavened cakes, and put them on this rock, and pour the broth over them." And he did so.<sup>21</sup>Then the angel of the LORD reached out the tip of the staff that was in his hand and touched the meat and the unleavened cakes. And fire sprang up from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened cakes. And the angel of the LORD vanished from his sight.<sup>22</sup>Then Gideon perceived that he was the angel of the LORD. And Gideon said, "Alas, O Lord GOD! For now I have seen the angel of the LORD face to face."<sup>23</sup>But the LORD said to him, "Peace be to you. Do not fear; you shall not die."<sup>24</sup>Then Gideon built an altar there to the LORD and called it, The LORD Is Peace. To this day it still stands at Ophrah, which belongs to the Abiezrites.<sup>25</sup>That night the LORD said to him, "Take your father's bull, and the second bull seven years old, and pull down the altar of Baal that your father has, and cut down the Asherah that is beside it<sup>26</sup>and build an altar to the LORD your God on the top of the stronghold here, with stones laid in due order. Then take the second bull and offer it as a burnt offering with the wood of the Asherah that you shall cut down."<sup>27</sup>So Gideon took ten men of his servants and did as the LORD had told him. But because he was too afraid of his family and the men of the town to do it by day, he did it by night.<sup>28</sup>When the men of the town rose early in the morning, behold, the altar of Baal was broken down, and the Asherah beside it was cut down, and the second bull was offered on the altar that had been built.<sup>29</sup>And they said to one another, "Who has done this thing?" And after they had searched and inquired, they said, "Gideon the son of Joash has done this thing."<sup>30</sup>Then the men of the town said to Joash, "Bring out your son, that he may die, for he has broken down the altar of Baal and cut down the Asherah beside it."<sup>31</sup>But Joash said to all who stood against him, "Will you contend for Baal? Or will you save him? Whoever contends for him shall be put to death by morning. If he is a god, let him contend for himself, because his altar has been broken down."<sup>32</sup>Therefore on that day Gideon was called Jerubbaal, that is to say, "Let Baal contend against him," because he broke down his altar.<sup>33</sup>Now all the Midianites and the Amalekites and the people of the East came together, and they crossed the Jordan and encamped in the Valley of Jezreel.<sup>34</sup>But the Spirit of the LORD clothed Gideon, and he sounded the trumpet, and the Abiezrites were called out to follow him.<sup>35</sup>And he sent messengers throughout all Manasseh, and they too were called out to follow him. And he sent messengers to Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, and they went up to meet them.<sup>36</sup>Then Gideon said to God, "If you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said,<sup>37</sup>behold, I am laying a fleece of wool on the threshing floor. If there is dew on the fleece alone, and it is dry on all the ground, then I shall know that you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said."<sup>38</sup>And it was so. When he rose early next morning and squeezed the fleece, he wrung enough dew from the fleece to fill a bowl with water.<sup>39</sup>Then Gideon said to God, "Let not your anger burn against me; let me speak just once more. Please let me test just once more with the fleece. Please let it be dry on the fleece only, and on all the ground let there be dew."<sup>40</sup>And God did so that night; and it was dry on the fleece only, and on all the ground there was dew.
6.overview:
With Gideon the cycle reaches its most fully developed and most psychologically searching telling. Israel again does evil, and God hands them to Midian — a devastation so total that the people hide in caves and dens while the Midianite raiders, 'like locusts in abundance,' strip the land bare year after year. Into this misery Israel cries out, and God's first response is not a deliverer but a prophet, who reminds them that their suffering is the fruit of their own disobedience.

Then the angel of the LORD comes to a man threshing wheat in a winepress — hiding his harvest from the Midianites — and greets him with words that must have sounded absurd: 'The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor.' Gideon is no mighty man; he is a frightened farmer from the weakest clan in Manasseh, the least in his father's house. The chapter is the story of how God transforms a fearful, doubting man into a deliverer — not by rebuking his weakness but by patiently meeting him in it.

God commissions Gideon, who immediately raises objections; God answers with a promise and a sign. Gideon builds an altar, 'The LORD Is Peace.' That very night God commands him to tear down his father's altar to Baal — and Gideon does it, but by night, 'because he was too afraid.' Even his obedience trembles. When the Spirit clothes him and he summons the tribes, he still cannot move without further reassurance, laying out the famous fleece — once wet, once dry — testing the patience of God twice over.

The glory of chapter 6 is the patience of God with a doubting servant. He does not thunder at Gideon's fear or cast him off for his repeated demands for signs; he stoops, reassures, and condescends to weak faith again and again. Here is the gospel character of God, who does not break the bruised reed or quench the smoldering wick (Isa. 42:3), who calls things that are not as though they were, naming a coward 'mighty man of valor' before he is anything of the kind — and then making him so. Gideon is every weak believer; his God is our God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Midian's Oppression and the Prophet's Rebuke
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel does evil; God gives them to Midian, whose raids devastate the land and drive Israel into caves. When they cry out, God first sends a prophet to remind them their suffering springs from their own disobedience.
verseByVerse.theology: God's first answer to Israel's cry is the word — a prophet who diagnoses the sin behind the suffering. Deliverance must begin with repentance, not mere relief.
verseByVerse.examples: Before God sends rescue, he often sends conviction. The cry of distress must become the cry of repentance.

verseByVerse.quote: The people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD gave them into the hand of Midian seven years... whenever the Israelites planted crops, the Midianites and the Amalekites... would come up against them... like locusts in abundance... So Israel was brought very low because of Midian. And the people of Israel cried out for help to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary: The cycle turns again, and the oppression is the most economically devastating yet. The Midianites, with the Amalekites and 'the people of the East,' descend each harvest 'like locusts in abundance,' their camels 'without number,' devouring the produce of the land and leaving 'no sustenance in Israel.' This is not a single conquering army but an annual plague of raiders who let Israel plant and then stripped them at harvest, a calculated cruelty that drove the people into 'dens... caves and strongholds' in the mountains. 'Israel was brought very low.'
