Davis notes the deliberate humiliation: the covenant people, heirs of a land flowing with milk and honey, are reduced to cowering in caves while pagan nomads eat their bread. Sin always impoverishes; it promises plenty and delivers locusts. The land God gave for blessing becomes, under disobedience, a place of want and fear. And so 'the people of Israel cried out for help to the LORD.' The cry is the third stage of the cycle, and it is, for all its desperation, a mercy — affliction has driven them back to the God they forsook. The locusts of Midian are doing the work the thorns and snares of chapter 2 were meant to do, emptying the far country until the prodigal turns homeward. (cf. Deut. 28:38–42; Luke 15:14–17)

verseByVerse.quote: When the people of Israel cried out to the LORD on account of the Midianites, the LORD sent a prophet to the people of Israel. And he said to them, "...I delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians... And I said to you, 'I am the LORD your God; you shall not fear the gods of the Amorites...' But you have not obeyed my voice."
verseByVerse.commentary: Israel cries out, and we expect God to raise up a deliverer at once, as he did for Othniel and Ehud. Instead, surprisingly, 'the LORD sent a prophet.' Before rescue, God sends a sermon. The unnamed prophet rehearses the gospel of the Exodus — 'I delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians' — recites the first commandment — 'you shall not fear the gods of the Amorites' — and lays the charge: 'But you have not obeyed my voice.' Davis observes the spiritual wisdom of this delay. Israel's cry, so far, is the cry of the afflicted who want their pain to stop, not yet the cry of the penitent who hate their sin. God will not deliver them while they remain blind to the root of their misery. So before the deliverer comes the diagnostician; before the cure, the conviction. The prophet does not announce salvation; he announces sin. This is God's gracious order: he wounds before he heals, convicts before he comforts, sends the law before the gospel. The cry of distress must be deepened into the cry of repentance. How often we want God to remove the consequences while leaving the sin untouched, to lift the locusts without dealing with the idolatry that summoned them. God loves us too well for that. He sends the prophet first. (cf. Ps. 81:8–13; Hos. 5:15)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–24 — The Angel of the LORD Calls Gideon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The angel of the LORD finds Gideon threshing wheat in a winepress and calls him 'mighty man of valor.' Gideon objects from weakness and doubt; God commissions him with a promise and confirms it with fire from the rock. Gideon builds the altar 'The LORD Is Peace.'
verseByVerse.theology: God calls things that are not as though they were, naming a coward 'mighty man of valor.' The presence of the LORD, not the strength of the man, is the ground of every commission.
verseByVerse.examples: God meets us in our hiding places and calls us by who we will become in him, not by what we are in ourselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the angel of the LORD came and sat under the terebinth at Ophrah... while his son Gideon was beating out wheat in the winepress to hide it from the Midianites. And the angel of the LORD appeared to him and said to him, "The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor."
verseByVerse.commentary: The scene is almost comic in its irony. The angel of the LORD finds Gideon 'beating out wheat in the winepress to hide it from the Midianites.' A winepress was a sunken pit for treading grapes, no place to thresh wheat, which needed an open, windy threshing floor to winnow the chaff. Gideon is crouched in a hole, doing the wrong job in the wrong place, furtively, terrified that the raiders will spot him and steal his grain. And to this frightened, hiding man the angel says, 'The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor.' The greeting is, on its face, absurd. Gideon is the picture of fear, not valor. But this is precisely how God speaks. He calls things that are not as though they were (Rom. 4:17); he names the coward by the warrior he will become. Davis loves the gap between the man Gideon is and the man God addresses — God does not see Gideon as he is in the winepress but as he will be by grace. And note the foundation of the whole greeting: 'The LORD is with you.' Not 'you are strong,' but 'the LORD is with you.' That is the secret of every deliverer in the book and the only ground of any valor. The God who finds us in our winepresses calls us by our calling, not our cowardice. (cf. Rom. 4:17; 1 Cor. 1:27–28)

verseByVerse.quote: And Gideon said to him, "Please, my lord, if the LORD is with us, why then has all this happened to us? ...the LORD has forsaken us..." And the LORD turned to him and said, "Go in this might of yours and save Israel from the hand of Midian; do not I send you?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Gideon's reply is the cry of every disillusioned believer: 'If the LORD is with us, why then has all this happened to us?... the LORD has forsaken us.' He has the Exodus stories — 'where are all his wonderful deeds that our fathers recounted?' — but they feel like ancient history, irrelevant to the misery of the winepress. His theology is half right and half despairing: he believes God once acted but assumes God has now abandoned them. Davis notes that Gideon mistakes the discipline for desertion; he reads the consequences of Israel's sin as evidence that God has quit. Then comes the stunning commission: 'Go in this might of yours and save Israel from the hand of Midian; do not I send you?' What might? Gideon has shown none. But God has just named it — the might is not Gideon's prowess but Gideon's sending. 'Do not I send you?' The strength lies entirely in the Sender. This is the pattern of every call of God: he does not wait for us to be strong; he sends us, and the sending is the strength. Moses pled inadequacy, Jeremiah his youth, Gideon his fear — and to each God said, in effect, 'I send you, and I will be with you.' The 'might' of the Christian is the commission of Christ: 'Go... and behold, I am with you always' (Matt. 28:19–20). (cf. Exod. 3:11–12; Matt. 28:18–20)

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "Please, Lord, how can I save Israel? Behold, my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house." And the LORD said to him, "But I will be with you, and you shall strike the Midianites as one man."
verseByVerse.commentary: Gideon objects again, and his objection is a careful inventory of his insignificance: 'my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house.' He is the least member of the weakest clan of a middling tribe — the bottom of the bottom. By every human reckoning, he is the wrong man. But this is exactly why God chose him. Davis observes that Gideon's protest is not false modesty but an accurate self-assessment that misses the point entirely. The question 'how can I save Israel?' assumes the saving depends on Gideon's resources. God's answer sweeps the whole objection aside with five words: 'But I will be with you.' The 'I' is everything. It does not matter that Gideon is the least of the weakest, because the salvation does not rest on Gideon. The same promise carried Moses, Joshua, Jeremiah — 'I will be with you' — and the same promise carries every servant God sends. Indeed, God positively delights in the weakest instrument, 'so that no human being might boast in his presence' (1 Cor. 1:29). Gideon's smallness is not an obstacle to overcome but a qualification to embrace. 'You shall strike the Midianites as one man' — the whole host defeated as easily as a single foe, because the battle belongs to the God who is with him. Our inadequacy, honestly confessed, is the very soil in which God's sufficiency is displayed. (cf. 1 Cor. 1:29; 2 Cor. 12:9)

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "If now I have found favor in your eyes, then show me a sign that it is you who speak with me." ...Then the angel of the LORD reached out the tip of the staff... and touched the meat and the unleavened cakes. And fire sprang up from the rock and consumed the meat... and the angel of the LORD vanished from his sight.
verseByVerse.commentary: Still uncertain, Gideon asks for a sign and brings an offering — a young goat and unleavened cakes — set on a rock at the angel's direction. The angel touches it with the tip of his staff, 'and fire sprang up from the rock and consumed' the offering, and the angel vanished. The sign is unmistakably divine: fire from the rock, the same fire of God that fell on Israel's altars and would fall on Elijah's sacrifice at Carmel. Note God's patience here, the great theme of the chapter. Gideon has already received a personal commission from the angel of the LORD and a direct promise of his presence, and still he asks for a sign. A lesser master might have rebuked the demand as unbelief. But God condescends, grants the sign, sends the fire. Davis stresses that this divine patience is not weakness but grace: God meets weak faith where it is and strengthens it rather than crushing it. The fire that consumes the offering also accepts it — Gideon's gift is received, and with it Gideon himself. There is gospel here. The fire that should have fallen on the sinner falls instead on the substitute offering, the consumed goat. So at the cross the fire of God's judgment fell on the true Sacrifice, that the trembling, doubting sinner might be accepted, not consumed. The God who answered Gideon's doubt with fire from the rock still meets our weak faith with patient grace. (cf. Lev. 9:24; 1 Kings 18:38)

verseByVerse.quote: Then Gideon perceived that he was the angel of the LORD. And Gideon said, "Alas, O Lord GOD! For now I have seen the angel of the LORD face to face." But the LORD said to him, "Peace be to you. Do not fear; you shall not die." Then Gideon built an altar there to the LORD and called it, The LORD Is Peace.
verseByVerse.commentary: The fire and the vanishing reveal who the visitor was, and Gideon is terrified: 'Alas, O Lord GOD! For now I have seen the angel of the LORD face to face.' He fears death, for the conviction ran deep in Israel that to see God was to die (Exod. 33:20). His terror is the right instinct of a sinner before the holy God. But the LORD answers with words that are pure gospel: 'Peace be to you. Do not fear; you shall not die.' The God whose holiness should have consumed the sinner speaks peace instead. Gideon responds by building an altar and naming it 'The LORD Is Peace' (Yahweh Shalom). Ferguson draws out the wonder: the sinner who deserved death receives peace, and so the place of dread becomes a place of worship. This is the heart of the gospel — that the holy God, who could justly destroy us, instead says 'Peace,' because the death we feared has been borne by another. Gideon did not die; the goat on the rock was consumed in his place. And the name endures as a banner over the believer's life: the LORD is our peace. Paul will say that Christ 'himself is our peace,' who made peace by the blood of his cross (Eph. 2:14; Col. 1:20). Every trembling sinner who has seen the holy God and feared death hears the same word at Calvary: 'Peace be to you. Do not fear.' (cf. Eph. 2:14; Col. 1:20)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–32 — Tearing Down the Altar of Baal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: That night God commands Gideon to tear down his father's altar to Baal and the Asherah beside it and build an altar to the LORD. Gideon obeys, but by night out of fear. When the town demands his death, his father Joash defends him: 'Let Baal contend for himself.'
verseByVerse.theology: Reformation begins at home, at the family altar. A god who needs men to defend him is no god at all. True deliverance starts with the destruction of idolatry.
verseByVerse.examples: Obedience may tremble and still be obedience. Yet God calls us to tear down the idols nearest us before we fight the enemies far away.

verseByVerse.quote: That night the LORD said to him, "Take your father's bull... and pull down the altar of Baal that your father has, and cut down the Asherah that is beside it..." So Gideon took ten men of his servants and did as the LORD had told him. But because he was too afraid of his family and the men of the town to do it by day, he did it by night.
verseByVerse.commentary: Before Gideon can fight Midian, God deals with the idolatry in his own backyard — literally. 'Pull down the altar of Baal that your father has.' The shocking detail is that the altar of Baal stood in Gideon's own family compound; his father Joash maintained it. Reformation must begin at home before it can spread to the nation. Israel cannot be delivered from Midian while it bows to Baal; the war against the external enemy waits upon the war against the internal idol. Gideon obeys — but the narrator is unflinchingly honest about how: 'because he was too afraid of his family and the men of the town to do it by day, he did it by night.' His obedience is real but trembling, done under cover of darkness. Davis notes the tender realism here: God accepts the obedience of a frightened man. Gideon is no fearless reformer striding out at noon; he is a scared man who nonetheless does the right thing, even if by moonlight. There is great comfort in this. God does not wait for our courage to be perfect before he uses our obedience. The obedience that trembles is still obedience; the step taken in fear still counts as faith. What matters is that Gideon did it. He tore down the family idol, fear and all. The Lord works with us as we are, growing our courage as we go, accepting the obedience of the night while leading us toward the boldness of the day. (cf. Deut. 7:5; Phil. 1:6)

verseByVerse.quote: When the men of the town rose early in the morning, behold, the altar of Baal was broken down... Then the men of the town said to Joash, "Bring out your son, that he may die..." But Joash said... "If he is a god, let him contend for himself, because his altar has been broken down." Therefore on that day Gideon was called Jerubbaal.
verseByVerse.commentary: Morning reveals the wreckage, and the town erupts, demanding Gideon's death for the sacrilege. The irony is bitter: these Israelites are ready to kill a man for destroying the altar of a Canaanite god — they will defend Baal to the death while their own God is forgotten. But Gideon's father Joash, the very owner of the demolished altar, rises to a startling defense: 'Will you contend for Baal?... If he is a god, let him contend for himself.' The logic is devastating and self-evident. A god who cannot defend his own altar, who needs a mob of men to avenge him, is no god at all. The true and living God needs no human protection; it is the idol, mute and impotent, that requires its worshipers to fight its battles. So Gideon earns the name Jerubbaal — 'Let Baal contend' — a standing taunt against the helpless idol every time his name is spoken. Davis relishes the theological point that runs from here to Isaiah's mockery of the idol-makers (Isa. 44): the gods of the nations are nothing, and the proof is that they cannot save themselves. The living God, by contrast, contends for his people; we do not contend for him. Every idol we are tempted to defend — our reputation, our comforts, our self-made securities — should hear Joash's challenge: if it is a god, let it save itself. It cannot. Only the LORD saves. (cf. Isa. 44:9–20; Ps. 115:4–8)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 33–40 — The Spirit and the Fleece
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Midianite host gathers; the Spirit of the LORD clothes Gideon, who sounds the trumpet and rallies the tribes. Yet still uncertain, he tests God twice with the fleece — once wet on dry ground, once dry on wet ground — and God patiently grants both signs.
verseByVerse.theology: The Spirit clothes the deliverer, the source of his power. God's patience with Gideon's repeated testing reveals a God who condescends to weak faith rather than crushing it.
verseByVerse.examples: God is patient with our doubts even as he calls us beyond them. Yet the fleece is a warning as much as a comfort: do not make a habit of demanding signs God has already given.

verseByVerse.quote: Now all the Midianites and the Amalekites and the people of the East came together... But the Spirit of the LORD clothed Gideon, and he sounded the trumpet, and the Abiezrites were called out to follow him. And he sent messengers throughout all Manasseh... Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, and they went up to meet them.
verseByVerse.commentary: The crisis comes: the vast confederation of Midian, Amalek, and the people of the East crosses the Jordan and encamps in the Valley of Jezreel. And here is the decisive turn: 'the Spirit of the LORD clothed Gideon.' The Hebrew is vivid — the Spirit 'clothed himself with' Gideon, or wrapped Gideon like a garment. The fearful farmer of the winepress is now invested with the power of God himself. This is the secret of every judge — Othniel, the Spirit was upon him; now Gideon, the Spirit clothes him. Ferguson notes that the same Spirit who empowered the judges for deliverance anticipates the fuller anointing of Pentecost, when the Spirit would clothe the church with power from on high (Luke 24:49). The man cannot save Israel; the Spirit-clothed man can. And immediately the empowering bears fruit: Gideon sounds the trumpet, and the tribes rally — Manasseh, Asher, Zebulun, Naphtali. The coward becomes a commander; the hider in the winepress now blows the trumpet of war. What changed? Not Gideon's character but the descent of the Spirit. This is the great hope of every weak servant of God: we are not asked to manufacture courage from within but to be clothed with power from above. The Spirit who clothed Gideon is given to all who belong to Christ, equipping the least of saints for the work to which God calls them. (cf. Luke 24:49; Acts 1:8)

verseByVerse.quote: Then Gideon said to God, "If you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said, behold, I am laying a fleece of wool on the threshing floor. If there is dew on the fleece alone, and it is dry on all the ground, then I shall know..." ...And God did so that night.
verseByVerse.commentary: Even Spirit-clothed and trumpet-blowing, Gideon still cannot quite believe. He lays out a fleece: if it is wet with dew while the ground stays dry, he will know God will save by his hand. God does it. Then, incredibly, Gideon asks for the reverse — fleece dry, ground wet — softening his request with 'Let not your anger burn against me.' He knows he is pressing. And God, astonishingly, does that too. Interpreters rightly note that this is not a model to imitate; Gideon already had the angel's word, the fire from the rock, and the clothing of the Spirit. The fleece is a concession to weak faith, not a pattern for guidance. Yet the dominant note Davis hears is the staggering patience of God. The Lord could have rebuked Gideon's repeated testing; instead he condescends, twice, to the timidity of his servant. Here is the God who does not break the bruised reed or quench the smoldering wick (Isa. 42:3), who meets us in our weakness and stoops to our frailty. There is profound comfort in a God so gentle with a faith so small — and a gentle summons, too, to grow beyond the fleece into the faith that trusts the bare word. The Lord who answered Gideon's fleece would answer doubting Thomas's demand to touch the wounds, then say, 'Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.' (cf. Isa. 42:3; John 20:27–29)

6.theology:
God Calls the Weak by What They Will Become. The angel greets a cowering farmer as 'mighty man of valor,' for God calls things that are not as though they were (Rom. 4:17). The ground of the call is never the strength of the man but the promise 'I will be with you.'

The Patience of God with Weak Faith. Sign upon sign — fire from the rock, the Spirit's clothing, the fleece wet and dry — God condescends again and again to Gideon's doubt without crushing it. He does not break the bruised reed (Isa. 42:3). This is the gospel character of God toward trembling sinners.

The LORD Is Peace. The sinner who feared death for seeing God receives the word 'Peace be to you.' The altar 'The LORD Is Peace' anticipates the cross, where the holy God speaks peace to sinners because the judgment fell on the substitute. Christ himself is our peace (Eph. 2:14).
6.examples:
Then: A frightened farmer threshing wheat in a winepress was called by God, met patiently in his doubt sign after sign, clothed with the Spirit, and transformed from the least of the weakest clan into the deliverer of Israel — though even his obedience trembled and tore down the family idol only by night.

Now: God meets you in your hiding place and calls you not by your cowardice but by who you will become in him. Let his patience with Gideon's fleece comfort your weak faith — and his commission summon you beyond it. Tear down the idol nearest you, even if your hand trembles, and go in the might of the One who sends you: 'I will be with you.'

7.title: Gideon's 300
7.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) and all the people who were with him rose early and encamped beside the spring of Harod. And the camp of Midian was north of them, by the hill of Moreh, in the valley.<sup>2</sup>The LORD said to Gideon, "The people with you are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hand, lest Israel boast over me, saying, 'My own hand has saved me.'<sup>3</sup>Now therefore proclaim in the ears of the people, saying, 'Whoever is fearful and trembling, let him return home and hurry away from Mount Gilead.'" Then 22,000 of the people returned, and 10,000 remained.<sup>4</sup>And the LORD said to Gideon, "The people are still too many. Take them down to the water, and I will test them for you there, and anyone of whom I say to you, 'This one shall go with you,' shall go with you, and anyone of whom I say to you, 'This one shall not go with you,' shall not go."<sup>5</sup>So he brought the people down to the water. And the LORD said to Gideon, "Every one who laps the water with his tongue, as a dog laps, you shall set by himself. Likewise, every one who kneels down to drink."<sup>6</sup>And the number of those who lapped, putting their hands to their mouths, was 300 men, but all the rest of the people knelt down to drink water.<sup>7</sup>And the LORD said to Gideon, "With the 300 men who lapped I will save you and give the Midianites into your hand, and let all the others go every man to his home."<sup>8</sup>So the people took provisions in their hands, and their trumpets. And he sent all the rest of Israel every man to his tent, but retained the 300 men. And the camp of Midian was below him in the valley.<sup>9</sup>That same night the LORD said to him, "Arise, go down against the camp, for I have given it into your hand.<sup>10</sup>But if you are afraid to go down, go down to the camp with Purah your servant.<sup>11</sup>And you shall hear what they say, and afterward your hands shall be strengthened to go down against the camp." Then he went down with Purah his servant to the outposts of the armed men who were in the camp.<sup>12</sup>And the Midianites and the Amalekites and all the people of the East lay along the valley like locusts in abundance, and their camels were without number, as the sand that is on the seashore in abundance.<sup>13</sup>When Gideon came, behold, a man was telling a dream to his comrade. And he said, "Behold, I dreamed a dream, and behold, a cake of barley bread tumbled into the camp of Midian and came to the tent and struck it so that it fell and turned it upside down, so that the tent lay flat."<sup>14</sup>And his comrade answered, "This is no other than the sword of Gideon the son of Joash, a man of Israel; God has given into his hand Midian and all the camp."<sup>15</sup>As soon as Gideon heard the telling of the dream and its interpretation, he worshiped. And he returned to the camp of Israel and said, "Arise, for the LORD has given the host of Midian into your hand."<sup>16</sup>And he divided the 300 men into three companies and put trumpets into the hands of all of them and empty jars, with torches inside the jars.<sup>17</sup>And he said to them, "Look at me, and do likewise. When I come to the outskirts of the camp, do as I do.<sup>18</sup>When I blow the trumpet, I and all who are with me, then blow the trumpets also on every side of all the camp and shout, 'For the LORD and for Gideon.'"<sup>19</sup>So Gideon and the hundred men who were with him came to the outskirts of the camp at the beginning of the middle watch, when they had just set the watch. And they blew the trumpets and smashed the jars that were in their hands.<sup>20</sup>Then the three companies blew the trumpets and broke the jars. They held in their left hands the torches, and in their right hands the trumpets to blow. And they cried out, "A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!"<sup>21</sup>Every man stood in his place around the camp, and all the army ran. They cried out and fled.<sup>22</sup>When they blew the 300 trumpets, the LORD set every man's sword against his comrade and against all the army. And the army fled as far as Beth-shittah toward Zererah, as far as the border of Abel-meholah, by Tabbath.<sup>23</sup>And the men of Israel were called out from Naphtali and from Asher and from all Manasseh, and they pursued after Midian.<sup>24</sup>Gideon sent messengers throughout all the hill country of Ephraim, saying, "Come down against the Midianites and capture the waters against them, as far as Beth-barah, and also the Jordan." So all the men of Ephraim were called out, and they captured the waters as far as Beth-barah, and also the Jordan.<sup>25</sup>And they captured the two princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. They killed Oreb at the rock of Oreb, and Zeeb they killed at the winepress of Zeeb. Then they pursued Midian, and they brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon across the Jordan.
7.overview:
Chapter 7 is the great demonstration of the book's central theology of grace: salvation is the LORD's, and he will arrange the battle so that no one can claim otherwise. Gideon musters thirty-two thousand men against the Midianite host. And then God does the unthinkable — he tells Gideon the army is too big. 'The people with you are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hand, lest Israel boast over me, saying, My own hand has saved me.'

So God reduces the army. First, the fearful are sent home — and twenty-two thousand leave, two-thirds of the force melting away. Then God applies a second test at the water: those who lap like dogs are kept, those who kneel to drink are dismissed. The army shrinks from ten thousand to three hundred. Against a host 'like locusts in abundance,' with camels beyond number, God will save Israel with three hundred men. The math is deliberately absurd, the point unmistakable: this can only be God.

God graciously stoops once more to Gideon's lingering fear, sending him by night into the enemy camp to overhear a Midianite recount a dream of a barley loaf tumbling into the camp and flattening a tent — and his comrade interpreting it as Gideon's sword. Encouraged, Gideon worships, then deploys his three hundred with trumpets, empty jars, and torches hidden inside them. At the signal they smash the jars, raise the torches and trumpets, and cry, 'A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!' The Midianites panic in the darkness, turn their swords on each other, and flee.

The torches in clay jars are one of Scripture's most luminous images. The light was hidden in fragile, breakable vessels, and only when the jars were shattered did the light blaze out and the enemy scatter. Paul will seize the very picture: 'we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us' (2 Cor. 4:7). It is when we are broken that the glory shines; it is in our weakness that his strength is made perfect. The three hundred, the smashed jars, the borrowed light — all preach that salvation belongs to the LORD.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — God Reduces the Army to Three Hundred
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God declares Gideon's 32,000 too many, lest Israel boast. He sends home the fearful (22,000 leave), then sifts the rest at the water until only 300 remain — those who lapped from their hands.
verseByVerse.theology: God deliberately weakens his people's resources so that the glory of salvation goes to him alone. 'My own hand has saved me' is the boast God will not permit.
verseByVerse.examples: God often subtracts our strength to make room for his. He saves by the few and the weak so that no flesh may glory in his presence.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Gideon, "The people with you are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hand, lest Israel boast over me, saying, 'My own hand has saved me.' Now therefore proclaim... 'Whoever is fearful and trembling, let him return home.'" Then 22,000 of the people returned, and 10,000 remained.
verseByVerse.commentary: Gideon has mustered thirty-two thousand men, already badly outnumbered by the Midianite host. And then God says the most counterintuitive thing imaginable: 'The people with you are too many.' Too many? Against an enemy 'like locusts in abundance'? But God states his reason with crystal clarity: 'lest Israel boast over me, saying, My own hand has saved me.' Here is the theological heart of the entire book laid bare. God is not merely concerned to defeat Midian; he is concerned that the glory of the victory go to him and not to Israel. A win with thirty-two thousand men could be credited to military strength; God will leave no room for such a boast. So he begins to subtract. The fearful are dismissed first, and twenty-two thousand — over two-thirds — go home. Davis observes the deliberate divine strategy: God weakens his people to display his strength, shrinking their resources until only his power can account for the outcome. This is how God works still. He often strips away our props — our numbers, our cleverness, our securities — precisely so that when deliverance comes we cannot say, 'My own hand has saved me.' The boast God forbids is the boast in self. He saves by the few so that all the praise is his. (cf. 1 Cor. 1:29; Deut. 8:17–18)

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Gideon, "The people are still too many..." ..."Every one who laps the water with his tongue, as a dog laps, you shall set by himself..." And the number of those who lapped... was 300 men... And the LORD said to Gideon, "With the 300 men who lapped I will save you and give the Midianites into your hand."
verseByVerse.commentary: Ten thousand is still too many. God applies a second, stranger sieve at the water: those who lap with their hands to mouth, like a dog, are kept; those who kneel down to drink are sent home. Three hundred lap; the rest are dismissed. Much ink has been spilled over whether the lappers were more alert and battle-ready, but the text gives no such rationale, and that silence is the point. The criterion is essentially arbitrary because God is not selecting the best soldiers; he is simply reducing the number until victory is humanly impossible. From thirty-two thousand to three hundred — less than one percent of the original force — against a host beyond counting. Davis stresses that the absurdity is deliberate and theological: God engineers a situation in which only divine power can explain the result. 'With the 300 men who lapped I will save you.' The 'I will save you' is the whole sentence; the three hundred are almost incidental, mere witnesses to a salvation God works. This is the gospel pattern writ large. God saves not the strong and many but the weak and few, that no flesh may glory. The cross itself is the ultimate reduction — one man, abandoned, dying in apparent defeat — through whom God saved a world, so that salvation could never be claimed as the achievement of human strength but only received as the gift of divine grace. (cf. 1 Cor. 1:27–29; Zech. 4:6)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–15 — The Dream of the Barley Loaf
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God, knowing Gideon's fear, sends him by night into the enemy camp, where he overhears a Midianite recount a dream of a barley loaf flattening a tent, and his comrade interpret it as the sword of Gideon. Gideon worships and returns emboldened.
verseByVerse.theology: God condescends again to Gideon's fear, granting reassurance through the mouths of his enemies. Even the dreams of pagans serve the purposes of God.
verseByVerse.examples: God meets our fear with fresh assurance. The proper response to such grace is worship, then bold obedience.

verseByVerse.quote: That same night the LORD said to him, "Arise, go down against the camp, for I have given it into your hand. But if you are afraid to go down, go down to the camp with Purah your servant..." ...a man was telling a dream to his comrade. And he said, "...a cake of barley bread tumbled into the camp of Midian and... the tent fell flat." And his comrade answered, "This is... the sword of Gideon..."
verseByVerse.commentary: God knows his man. The command comes — 'go down against the camp, for I have given it into your hand' — but it is immediately followed by a tender concession: 'But if you are afraid to go down, go down... with Purah your servant.' God reads Gideon's lingering fear and provides for it without rebuke, even pointing him toward the reassurance he will find. So Gideon creeps to the edge of the vast camp and overhears a Midianite recounting a dream: 'a cake of barley bread tumbled into the camp... and the tent fell flat.' Barley was the bread of the poor; a tumbling barley loaf flattening a tent is an image of the despised and lowly overthrowing the mighty. And his comrade, terrified, interprets it himself: 'This is... the sword of Gideon... God has given into his hand Midian.' The enemy's own dream preaches Gideon's victory. Davis savors the providence: God so governs even the subconscious of a pagan soldier that the enemy camp is already trembling, already interpreting its own doom, before a single jar is broken. The God who would save by three hundred has already conquered the enemy's nerve. Israel's God rules the dreams of his foes; the barley loaf, the lowly instrument, is exactly the means by which he delights to topple the tents of the proud. Gideon has not yet lifted a hand, and the battle is half won in the enemy's own heart. (cf. Prov. 21:1; Job 4:13–14)

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Gideon heard the telling of the dream and its interpretation, he worshiped. And he returned to the camp of Israel and said, "Arise, for the LORD has given the host of Midian into your hand."
verseByVerse.commentary: Gideon's response to the overheard dream is the right response to every fresh assurance of God: 'he worshiped.' Before he fights, before he organizes, before he speaks a word to his men, he bows. The fearful man who needed the fleece twice, who needed to creep into the enemy camp for one more confirmation, now hears God's promise echoed from a Midianite's mouth and falls down in worship. Davis notes the transformation: the doubting Gideon of chapter 6 has become the worshiping, confident Gideon of chapter 7, and the hinge was God's patient, repeated grace. Faith strengthened by God's reassurance overflows into worship. And worship immediately produces bold action: 'Arise, for the LORD has given the host of Midian into your hand.' Note the tense — 'has given,' past, settled, accomplished in heaven though the battle is still future on earth. Gideon now speaks the very language God spoke to him, with conviction. This is the proper order of the Christian life: assurance leads to worship, and worship arms us for obedience. The man who has bowed before God can stand before any enemy. Gideon will lead three hundred against a host beyond number, and he will do it not in nervous bravado but in the settled confidence of one who has worshiped the God who has already given the victory. (cf. Exod. 4:31; Ps. 95:6)

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gideon arms his 300 with trumpets and empty jars hiding torches. At the signal they smash the jars, raise the blazing torches, blow the trumpets, and cry, 'A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!' The Midianites panic, turn their swords on each other, and flee.
verseByVerse.theology: The light was hidden in fragile clay jars and blazed out only when they were broken — the treasure in jars of clay (2 Cor. 4:7). Victory came by trumpet, torch, and shout, not by sword; the LORD himself routed the enemy.
verseByVerse.examples: It is when we are broken that the glory shines. God's surpassing power is displayed precisely in our fragility and weakness.

verseByVerse.quote: And he divided the 300 men into three companies and put trumpets into the hands of all of them and empty jars, with torches inside the jars. And he said to them, "...when I blow the trumpet... then blow the trumpets also on every side of all the camp and shout, 'For the LORD and for Gideon.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Gideon's battle plan is so unmilitary it could only be of God. He divides his three hundred into three companies and arms each man not with a sword in each hand but with a trumpet in one and a clay jar in the other, with a torch burning inside the jar. The jar hides and protects the flame; the trumpet is for noise, not fighting. Both hands are full of instruments of light and sound — neither hand holds a weapon for the attack. Davis points out the deliberate strategy of weakness: God's army will win without striking a blow, by torch and trumpet and shout alone. The torch concealed within the clay jar is the image that will echo through Scripture. The light is real but hidden, carried in a fragile, breakable vessel — useless until the vessel is shattered. Paul saw the whole gospel in it: 'we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us' (2 Cor. 4:7). The believer is the clay jar; the light of Christ is the treasure within; and it is precisely in our breaking — our weakness, our affliction, our shattering — that the glory blazes out for all to see. Gideon's men were told to break the very jars that hid their torches. So God often must break us before the light he has put within us can shine. (cf. 2 Cor. 4:7; Matt. 5:14–16)

verseByVerse.quote: So Gideon and the hundred men who were with him came to the outskirts of the camp at the beginning of the middle watch... And they blew the trumpets and smashed the jars... And they held in their left hands the torches, and in their right hands the trumpets to blow. And they cried out, "A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!"
verseByVerse.commentary: At the start of the middle watch — just after the guard had changed, when the camp was most disoriented — the three hundred strike. In a single coordinated instant they blow the trumpets, smash the jars, and raise the suddenly-blazing torches, crying, 'A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!' Imagine it from inside the Midianite camp: in the dead of night, three hundred trumpets blare from every side, three hundred jars shatter, three hundred torches flare in the darkness, and a war cry rolls in from all directions. Each trumpet normally signaled a company; three hundred trumpets implied an army of overwhelming size encircling them. The battle cry itself is theologically precise — 'A sword for the LORD and for Gideon' — naming the LORD first. Davis notes the irony: they shout 'a sword,' yet their hands hold torches and trumpets, not swords. The only sword that matters is the LORD's. The light that had been hidden in the jars now blazes out the moment the jars are broken — the treasure revealed through the shattered vessel. The deliverance comes not by the strength of the three hundred but by the terror God sends into the enemy through light, sound, and the broken clay. When God's people are broken open in obedience, the light within scatters the darkness. (cf. 2 Cor. 4:7; Eph. 5:8)

verseByVerse.quote: Every man stood in his place around the camp, and all the army ran. They cried out and fled. ...the LORD set every man's sword against his comrade and against all the army. And the army fled...
verseByVerse.commentary: Here is the climax, and it is pure grace: 'Every man stood in his place around the camp' — the three hundred did not charge, did not fight; they simply held their ground with torch and trumpet — 'and all the army ran. They cried out and fled.' The victory is won without an Israelite sword drawn. And the decisive line names the true Warrior: 'the LORD set every man's sword against his comrade.' In the panic and darkness, with trumpets blaring from every direction and torches flaring, the Midianites could not tell friend from foe and turned their swords on one another. God did not merely help Israel defeat Midian; God caused Midian to destroy itself. The enemy's own swords became the instrument of God's judgment. Davis underlines the theology the whole chapter has been building toward: this can only be God. Three hundred men standing still, holding torches, and a host beyond number slaughtering itself in the dark — no one could ever say 'my own hand has saved me.' The salvation belongs entirely to the LORD. This is how God overthrows the kingdom of darkness still: not chiefly by our striving but by his own power, turning the enemy's weapons against himself, as he did supremely at the cross, where the very death the powers inflicted on Christ became the death of death and the disarming of every hostile power (Col. 2:15). (cf. 1 Sam. 14:20; 2 Chron. 20:22–23)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–25 — The Pursuit and the Ephraimites
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel is summoned to pursue the fleeing Midianites; the Ephraimites capture and kill the Midianite princes Oreb and Zeeb, bringing their heads to Gideon across the Jordan.
verseByVerse.theology: After God wins the decisive victory, his people share in the pursuit and the spoil — grace empowers and then includes the saved in the triumph.
verseByVerse.examples: When God grants the breakthrough, his people join the work of consolidating it. The victory God begins, his people are invited to complete.

verseByVerse.quote: And the men of Israel were called out from Naphtali and from Asher and from all Manasseh, and they pursued after Midian. Gideon sent messengers throughout all the hill country of Ephraim... And they captured the two princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb... and they brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon across the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary: The decisive victory belonged to God and the three hundred, but now the wider nation is summoned to share in the pursuit. Men from Naphtali, Asher, and all Manasseh chase the fleeing host, and the Ephraimites are called to seize the Jordan fords, cutting off the enemy's escape. They capture and execute the two Midianite princes, Oreb ('Raven') and Zeeb ('Wolf'), and bring their heads to Gideon. The rout has become a pursuit; the broken enemy is run down and his leaders destroyed. Davis notes the pattern: God wins the breakthrough by his own power and a tiny remnant, and then graciously includes the broader people in finishing the work and sharing the triumph. The salvation is God's, but the saved are not left as mere spectators; they are drawn into the pursuit. There is, however, a faint cloud on the horizon. The mention of Ephraim and the Jordan crossing sets up the quarrel that opens chapter 8, where the proud Ephraimites will pick a fight with Gideon over not being called sooner. Even in victory, the seeds of Israel's chronic tribal pride are sprouting. But for now the note is triumphant: the enemy that stripped the land like locusts is shattered, its princes slain, and the people of God share in the spoils of a deliverance that was, from first to last, the work of the LORD. (cf. Isa. 10:26; Ps. 83:11)

7.theology:
Lest Israel Boast: Salvation Is the LORD's. God reduced the army from 32,000 to 300 for one stated reason — 'lest Israel boast over me, saying, My own hand has saved me' (v. 2). The deliberate impossibility of the odds ensures that all glory goes to God. This is the theological heart of the whole book.

Treasure in Jars of Clay. The light was hidden in fragile jars and blazed out only when they were broken (vv. 16–20). Paul saw the gospel here: 'we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us' (2 Cor. 4:7). God's glory shines through our brokenness.

The LORD Routs the Enemy. 'The LORD set every man's sword against his comrade' (v. 22). The three hundred never drew a sword; God caused the enemy to destroy itself. As at the cross, God overthrows the powers of darkness by his own power, turning their weapons against them (Col. 2:15).
7.examples:
Then: God whittled Gideon's army down to three hundred, armed them with trumpets and torches hidden in clay jars, and routed a countless host without a sword drawn by Israel — the enemy slaughtering itself in the dark — so that no one could say, 'My own hand has saved me.'

Now: When God subtracts your strength — your numbers, your props, your securities — he is making room for his power, that you may never boast in yourself. And do not despise your brokenness: it is when the clay jar is shattered that the light within blazes out. His surpassing power is displayed precisely in your weakness. The battle is the Lord's.

8.title: Gideon's Failure
8.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the men of Ephraim said to him, "What is this that you have done to us, not to call us when you went to fight against Midian?" And they accused him fiercely.<sup>2</sup>And he said to them, "What have I done now in comparison with you? Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the grape harvest of Abiezer?<sup>3</sup>God has given into your hands the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. What have I been able to do in comparison with you?" Then their anger against him subsided when he said this.<sup>4</sup>And Gideon came to the Jordan and crossed over, he and the 300 men who were with him, exhausted yet pursuing.<sup>5</sup>So he said to the men of Succoth, "Please give loaves of bread to the people who follow me, for they are exhausted, and I am pursuing after Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian."<sup>6</sup>And the officials of Succoth said, "Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand, that we should give bread to your army?"<sup>7</sup>So Gideon said, "Well then, when the LORD has given Zebah and Zalmunna into my hand, I will flail your flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and with briers."<sup>8</sup>And from there he went up to Penuel, and spoke to them in the same way, and the men of Penuel answered him as the men of Succoth had answered.<sup>9</sup>And he said to the men of Penuel, "When I come again in peace, I will break down this tower."<sup>10</sup>Now Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor with their army, about 15,000 men, all who were left of all the army of the people of the East, for there had fallen 120,000 men who drew the sword.<sup>11</sup>And Gideon went up by the way of the tent dwellers east of Nobah and Jogbehah and attacked the army, for the army felt secure.<sup>12</sup>And Zebah and Zalmunna fled, and he pursued them and captured the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and he threw all the army into a panic.<sup>13</sup>Then Gideon the son of Joash returned from the battle by the ascent of Heres.<sup>14</sup>And he captured a young man of Succoth and questioned him. And he wrote down for him the officials and elders of Succoth, seventy-seven men.<sup>15</sup>And he came to the men of Succoth and said, "Behold Zebah and Zalmunna, about whom you taunted me, saying, 'Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand, that we should give bread to your men who are exhausted?'"<sup>16</sup>And he took the elders of the city, and he took thorns of the wilderness and briers and with them taught the men of Succoth a lesson.<sup>17</sup>And he broke down the tower of Penuel and killed the men of the city.<sup>18</sup>Then he said to Zebah and Zalmunna, "Where are the men whom you killed at Tabor?" They answered, "As you are, so were they. Every one of them resembled the son of a king."<sup>19</sup>And he said, "They were my brothers, the sons of my mother. As the LORD lives, if you had saved them alive, I would not kill you."<sup>20</sup>So he said to Jether his firstborn, "Rise and kill them!" But the young man did not draw his sword, for he was afraid, because he was still a young man.<sup>21</sup>Then Zebah and Zalmunna said, "Rise yourself and fall upon us, for as the man is, so is his strength." And Gideon arose and killed Zebah and Zalmunna, and he took the crescent ornaments that were on the necks of their camels.<sup>22</sup>Then the men of Israel said to Gideon, "Rule over us, you and your son and your grandson also, for you have saved us from the hand of Midian."<sup>23</sup>Gideon said to them, "I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you; the LORD will rule over you."<sup>24</sup>And Gideon said to them, "Let me make a request of you: every one of you give me the earrings from his spoil." (For they had golden earrings, because they were Ishmaelites.)<sup>25</sup>And they answered, "We will willingly give them." And they spread a cloak, and every man threw in it the earrings of his spoil.<sup>26</sup>And the weight of the golden earrings that he requested was 1,700 shekels of gold, besides the crescent ornaments and the pendants and the purple garments worn by the kings of Midian, and besides the collars that were around the necks of their camels.<sup>27</sup>And Gideon made an ephod of it and put it in his city, in Ophrah. And all Israel whored after it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his family.<sup>28</sup>So Midian was subdued before the people of Israel, and they raised their heads no more. And the land had rest for forty years in the days of Gideon.<sup>29</sup>Jerubbaal the son of Joash went and lived in his own house.<sup>30</sup>Now Gideon had seventy sons, his own offspring, for he had many wives.<sup>31</sup>And his concubine who was in Shechem also bore him a son, and he called his name Abimelech.<sup>32</sup>And Gideon the son of Joash died in a good old age and was buried in the tomb of Joash his father, at Ophrah of the Abiezrites.<sup>33</sup>As soon as Gideon died, the people of Israel turned again and whored after the Baals and made Baal-berith their god.<sup>34</sup>And the people of Israel did not remember the LORD their God, who had delivered them from the hand of all their enemies on every side,<sup>35</sup>and they did not show steadfast love to the family of Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) in return for all the good that he had done to Israel.
8.overview:
Chapter 8 is the tragic underside of Gideon's story, the slow corruption of a deliverer. The man who tore down Baal's altar and routed Midian with three hundred now begins a downward drift that ends in idolatry and family disaster. The chapter opens with the proud Ephraimites quarreling over not being called to the battle sooner; Gideon soothes them with a diplomatic answer. But as he pursues the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna across the Jordan, a harder edge appears.

The towns of Succoth and Penuel refuse Gideon's exhausted men bread, doubting he will win. Gideon's response is vengeful and disproportionate — he threatens them, and on his return he flays the elders of Succoth with thorns and tears down the tower of Penuel, killing its men. The deliverer is becoming a tyrant. He captures and personally executes Zebah and Zalmunna, partly in blood-vengeance for his own brothers they had killed.

Then comes the chapter's great moment of apparent humility. Israel offers Gideon the crown — 'Rule over us, you and your son and your grandson.' Gideon refuses with seemingly perfect theology: 'I will not rule over you... the LORD will rule over you.' But in the very next breath he asks for the golden earrings of the plunder, fashions them into an ephod, and sets it up in his city. 'All Israel whored after it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his family.' The man who destroyed one idol erects another. He refuses the crown but takes the wealth and the worship; he declines to be king in name while behaving like one — naming a son Abimelech, 'my father is king.'

Here is the sobering theology of the chapter: the deliverer himself becomes the snare. Gideon's tragedy is the tragedy of every human savior — even the Spirit-clothed, idol-breaking hero finishes flawed, drawing the worship to himself and leaving a legacy of apostasy. Israel does not need a better Gideon; Israel needs a Deliverer who will not fail in the end, who will not turn the people's gratitude into idolatry, who when offered every kingdom will worship God alone. Gideon's golden ephod cries out for the King who is himself without sin.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Ephraimites angrily confront Gideon for not summoning them earlier to the battle. Gideon defuses them with a soft, flattering answer.
verseByVerse.theology: A soft answer turns away wrath. Yet Ephraim's wounded pride foreshadows the tribal jealousy that will tear Israel apart.
verseByVerse.examples: Gentleness can disarm conflict. But the craving for recognition, even in God's work, is a root of bitter division.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the men of Ephraim said to him, "What is this that you have done to us, not to call us when you went to fight against Midian?" And they accused him fiercely. And he said to them, "What have I done now in comparison with you? Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abiezer?" ...Then their anger against him subsided.
verseByVerse.commentary: Hardly has the victory been won when the Ephraimites pick a quarrel. 'What is this that you have done to us, not to call us...?' They are not angry that Midian oppressed Israel; they are angry that they missed the glory. Wounded tribal pride, not zeal for God, drives their fierce accusation. Gideon responds with remarkable diplomacy, a soft answer that magnifies them and minimizes himself: 'Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim' — your capture of Oreb and Zeeb — 'better than the vintage of Abiezer?' — my whole campaign? He gives them the credit, and their anger subsides. Davis credits the wisdom of the answer; 'a soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger' (Prov. 15:1), and Gideon proves it. Yet there is a darker undertone. Ephraim's touchiness about honor is a symptom of the tribal jealousy that will eventually tear Israel apart — indeed, Jephthah will face the same Ephraimite pride in chapter 12 and answer it not with soft words but with civil war and the slaughter at the fords. The craving for recognition, even in the work of God, is a poison. How often ministry is wounded not by enemies without but by the bruised egos within, by those more concerned to be called than to see God glorified. Gideon's gentleness is admirable; Ephraim's pride is a warning. (cf. Prov. 15:1; Phil. 2:3)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–9 — Succoth and Penuel Refuse Aid
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pursuing the Midianite kings, Gideon's exhausted men ask Succoth and Penuel for bread. Both towns refuse, doubting his victory. Gideon vows vengeance on them.
verseByVerse.theology: The towns' refusal exposes a failure of faith and solidarity within Israel itself. Gideon's vow of vengeance shows his own hardening heart.
verseByVerse.examples: Cynical refusal to help God's work when the outcome looks uncertain is its own kind of unbelief. Yet vengeance is not ours to take.

verseByVerse.quote: And Gideon came to the Jordan and crossed over, he and the 300 men with him, exhausted yet pursuing. So he said to the men of Succoth, "Please give loaves of bread to the people who follow me..." And the officials of Succoth said, "Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand...?" ...he said, "Well then, when the LORD has given Zebah and Zalmunna into my hand, I will flail your flesh with the thorns..."
verseByVerse.commentary: The three hundred are 'exhausted yet pursuing' — a phrase that captures the dogged faith of those who press on past their strength. Gideon asks the Israelite towns of Succoth and Penuel for bread, a reasonable request from kinsmen to weary soldiers fighting their common enemy. But both towns sneer and refuse: 'Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand?' In other words, you have not won yet; why should we risk Midianite reprisal by helping a man who may lose? Their refusal is unbelief and self-interest dressed as prudence. They will not commit until they see the victory secured. Davis notes the cynicism: they hedge their bets, declining to aid God's deliverer until success is guaranteed. There is a rebuke here for the faith that will only help God's work once it looks like a sure thing. But Gideon's reaction is no better. Instead of grieving their unbelief, he swells with vengeful fury, vowing to flail the elders of Succoth with thorns and tear down the tower of Penuel. The diplomat of verse 2 has become the avenger of verse 7. The narrator is charting Gideon's hardening; the meek man who hid in the winepress now threatens his own people with torture. Success, it seems, has begun to corrupt him. Vengeance belongs to the Lord, not to us (Rom. 12:19), but Gideon has begun to take it into his own hands. (cf. Rom. 12:19; 1 Sam. 25:21–22)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — The Capture of the Kings and Vengeance
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gideon defeats the remaining Midianite host and captures Zebah and Zalmunna. Returning, he makes good his threats — punishing the elders of Succoth with thorns and destroying the tower of Penuel, killing its men.
verseByVerse.theology: God grants the full victory, but Gideon's brutal reprisals against Israelite towns reveal a deliverer increasingly driven by personal vengeance rather than zeal for God.
verseByVerse.examples: The line between righteous justice and personal vengeance is easily crossed. Power and success can harden even a once-humble heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor with their army... So Gideon... captured the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and he threw all the army into a panic. ...he took the elders of the city, and he took thorns of the wilderness and briers and with them taught the men of Succoth a lesson. And he broke down the tower of Penuel and killed the men of the city.
verseByVerse.commentary: Gideon completes the military victory, surprising the remnant of the Midianite army at Karkor and capturing the two kings Zebah and Zalmunna. God has given him everything he asked — the kings are in his hand, exactly as he had vowed. But the use he makes of his triumph is troubling. He carries out his threats against his own people: the elders of Succoth are punished with thorns and briers, and the tower of Penuel is torn down and its men killed. Davis observes the sobering trajectory — Gideon now wages war against Israelite towns with the same ferocity he showed against Midian. Whatever the towns deserved for their cynical refusal, the punishment is disproportionate and personal; the men of Penuel are killed, not merely rebuked. The Spirit-clothed deliverer is slipping into the role of the vengeful warlord. There is a hard lesson here about the corrupting power of success. The same man who trembled in a winepress, who needed two fleeces and a midnight reconnaissance to believe God, now strides through the land settling scores with thorns and the sword. Victory has not sanctified him; it has emboldened his flesh. Power tests the heart as adversity never could. Gideon passed the test of weakness magnificently; he is failing the test of strength. The crown he will soon refuse he is already, in spirit, beginning to wear. (cf. Prov. 16:32; Deut. 32:35)

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to Zebah and Zalmunna, "Where are the men whom you killed at Tabor?" They answered, "...they were like you, every one of them resembling the son of a king." And he said, "They were my brothers, the sons of my mother..." ...So Gideon arose and killed Zebah and Zalmunna...
verseByVerse.commentary: The interrogation of the captured kings reveals a personal motive beneath Gideon's pursuit. The men they killed at Tabor were Gideon's own brothers, 'the sons of my mother.' This was blood-vengeance as much as national deliverance; Gideon hunted these kings partly to avenge his family. He commands his young son Jether to execute them — an attempt to confer the honor of the kill on his heir, another hint of the dynastic ambition stirring in him — but the boy is too afraid. So Gideon does it himself. The kings die with a grim dignity, even noting that the slain brothers 'resembled the son of a king' — and the reader catches the irony, for Gideon's family carried itself with royal bearing. Davis notes how the personal and the public have become tangled in Gideon; the LORD's battle and Gideon's vendetta are no longer cleanly distinguishable. The deliverance that began as pure grace — God saving a helpless people through a fearful nobody — has acquired the stains of personal grievance and family pride. This is the perennial danger for every servant of God: that the Lord's work and our own agendas blur together until we can no longer tell whether we fight for his glory or our own. The honor Gideon tried to give his son foreshadows the dynastic disaster of Abimelech in chapter 9. (cf. Num. 35:19; Jer. 17:9)

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel offers Gideon a hereditary monarchy for delivering them. Gideon refuses with seemingly perfect theology: 'The LORD will rule over you.'
verseByVerse.theology: Gideon's words confess the great truth that the LORD alone is Israel's true King. Yet his subsequent actions betray a dynastic ambition his words deny.
verseByVerse.examples: It is possible to confess the right theology with our lips while contradicting it with our lives. The LORD alone is King.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the men of Israel said to Gideon, "Rule over us, you and your son and your grandson also, for you have saved us from the hand of Midian." Gideon said to them, "I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you; the LORD will rule over you."
verseByVerse.commentary: Israel offers Gideon a hereditary throne — 'you and your son and your grandson' — and on its face Gideon's refusal is magnificent theology: 'I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you; the LORD will rule over you.' This is the very heart of Israel's covenant ideal. Yahweh is Israel's true King; for a man to claim the throne is to usurp the kingship of God. Gideon's words echo the right order of things, the theocratic conviction that would make Israel uneasy about monarchy right up to Samuel's day. If Gideon had only meant it, the chapter might have ended in glory. But the tragedy of the next verses is that his deeds will betray his creed. Davis catches the painful gap: Gideon says the King is the LORD, and then proceeds to take royal plunder, set up a royal shrine, accumulate a royal household of wives and concubines, and name a son Abimelech, 'my father is king.' He declines the title while grasping the substance. Here is one of Scripture's most searching warnings: it is entirely possible to confess sound theology with the mouth while denying it with the life. The right words about God's kingship are no proof of submission to it. Gideon's lips crown the LORD; Gideon's life reaches for the crown himself. The orthodoxy of the tongue must be matched by the obedience of the heart, or it becomes a cloak for idolatry. (cf. 1 Sam. 8:7; Matt. 7:21)

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gideon asks for the golden earrings of the plunder, fashions them into an ephod, and sets it up in Ophrah. All Israel 'whored after it,' and it became a snare to Gideon and his family.
verseByVerse.theology: The man who tore down one idol erects another. The deliverer himself becomes the snare — the tragic flaw of every human savior.
verseByVerse.examples: Even good things — even religious objects — become idols when they draw worship to themselves. The savior who becomes the snare cries out for the sinless King.

verseByVerse.quote: And Gideon said to them, "Let me make a request of you: every one of you give me the earrings from his spoil." ...And Gideon made an ephod of it and put it in his city, in Ophrah. And all Israel whored after it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his family.
verseByVerse.commentary: In the very breath after refusing the crown, Gideon makes a request that unravels his confession. He asks for the golden earrings of the plunder — a staggering weight of gold — and fashions them into an 'ephod.' Whatever its exact form, perhaps a richly ornamented priestly garment or cult object, Gideon sets it up in his own city of Ophrah, establishing a rival center of worship apart from the tabernacle. And the result is catastrophic: 'all Israel whored after it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his family.' The verb 'whored' is the language of spiritual adultery used throughout the book for idolatry; the very word once applied to Baal worship now describes Israel's devotion to Gideon's ephod. The unbearable irony, which Davis drives home, is that the man who began by tearing down the altar of Baal ends by erecting a snare of his own — and the man named Jerubbaal, 'let Baal contend,' becomes the source of fresh idolatry. The ephod was probably intended as a memorial to God's victory, even an instrument of worship; but good intentions could not keep it from becoming an idol. This is the deepest tragedy of the chapter and a parable of every human deliverer: the savior himself becomes the snare. Even the gold dedicated to God, even the religious object, even the memorial of grace, will be 'whored after' by the idolatrous heart. Only a Savior who is himself sinless can refuse every crown of self-glory and lead his people to worship God alone. (cf. Exod. 32:2–4; 1 Cor. 10:14)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–35 — Gideon's Death and Israel's Relapse
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The land has rest forty years. Gideon lives like a king with many wives and seventy sons, and names a son by his Shechemite concubine 'Abimelech.' When Gideon dies, Israel immediately whores after Baal again and forgets both the LORD and Gideon's house.
verseByVerse.theology: The cycle repeats: the moment the deliverer dies, Israel relapses. Gideon's royal household and the ominous name Abimelech set the stage for the horror of chapter 9.
verseByVerse.examples: Human deliverance always wears off at the deliverer's death. Ingratitude toward God and his servants is the dark fruit of the unconverted heart.

verseByVerse.quote: So Midian was subdued before the people of Israel... And the land had rest forty years in the days of Gideon. ...Now Gideon had seventy sons, his own offspring... and his concubine who was in Shechem also bore him a son, and he called his name Abimelech. ...As soon as Gideon died, the people of Israel turned again and whored after the Baals...
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter closes with the familiar rhythm of the cycle and a heavy sense of foreboding. Midian is subdued, and the land has rest forty years — a generation of peace, the fruit of God's deliverance. But the narrator's portrait of Gideon's later life is unmistakably royal: he takes 'many wives' and fathers 'seventy sons' — a harem and a dynasty, the marks of an oriental king. He has refused the title but lives the role. Most ominous is the son born to his Shechemite concubine, whom he names Abimelech — 'my father is king.' The name betrays what Gideon's confession denied; whatever his lips said about the LORD ruling, his heart was royal, and his son's very name proclaims it. This name will become the title of chapter 9's nightmare. Then the cycle turns with brutal speed: 'As soon as Gideon died, the people of Israel turned again and whored after the Baals.' The deliverance lasted exactly as long as the deliverer lived. They forgot the LORD their God who had delivered them, and they showed no kindness to Gideon's house. Davis notes the double ingratitude — toward God and toward his servant — that marks the depraved heart. Once more the book's great cry rises: the deliverer dies, and all is undone. Israel needs the King whose death is not the end but the very means of salvation, whose rising secures a rest that no relapse can destroy. (cf. Judg. 2:19; Ps. 106:13)

8.theology:
The Corruption of Success. The fearful man of the winepress, once tested by weakness, fails the test of strength. Victory hardens Gideon into a vengeful avenger and an aspiring king. Power tries the heart as adversity never could; success is the more dangerous trial.

The Deliverer Becomes the Snare. The man who tore down Baal's altar erects the golden ephod, and 'all Israel whored after it' (v. 27). Every human savior finishes flawed, drawing worship to himself. This is the book's argument that Israel needs not a better Gideon but a sinless King.

Orthodox Lips, Idolatrous Life. Gideon confesses 'the LORD will rule over you' (v. 23) and then lives like a king, naming his son 'my father is king.' Sound theology on the tongue can mask rebellion in the heart. Not those who say but those who do the Father's will (Matt. 7:21).
8.examples:
Then: The hero who broke Baal's altar and routed Midian with three hundred ended his days taking vengeance on his own people, refusing the crown with his lips while grasping its substance, and erecting a golden ephod that snared all Israel into idolatry — and the moment he died, Israel relapsed.

Now: Beware the test of success more than the test of hardship; many who stood in weakness fall in strength. Beware the idols we make even of good and religious things, which draw to themselves the worship due to God alone. And beware the orthodox confession that the life contradicts. Look away from every Gideon to the sinless King who, offered all the kingdoms, worshiped God alone.

9.title: Abimelech the Bramble King
9.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Abimelech the son of Jerubbaal went to Shechem to his mother's relatives and said to them and to the whole clan of his mother's family,<sup>2</sup>"Say in the ears of all the leaders of Shechem, 'Which is better for you, that all seventy of the sons of Jerubbaal rule over you, or that one rule over you?' Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh."<sup>3</sup>And his mother's relatives spoke all these words on his behalf in the ears of all the leaders of Shechem, and their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, "He is our brother."<sup>4</sup>And they gave him seventy pieces of silver out of the house of Baal-berith with which Abimelech hired worthless and reckless fellows, who followed him.<sup>5</sup>And he went to his father's house at Ophrah and killed his brothers the sons of Jerubbaal, seventy men, on one stone. But Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left, for he hid himself.<sup>6</sup>And all the leaders of Shechem came together, and all Beth-millo, and they went and made Abimelech king, by the oak of the pillar at Shechem.<sup>7</sup>When it was told to Jotham, he went and stood on top of Mount Gerizim and cried aloud and said to them, "Listen to me, you leaders of Shechem, that God may listen to you.<sup>8</sup>The trees once went out to anoint a king over them, and they said to the olive tree, 'Reign over us.'<sup>9</sup>But the olive tree said to them, 'Shall I leave my abundance, by which gods and men are honored, and go hold sway over the trees?'<sup>10</sup>And the trees said to the fig tree, 'You come and reign over us.'<sup>11</sup>But the fig tree said to them, 'Shall I leave my sweetness and my good fruit and go hold sway over the trees?'<sup>12</sup>And the trees said to the vine, 'You come and reign over us.'<sup>13</sup>But the vine said to them, 'Shall I leave my wine that cheers God and men and go hold sway over the trees?'<sup>14</sup>Then all the trees said to the bramble, 'You come and reign over us.'<sup>15</sup>And the bramble said to the trees, 'If in good faith you are anointing me king over you, then come and take refuge in my shade, but if not, let fire come out of the bramble and devour the cedars of Lebanon.'<sup>16</sup>"Now therefore, if you acted in good faith and integrity when you made Abimelech king, and if you have dealt well with Jerubbaal and his house and have done to him as his deeds deserved—<sup>17</sup>for my father fought for you and risked his life and delivered you from the hand of Midian,<sup>18</sup>and you have risen up against my father's house this day and have killed his sons, seventy men on one stone, and have made Abimelech, the son of his female servant, king over the leaders of Shechem, because he is your relative—<sup>19</sup>if you then have acted in good faith and integrity with Jerubbaal and with his house this day, then rejoice in Abimelech, and let him also rejoice in you.<sup>20</sup>But if not, let fire come out from Abimelech and devour the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo; and let fire come out from the leaders of Shechem and from Beth-millo and devour Abimelech."<sup>21</sup>And Jotham ran away and fled and went to Beer and lived there, because of Abimelech his brother.<sup>22</sup>Abimelech ruled over Israel three years.<sup>23</sup>And God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem, and the leaders of Shechem dealt treacherously with Abimelech,<sup>24</sup>that the violence done to the seventy sons of Jerubbaal might come, and their blood be laid on Abimelech their brother, who killed them, and on the men of Shechem, who strengthened his hands to kill his brothers.<sup>25</sup>And the leaders of Shechem put men in ambush against him on the mountaintops, and they robbed all who passed by them along that way. And it was told to Abimelech.<sup>26</sup>And Gaal the son of Ebed moved into Shechem with his relatives, and the leaders of Shechem put confidence in him.<sup>27</sup>And they went out into the field and gathered the grapes from their vineyards and trod them and held a festival; and they went into the house of their god and ate and drank and reviled Abimelech.<sup>28</sup>And Gaal the son of Ebed said, "Who is Abimelech, and who are we of Shechem, that we should serve him? Is he not the son of Jerubbaal, and is not Zebul his officer? Serve the men of Hamor the father of Shechem; but why should we serve him?<sup>29</sup>Would that this people were under my hand! Then I would remove Abimelech. I would say to Abimelech, 'Increase your army, and come out.'"<sup>30</sup>When Zebul the ruler of the city heard the words of Gaal the son of Ebed, his anger was kindled.<sup>31</sup>And he sent messengers to Abimelech secretly, saying, "Behold, Gaal the son of Ebed and his relatives have come to Shechem, and they are stirring up the city against you.<sup>32</sup>Now therefore, go by night, you and the people who are with you, and set an ambush in the field.<sup>33</sup>Then in the morning, as soon as the sun is up, rise early and rush upon the city. And when he and the people who are with him come out against you, you may do to them as your hand finds to do."<sup>34</sup>So Abimelech and all the men who were with him rose up by night and set an ambush against Shechem in four companies.<sup>35</sup>And Gaal the son of Ebed went out and stood in the entrance of the gate of the city, and Abimelech and the people who were with him rose from the ambush.<sup>36</sup>And when Gaal saw the people, he said to Zebul, "Look, people are coming down from the mountaintops!" And Zebul said to him, "You mistake the shadow of the mountains for men."<sup>37</sup>Gaal spoke again and said, "Look, people are coming down from the center of the land, and one company is coming from the direction of the Diviners' Oak."<sup>38</sup>Then Zebul said to him, "Where is your mouth now, you who said, 'Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him?' Are not these the people whom you despised? Go out now and fight with them."<sup>39</sup>And Gaal went out at the head of the leaders of Shechem and fought with Abimelech.<sup>40</sup>And Abimelech chased him, and he fled before him. And many fell wounded, up to the entrance of the gate.<sup>41</sup>And Abimelech lived at Arumah, and Zebul drove out Gaal and his relatives, so that they could not dwell at Shechem.<sup>42</sup>On the following day, the people went out into the field, and Abimelech was told.<sup>43</sup>He took his people and divided them into three companies and set an ambush in the fields. And he looked and saw the people coming out of the city. So he rose against them and killed them.<sup>44</sup>Abimelech and the company that was with him rushed forward and stood at the entrance of the gate of the city, while the two companies rushed upon all who were in the field and killed them.<sup>45</sup>And Abimelech fought against the city all that day. He captured the city and killed the people who were in it, and he razed the city and sowed it with salt.<sup>46</sup>When all the leaders of the Tower of Shechem heard of it, they entered the stronghold of the house of El-berith.<sup>47</sup>Abimelech was told that all the leaders of the Tower of Shechem were gathered together.<sup>48</sup>And Abimelech went up to Mount Zalmon, he and all the people who were with him. And Abimelech took an axe in his hand and cut down a bundle of brushwood and took it up and laid it on his shoulder. And he said to the men who were with him, "What you have seen me do, hurry and do as I have done."<sup>49</sup>So every one of the people cut down his bundle and following Abimelech put it against the stronghold, and they set the stronghold on fire over them, so that all the people of the Tower of Shechem also died, about 1,000 men and women.<sup>50</sup>Then Abimelech went to Thebez and encamped against Thebez and captured it.<sup>51</sup>But there was a strong tower within the city, and all the men and women and all the leaders of the city fled to it and shut themselves in, and they went up to the roof of the tower.<sup>52</sup>And Abimelech came to the tower and fought against it and drew near to the door of the tower to burn it with fire.<sup>53</sup>And a certain woman threw an upper millstone on Abimelech's head and crushed his skull.<sup>54</sup>Then he called quickly to the young man his armor-bearer and said to him, "Draw your sword and kill me, lest they say of me, 'A woman killed him.'" And his young man thrust him through, and he died.<sup>55</sup>And when the men of Israel saw that Abimelech was dead, everyone departed to his home.<sup>56</sup>Thus God returned the evil of Abimelech, which he committed against his father in killing his seventy brothers.<sup>57</sup>And God also made all the evil of the men of Shechem return on their heads, and upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal.
9.overview:
Chapter 9 is the dark sequel to Gideon's golden ephod, the story of the anti-judge Abimelech. Where every other judge was raised up by God, Abimelech seizes power by murder. He is not sent; he grasps. He is not Spirit-clothed; he is ambition incarnate. If the judges are flawed types of Christ, Abimelech is a type of the antichrist — the self-appointed king who comes in his own name, builds his throne on blood, and brings ruin on all who follow him.
