Abimelech persuades the men of Shechem to back his bid, hires reckless men with idol money, and murders his seventy brothers 'on one stone.' Only the youngest, Jotham, escapes. From Mount Gerizim Jotham shouts down the parable of the trees who sought a king: the fruitful olive, fig, and vine all decline the throne, and only the worthless, fire-prone bramble accepts — and its acceptance carries a threat of fire.

Jotham's curse comes true with terrible precision. God sends 'an evil spirit between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem,' and they turn on each other. Abimelech destroys Shechem, sows it with salt, and burns a thousand people alive in its tower. Then, besieging Thebez, he is felled by a millstone dropped by a woman, and dies begging his armor-bearer to kill him lest it be said a woman slew him.

The narrator's verdict is stark: 'Thus God returned the evil of Abimelech.' Sin reaps what it sows; the fire of the bramble consumes the bramble (Gal. 6:7). The chapter is a thunderous demonstration that God governs even the schemes of wicked men, repaying blood with blood and vindicating the murdered seventy — and a dark backdrop against which the true King, who builds his kingdom not on his brothers' blood but on his own, shines all the brighter.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Abimelech Seizes Power by Murder
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abimelech appeals to his Shechemite kinsmen, hires reckless men with temple silver, and murders his seventy brothers on one stone. Only Jotham escapes. Shechem crowns Abimelech king.
verseByVerse.theology: Abimelech is the anti-judge: not raised by God but self-appointed, building his throne on fratricide and idol money. He is the antithesis of the King who emptied himself for his brothers.
verseByVerse.examples: Ambition that grasps what God has not given builds on blood. The kingdom of self is founded on the destruction of rivals.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Abimelech the son of Jerubbaal went to Shechem to his mother's relatives and said to them... "Which is better for you, that all seventy of the sons of Jerubbaal rule over you, or that one rule over you? Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh." ...their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech...
verseByVerse.commentary: Abimelech opens his campaign with cynical manipulation. He appeals to his mother's kinsmen in Shechem on the basis of blood — 'I am your bone and your flesh' — and invents a threat that does not exist, suggesting the seventy sons of Gideon intend to rule them, when there is no evidence they sought any such thing. He offers himself as the convenient local alternative. Davis notes how Abimelech trades entirely on flesh and clan, never on calling or righteousness; he is the first man in the book to grasp at leadership rather than be raised to it by God. Every true judge was sent — Othniel raised up, Gideon called from the winepress, the Spirit clothing each one. Abimelech sends himself. The contrast is the heart of the chapter. He appeals to tribal self-interest ('better for you'), not to the glory of God or the good of Israel. This is the politics of the flesh, the campaign of ambition, and the Shechemites' hearts 'inclined to follow' him because he spoke to their pride and their pocketbooks. He stands in utter opposition to the King who would not grasp at glory but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:6–7). Abimelech reaches up to seize a throne; Christ reached down to wash feet. (cf. Phil. 2:6–7; John 5:43)

verseByVerse.quote: And they gave him seventy pieces of silver out of the house of Baal-berith with which Abimelech hired worthless and reckless fellows, who followed him. And he went to his father's house at Ophrah and killed his brothers the sons of Jerubbaal, seventy men, on one stone. But Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left, for he hid himself.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Shechemites finance Abimelech with seventy pieces of silver from the temple of Baal-berith — idol money for an idolatrous king — and with it he hires 'worthless and reckless fellows,' the violent hangers-on who attach themselves to any strongman. Then comes the atrocity: he goes to Ophrah and murders his seventy brothers 'on one stone.' The phrase is chilling in its efficiency — a butcher's block, an assembly-line slaughter of his own family to eliminate every rival to the throne. The number seventy echoes back to chapter 1, where the Canaanite tyrant Adoni-bezek had mutilated seventy kings; now an Israelite does far worse, murdering seventy of his own brothers. Davis observes that the line between Canaan and Israel has all but vanished — God's people now produce tyrants worse than the pagans they were sent to drive out. Only Jotham, the youngest, escapes by hiding, and the men of Shechem crown Abimelech king, ironically near the very place where Joshua had renewed the covenant (Josh. 24). The throne is built on fratricide and financed by idolatry. This is the kingdom of self, and its foundation stone is murder — the dark inverse of the King who builds his kingdom on his own blood shed for his brothers. (cf. Gen. 4:8; Heb. 2:11)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — Jotham's Parable of the Trees
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From Mount Gerizim Jotham shouts the fable of the trees seeking a king: the olive, fig, and vine all refuse to abandon their fruitfulness, but the worthless bramble accepts — offering false shade and threatening fire.
verseByVerse.theology: The worthy decline the crown to keep bearing fruit; the worthless grasp it and bring fire, not shade. Human kingship apart from God produces a furnace, not a refuge.
verseByVerse.examples: Those most fit to lead are often least eager for power; those least fit grasp it most greedily. The bramble king gives no shade, only fire.

verseByVerse.quote: ...he cried out, "...The trees once went out to anoint a king over them, and they said to the olive tree, 'Reign over us.' But the olive tree said to them, 'Shall I leave my abundance... and go hold sway over the trees?'" ...the fig tree... the vine... [all refused].
verseByVerse.commentary: The lone survivor climbs Mount Gerizim — the mountain of blessing in Israel's covenant ceremony — and shouts down a fable of devastating wit. The trees once went out to anoint a king. They asked the olive tree, but it refused: 'Shall I leave my abundance, by which gods and men are honored, and go hold sway over the trees?' They asked the fig tree, which would not forsake its sweetness and good fruit; and the vine, which would not abandon its wine 'that cheers God and men.' The worthy trees — the fruitful, useful ones — all decline the throne. Davis draws out the searching truth: those most fit to lead are often least eager for power, precisely because they are busy bearing fruit. The olive, fig, and vine each have a calling they will not abandon for the empty 'swaying over the trees.' There is wisdom here about the right attitude toward power and position. The mature servant of God does not crave the crown; he is content to be fruitful in his appointed place, producing oil and sweetness and wine for the good of others rather than lording it over them. The craving for preeminence is itself a mark of the bramble. The fruitful are too useful to be ambitious. Jesus would say it directly: the one who would be great must be the servant of all (Mark 10:43–44). (cf. Mark 10:43–44; 3 John 9)

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the trees said to the bramble, "You come and reign over us." And the bramble said to the trees, "If in good faith you are anointing me king over you, then come and take refuge in my shade, but if not, let fire come out of the bramble and devour the cedars of Lebanon."
verseByVerse.commentary: At last the trees turn to the bramble — a worthless, fruitless, low-growing thornbush, good for nothing but kindling and a hazard in the dry season. And the bramble eagerly accepts, with a speech full of menace: 'If in good faith you are anointing me king over you, then come and take refuge in my shade, but if not, let fire come out of the bramble and devour the cedars of Lebanon.' The absurdity is the point. A thornbush offering shade is laughable, for it has none to give; one cannot shelter under a bramble. Its only real power is to catch fire and, in burning, set ablaze even the mighty cedars. Davis presses the searing truth: the worthless grasp for power most greedily, and the bramble king gives no shade, only fire. Abimelech is the bramble — fruitless, destructive, offering Israel a kingship that can shelter no one and will end in flames. The threat in the bramble's speech is the prophecy of the whole chapter: fire will come out and devour. This stands in stark, glorious contrast to the true King, the Vine of John 15, who did not cling to glory but came down to give his people shade and fruit and life, laying down his own life for the trees of his planting. Jotham's bramble is the antithesis of Christ, who is himself the refuge that does not burn. (cf. John 15:1; Isa. 32:2)

verseByVerse.quote: "Now therefore, if you acted in good faith and integrity when you made Abimelech king... then rejoice in Abimelech... But if not, let fire come out from Abimelech and devour the leaders of Shechem... and let fire come out from the leaders of Shechem... and devour Abimelech." And Jotham ran away and fled...
verseByVerse.commentary: Jotham makes the parable's application explicit and unsparing. If Shechem has dealt honestly with Gideon's house, let them rejoice in Abimelech. But if they have acted treacherously — and they have, financing the slaughter of Gideon's seventy sons — then he pronounces the double curse: 'let fire come out from Abimelech and devour the leaders of Shechem... and let fire come out from the leaders of Shechem... and devour Abimelech.' The bramble and those who crowned it will consume each other in flames. It is a curse that is really a prophecy, a sentence Jotham announces but God will execute. Davis notes that Jotham appeals to 'good faith and integrity' — the moral order that Abimelech and Shechem have shattered — and entrusts the verdict to God by fleeing rather than fighting. He does not take vengeance into his own hands; he speaks the truth and leaves the outcome to the God who judges. There is wisdom in this. The wronged believer is not called to execute justice personally but to declare what is right and commit the matter to the righteous Judge. Jotham flees to Beer and lives; the curse he pronounced will do its slow, certain work. The God who governs all things will see that fire comes out exactly as Jotham said, for he will not be mocked, and the seventy sons' blood will not go unanswered. (cf. Rom. 12:19; Ps. 7:15–16)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–29 — The Evil Spirit and the Rebellion of Gaal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After three years God sends an evil spirit between Abimelech and Shechem, that the murder of the seventy might be avenged. Gaal son of Ebed arrives and stirs Shechem to rebellion.
verseByVerse.theology: God sovereignly governs even the treachery of wicked men, turning their mutual hatred into the instrument of his justice. The blood of the seventy will be repaid.
verseByVerse.examples: God needs no new weapons to judge the wicked; he simply lets their sin run its course among themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Abimelech ruled over Israel three years. And God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem... that the violence done to the seventy sons of Jerubbaal might come, and their blood be laid on Abimelech their brother, who killed them, and on the men of Shechem, who strengthened his hands to kill his brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary: Abimelech rules three years, and then the curse begins to work. The narrator states it with stark theological clarity: 'God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem.' Here is the sovereignty of God over even the wickedness of wicked men. The 'evil spirit' is best understood as a spirit of discord and ill will that God permits and directs; he does not author their sin, but he governs it, turning the murderers' mutual treachery into the instrument of his judgment. And the purpose is stated plainly: 'that the violence done to the seventy sons of Jerubbaal might come, and their blood be laid on Abimelech... and on the men of Shechem, who strengthened his hands.' Both the tyrant and his accomplices will be repaid. Davis underscores the bedrock truth: God's moral government is inescapable, and he often executes justice not by sending some new calamity but simply by letting sinners reap the sin they have sown among themselves. The murderers turn on each other; the conspirators devour one another. The blood of the innocent seventy cries from the ground, and God answers — not with a thunderbolt, but by setting the wicked against the wicked. He who shed innocent blood will have his own blood required. The God who governs the evil spirit between Abimelech and Shechem governs every scheme of every tyrant still. (cf. 1 Sam. 16:14; Gen. 4:10)

verseByVerse.quote: And Gaal the son of Ebed moved into Shechem with his relatives, and the leaders of Shechem put confidence in him. ...Gaal the son of Ebed said, "Who is Abimelech, and who are we of Shechem, that we should serve him?..."
verseByVerse.commentary: The instrument of discord arrives in the person of Gaal son of Ebed, a newcomer who wins the confidence of Shechem's leaders. At the vintage festival, amid the feasting and drinking in the house of their god, Gaal grows bold and drunkenly contemptuous of Abimelech: 'Who is Abimelech, and who are we of Shechem, that we should serve him?' He boasts that if the people were under his command, he would remove Abimelech. The very Shechemites who crowned Abimelech now itch to be rid of him, their loyalty as cheap and shifting as the silver they paid for murder. Davis notes the bitter logic of treachery: those who will betray for gain will betray again, and the man who gained a throne by violence cannot trust the violent men who gave it to him. There is no honor among the godless; the alliance of the wicked is a rope of sand. Gaal's drunken boast is the spark, but the fire was laid by God's evil spirit of discord, working out the curse. The whole sordid scene — the festival in the pagan temple, the drunken treason, the shifting loyalties — is a portrait of a society that has forgotten God and now feeds on itself. When men cast off the fear of the LORD, they do not become free; they become wolves to one another. Shechem's rebellion against the tyrant it created is the next turn of the wheel of judgment Jotham foretold. (cf. Prov. 26:24–26; Gal. 5:15)

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Warned by his officer Zebul, Abimelech ambushes Gaal and routs him, then captures Shechem, kills its people, sows the city with salt, and burns about a thousand people alive in the tower of Shechem.
verseByVerse.theology: Jotham's prophecy is fulfilled to the letter: fire comes out from Abimelech and devours the leaders of Shechem. Human kingship apart from God produces not refuge but a furnace.
verseByVerse.examples: The fire of ambition, once kindled, does not stay where it is lit; it spreads until it consumes both the kindler and all who warmed themselves at it.

verseByVerse.quote: When Zebul the ruler of the city heard the words of Gaal... his anger was kindled. And he sent messengers to Abimelech secretly... So Abimelech... fought with [Gaal]. And Gaal fled before him... Thus Zebul drove out Gaal and his relatives, so that they could not dwell at Shechem.
verseByVerse.commentary: Zebul, Abimelech's loyal officer within Shechem, secretly warns his master of Gaal's rebellion and counsels an ambush. Abimelech lies in wait, and when Gaal comes out at dawn, Zebul taunts him into battle. Gaal's drunken bravado collapses in the cold light of morning; he is routed and driven from the city, his rebellion crushed before it could rise. The treacherous are outmaneuvered by the more treacherous. Davis observes the grim spectacle of the wicked devouring one another — Zebul betraying Gaal to Abimelech, Abimelech preparing to destroy the very Shechem that made him king. There is no virtue in any party here; this is simply the curse working itself out, the evil spirit of discord doing its appointed labor. The reader feels the gathering momentum of judgment. Gaal, the would-be liberator, proves a drunken windbag who flees at the first clash; Zebul, the schemer, secures a temporary victory for a doomed master; and Abimelech, the bramble king, turns now in fury upon his own people. Every alliance among the godless is provisional, every loyalty for sale, every victory a prelude to the next betrayal. This is the kingdom of self at war with itself, and it can end only in ashes. The God who governs it is patiently bringing the blood of the seventy back upon the heads that shed it. (cf. Prov. 11:5; Ps. 9:15–16)

verseByVerse.quote: ...Abimelech captured the city and killed the people who were in it, and he razed the city and sowed it with salt. ...all the people of the Tower of Shechem... entered the stronghold of the house of El-berith. ...Abimelech... set the stronghold on fire over them, so that all the people of the Tower of Shechem also died, about 1,000 men and women.
verseByVerse.commentary: Abimelech's vengeance on the city that crowned him is total. He captures Shechem, slaughters its people, razes it to the ground, and sows it with salt — an act of permanent, symbolic destruction, declaring the soil forever cursed and barren. The king destroys the very city that made him king. Then the horror climaxes: about a thousand men and women take refuge in the stronghold of the temple of El-berith, the tower of Shechem. Abimelech and his men cut brushwood, pile it against the stronghold, and set it ablaze, and 'all the people of the Tower of Shechem also died, about a thousand men and women.' Jotham's prophecy is fulfilled to the letter: fire came out from Abimelech and devoured the leaders of Shechem. The bramble's fire, threatened in verse 15, has now consumed. Davis refuses to soften the scene, and neither should we: a thousand people burned alive in their false refuge is one of the most harrowing images in the book, a vision of what human kingship apart from God finally produces — not shade, but fire; not refuge, but a furnace. This is the bitter harvest of the golden ephod, the wages of seizing what God did not give, the end of a nation that does what is right in its own eyes. The fire of ambition, once kindled, does not stay where it is lit. Only the kingdom that comes down from heaven, founded on mercy not murder, offers a refuge that does not burn. (cf. Gal. 6:8; Ps. 11:6)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 50–57 — The Millstone of Thebez and God's Retribution
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Besieging Thebez, Abimelech approaches the tower to burn it, but a woman drops a millstone that crushes his skull. He begs his armor-bearer to kill him lest it be said a woman slew him. The narrator declares: thus God returned the evil of Abimelech and the men of Shechem.
verseByVerse.theology: God topples the proud through the weak — a woman's millstone, echoing Jael's tent peg and the seed of the woman crushing the serpent. God returns evil on the head that devised it; a man reaps what he sows.
verseByVerse.examples: Vengeance belongs to God, who repays all innocent blood. For those who shelter in the true King, there is a blood that speaks not vengeance but forgiveness.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Abimelech went to Thebez and... there was a strong tower within the city, and all... fled to it... And Abimelech came to the tower and fought against it... And a certain woman threw an upper millstone on Abimelech's head and crushed his skull. Then he called quickly to the young man his armor-bearer and said... "Draw your sword and kill me, lest they say of me, 'A woman killed him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Drunk on destruction, Abimelech marches against Thebez, but its people flee to a strong tower. As he approaches to burn it as he burned Shechem's, God's justice strikes with poetic precision: 'a certain woman threw an upper millstone on Abimelech's head and crushed his skull.' The mighty bramble king, who slaughtered seventy brothers and burned a thousand people, is felled by an anonymous woman with a household grinding-stone dropped from a tower. The reversal echoes Sisera, brought down by Jael's tent peg, and reaches back to Genesis 3:15 — the seed of the woman crushing the serpent's head. God delights to topple the proud through the weak and despised. Mortally wounded, Abimelech's last concern is not his soul but his reputation: 'kill me, lest they say of me, A woman killed him.' Even dying, vanity rules him; he fears the shame of a woman's blow more than death or judgment itself. So his armor-bearer runs him through. Davis notes the bitter futility — his attempt to hide the shame failed utterly, for the story was told and retold, remembered centuries later (2 Sam. 11:21). The man who built his throne on blood dies as a byword, undone by a woman and a millstone, clutching at his pride to the last breath. Pride goes before destruction; the proud heart is its own executioner. (cf. Gen. 3:15; Prov. 16:18)

verseByVerse.quote: Thus God returned the evil of Abimelech, which he committed against his father in killing his seventy brothers. And God also made all the evil of the men of Shechem return on their heads, and upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal.
verseByVerse.commentary: The narrator delivers the chapter's theological verdict, and he says it twice for emphasis: 'Thus God returned the evil of Abimelech... And God also made all the evil of the men of Shechem return on their heads.' Note the agent of every clause — God returned, God made return. Behind the millstone, the civil war, the evil spirit, the whole bloody unraveling, stands the moral government of God, who will not be mocked and who repays. Jotham's curse was no empty rhetoric but the announcement of a sentence God himself executed. Davis underscores the bedrock truth that anchors the chapter: a man reaps what he sows (Gal. 6:7). Abimelech sowed his brothers' blood and reaped his own; the men of Shechem sowed treachery and reaped fire. The justice is exact, the harvest unavoidable. And in this dark vindication there is, for the believer, profound hope. The God who avenged the murdered seventy is the God who hears all innocent blood crying from the ground (Gen. 4:10), who will set every wrong right in his time, who reserves vengeance to himself so that we need not seize it (Rom. 12:19). The bramble king's fire consumed the bramble. But for those who shelter in the true King, there is a refuge that does not burn and a blood that does not cry for vengeance but speaks a better word — the sprinkled blood of Jesus, which pleads not 'condemn' but 'forgive.' (cf. Gal. 6:7; Heb. 12:24)

9.theology:
The Anti-Judge. Every true judge was raised up by God and clothed with his Spirit; Abimelech seizes power by murder and rules by terror. He is the photographic negative of a deliverer, a type of the antichrist who comes in his own name — the antithesis of the King who emptied himself and gave his life for his brothers.

The Bramble King. Jotham's parable exposes a timeless truth: the worthy decline the crown to keep bearing fruit, while the worthless grasp it and bring fire, not shade. Human kingship apart from God produces not refuge but a furnace, pointing by contrast to the true Vine who gives life to his own.

God Returns the Evil: A Man Reaps What He Sows. 'Thus God returned the evil of Abimelech' (v. 56). The evil spirit, the civil war, the millstone — all are the moral government of God repaying blood with blood. He will not be mocked; vengeance is his (Gal. 6:7; Rom. 12:19).
9.examples:
Then: Abimelech murdered seventy brothers to seize a crown God never gave, ruled by terror, burned a thousand people in Shechem's tower, and died with his skull crushed by a woman's millstone — God returning his evil on his own head exactly as Jotham's curse foretold.

Now: Beware the bramble's ambition — the grasping for power, position, or recognition that God has not given. The fire of selfish ambition never stays where it is lit; it consumes the one who kindles it. Take comfort that God still governs the schemes of the wicked and repays all innocent blood — and flee for refuge to the King whose blood speaks not vengeance but forgiveness.

10.title: Tola, Jair, and Renewed Apostasy
10.text: <sup>1</sup>After Abimelech there arose to save Israel Tola the son of Puah, son of Dodo, a man of Issachar, and he lived at Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim.<sup>2</sup>And he judged Israel twenty-three years. Then he died and was buried at Shamir.<sup>3</sup>After him arose Jair the Gileadite, who judged Israel twenty-two years.<sup>4</sup>And he had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys, and they had thirty cities, called Havvoth-jair to this day, which are in the land of Gilead.<sup>5</sup>And Jair died and was buried in Kamon.<sup>6</sup>The people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals and the Ashtaroth, the gods of Syria, the gods of Sidon, the gods of Moab, the gods of the Ammonites, and the gods of the Philistines. And they forsook the LORD and did not serve him.<sup>7</sup>So the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of the Philistines and into the hand of the Ammonites,<sup>8</sup>and they crushed and oppressed the people of Israel that year. For eighteen years they oppressed all the people of Israel who were beyond the Jordan in the land of the Amorites, which is in Gilead.<sup>9</sup>And the Ammonites crossed the Jordan to fight also against Judah and against Benjamin and against the house of Ephraim, so that Israel was severely distressed.<sup>10</sup>And the people of Israel cried out to the LORD, saying, "We have sinned against you, because we have forsaken our God and have served the Baals."<sup>11</sup>And the LORD said to the people of Israel, "Did I not save you from the Egyptians and from the Amorites, from the Ammonites and from the Philistines?<sup>12</sup>The Sidonians also, and the Amalekites and the Maonites oppressed you, and you cried out to me, and I saved you out of their hand.<sup>13</sup>Yet you have forsaken me and served other gods; therefore I will save you no more.<sup>14</sup>Go and cry out to the gods whom you have chosen; let them save you in the time of your distress."<sup>15</sup>And the people of Israel said to the LORD, "We have sinned; do to us whatever seems good to you. Only please deliver us this day."<sup>16</sup>So they put away the foreign gods from among them and served the LORD, and he became impatient over the misery of Israel.<sup>17</sup>Then the Ammonites were called to arms, and they encamped in Gilead. And the people of Israel came together, and they encamped at Mizpah.<sup>18</sup>And the people, the leaders of Gilead, said one to another, "Who is the man who will begin to fight against the Ammonites? He shall be head over all the inhabitants of Gilead."
10.overview:
Chapter 10 sits as a hinge in the book. It opens with two of the so-called 'minor judges,' Tola and Jair, briefly noted — men who 'judged Israel' but of whom no deliverance is recorded, only years and burial places. Then the chapter pivots into one of the most theologically searching exchanges in all of Judges: a divine dialogue in which God, exasperated by Israel's relentless idolatry, declares he will save them no more — and then, against his own announced verdict, cannot bear their misery.

Israel's apostasy here reaches a new breadth. They serve not just the Baals and Ashtaroth but the gods of Syria, Sidon, Moab, Ammon, and Philistia — a whole pantheon of foreign deities. The narrator says they 'forsook the LORD and did not serve him.' God's anger is kindled, and he sells them into the hands of the Philistines and the Ammonites, who crush and oppress them for eighteen years.

When Israel cries out, God's response is unlike anything earlier in the book. Instead of immediately raising a deliverer, he confronts them: 'Did I not save you from the Egyptians, the Amorites, the Ammonites, the Philistines...? Yet you have forsaken me. Therefore I will save you no more. Go and cry out to the gods whom you have chosen; let them save you.' It is the language of a wounded husband, a holy sarcasm that exposes the folly of idolatry — let the gods you preferred rescue you now.

And here the chapter reaches its astonishing climax. Israel does the one thing that moves the heart of God: they confess their sin, put away their foreign gods, and serve the LORD. And then comes the most tender line — 'he became impatient over the misery of Israel,' or as older versions render it, 'his soul was grieved for the misery of Israel.' The God who said 'I will save you no more' cannot, in the end, abandon his people. Here the gospel blazes: the LORD's love is not finally conditioned on Israel's worthiness but rooted in his own covenant heart. He is grieved by their pain even when it is self-inflicted. This is the God who would one day be so moved by our misery that he gave his only Son — the God whose mercy triumphs over the judgment his justice demands.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Tola and Jair, the Minor Judges
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Tola judges Israel twenty-three years; Jair judges twenty-two years, noted for his thirty sons on thirty donkeys with thirty towns. No deliverance is recorded — only quiet years and burial.
verseByVerse.theology: God provides ordinary, unspectacular leadership as well as dramatic deliverers. Faithfulness in obscurity has its own worth in God's economy.
verseByVerse.examples: Not every servant of God is a Gideon or a Samson. Quiet, faithful stewardship matters, even when no great deeds are recorded.

verseByVerse.quote: After Abimelech there arose to save Israel Tola the son of Puah... and he judged Israel twenty-three years. Then he died... After him arose Jair the Gileadite, who judged Israel twenty-two years. And he had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys, and they had thirty cities...
verseByVerse.commentary: After the nightmare of Abimelech, the narrator offers a moment of quiet with two 'minor' judges. Tola 'arose to save Israel' and judged twenty-three years; Jair the Gileadite judged twenty-two, notable mainly for his thirty sons riding thirty donkeys and holding thirty towns — a mark of prosperity and influence. Of neither man is any battle or deliverance recorded; we are told their years, their families, and their graves. They are easy to skim past, and that is part of their lesson. Davis notes that after the spectacular violence of Abimelech, these understated notices come almost as relief — forty-five combined years of stable, unremarkable leadership, the long stretches of ordinary faithfulness that hold a society together between crises. Not every servant of God is a Gideon routing Midian or a Samson toppling temples. Most of God's work in the world is done by Tolas and Jairs — faithful people whose names appear once, whose deeds fill no dramatic chapter, who simply judged Israel and died. There is dignity in such obscurity. The kingdom advances not only through the famous few but through the faithful many whose quiet stewardship leaves little record but real fruit. God sees the unspectacular servant; the cup of cold water given in his name is not forgotten (Matt. 10:42). Tola 'arose to save Israel,' and that is enough for the LORD to have recorded his name forever. (cf. Matt. 10:42; 1 Cor. 4:2)

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel's idolatry reaches new breadth — serving the gods of seven nations and forsaking the LORD entirely. God sells them to the Philistines and Ammonites, who crush them for eighteen years.
verseByVerse.theology: Apostasy deepens with each turn of the cycle. Israel now serves a whole pantheon of foreign gods, abandoning the LORD altogether — and the oppression intensifies accordingly.
verseByVerse.examples: Idolatry is rarely content with one idol; the heart that leaves God collects substitutes. The further we drift, the heavier the bondage.

verseByVerse.quote: The people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals and the Ashtaroth, the gods of Syria, the gods of Sidon, the gods of Moab, the gods of the Ammonites, and the gods of the Philistines. And they forsook the LORD and did not serve him. So the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel...
verseByVerse.commentary: The cycle turns yet again — 'the people of Israel again did what was evil' — but now the apostasy reaches a staggering new breadth. Where earlier they served 'the Baals,' here they serve the gods of seven nations: Syria, Sidon, Moab, Ammon, Philistia, plus the Baals and Ashtaroth. They have assembled a whole pantheon, a veritable collector's cabinet of idols. And the summary verdict is total: 'they forsook the LORD and did not serve him.' Not partly, not occasionally — they abandoned him entirely. Davis observes the deepening of the spiral; each relapse in the book sinks lower than the last, and here Israel's idolatry becomes comprehensive, embracing every god but the true one. There is a spiritual law exposed here: idolatry is never satisfied with a single idol. The heart that forsakes the living God does not find one substitute and rest; it collects them, serving Sidon's gods on one day and Ammon's the next, ever restless, ever seeking, never filled. Augustine's words apply: the heart is restless until it rests in God, and so the apostate heart multiplies its idols in a hunger nothing false can satisfy. The consequence follows as surely as ever: God's anger is kindled, and the oppression that comes — Philistines and Ammonites crushing Israel for eighteen years — is heavier than before. The further the drift, the deeper the bondage. (cf. Jer. 2:13; Rom. 1:23)

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel cries out and confesses sin, but God responds with a stinging rehearsal of his past deliverances and a refusal: 'I will save you no more. Go and cry out to the gods whom you have chosen; let them save you.'
verseByVerse.theology: God's holy sarcasm exposes the folly of idolatry. The refusal is real but not final — it is meant to break Israel's shallow repentance into genuine turning.
verseByVerse.examples: God will sometimes withhold quick relief to expose the emptiness of our idols. He drives us to despair of false saviors so we will turn wholly to him.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel cried out to the LORD, saying, "We have sinned against you, because we have forsaken our God and have served the Baals." And the LORD said to the people of Israel, "...Yet you have forsaken me and served other gods; therefore I will save you no more. Go and cry out to the gods whom you have chosen; let them save you in the time of your distress."
verseByVerse.commentary: Israel cries out, and this time their cry even includes a confession: 'We have sinned against you, because we have forsaken our God.' But God's response is startling and unlike anything earlier in the book. Instead of immediately raising a deliverer, he rehearses his long record of salvation — from Egyptians, Amorites, Ammonites, Philistines, Sidonians, Amalekites, Maonites — 'and I saved you out of their hand. Yet you have forsaken me.' Then the devastating verdict: 'Therefore I will save you no more. Go and cry out to the gods whom you have chosen; let them save you.' This is holy sarcasm, the wounded irony of a betrayed husband. You preferred Baal and Chemosh and Dagon; very well, let them rescue you now. Davis and Ferguson both stress that this refusal is real but not final; it is the language of a God whose patience has been pressed to exposing the emptiness of Israel's idols. God knows their confession is still shallow — words wrung out by pain, not a heart truly broken. So he will not give the cheap relief that would leave the idolatry intact. He drives them instead to the bitter end of their false saviors: cry to the gods you chose, and watch them do nothing. Sometimes the severest mercy is the withheld rescue, the silence that forces us to discover that our idols cannot save, until we turn from them not merely with our lips but with our whole heart. (cf. Deut. 32:37–38; Jer. 2:28)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–16 — Genuine Repentance and God's Grieved Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel does not argue but submits, confessing sin and actually putting away their foreign gods to serve the LORD. And God 'became impatient over the misery of Israel' — his soul grieved, unable to bear their suffering.
verseByVerse.theology: True repentance is shown not in words alone but in putting away the idols and serving God. And the deepest revelation: God's love is rooted in his own heart, grieved by his people's misery even when self-inflicted.
verseByVerse.examples: Real repentance removes the idols, not merely regrets the consequences. And our God is not indifferent to our pain — his heart is moved even by misery we brought on ourselves.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel said to the LORD, "We have sinned; do to us whatever seems good to you. Only please deliver us this day." So they put away the foreign gods from among them and served the LORD...
verseByVerse.commentary: Now Israel's repentance turns a corner. They do not argue with God's verdict or bargain or excuse themselves. They submit utterly: 'We have sinned; do to us whatever seems good to you.' This is the language of true contrition — casting themselves on God's mercy with no claim, no demand, only 'please deliver us,' and even that as a plea, not a right. But the decisive proof of genuine repentance comes in the next clause: 'So they put away the foreign gods from among them and served the LORD.' Here is repentance that moves from the lips to the life. At Bochim, back in chapter 2, Israel wept but did nothing; their tears watered no fruit. Here they actually remove the idols. Davis marks the difference sharply: true repentance is not measured by the intensity of remorse but by the removal of the idol. They did not merely feel sorry; they put away their gods and served the LORD. This is the turning Paul describes among the Thessalonians, who 'turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God' (1 Thess. 1:9). Confession without the casting out of the idol is hollow; godly grief produces a repentance that acts, that strips the shelves of the household gods and bows again to the LORD alone. Israel finally does what Bochim never did — and it is precisely this that opens the door to the astonishing line that follows. (cf. 1 Thess. 1:9; 2 Cor. 7:10–11)

verseByVerse.quote: ...And he became impatient over the misery of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary: This brief clause is one of the most moving in all of Scripture, the emotional and theological summit of the chapter. God had just declared, 'I will save you no more.' And now, when Israel puts away its idols, 'he became impatient over the misery of Israel' — older versions render it, 'his soul was grieved for the misery of Israel,' or 'he could bear Israel's misery no longer.' The God who pronounced the refusal cannot, in the end, abide his people's suffering. His heart turns over within him. Ferguson and Sproul both linger here in wonder: this is the language of a love that is rooted not in Israel's worthiness — they had none — but in God's own covenant heart. His mercy is not finally conditioned on their deserving but flows from his own grieved compassion. And note the staggering tenderness: the misery that grieves him is misery they brought upon themselves by their own idolatry. He is moved by self-inflicted suffering, like a father whose heart breaks over a child reaping the bitter harvest of his own folly. Here the gospel blazes out of the dark book of Judges. This is the God of Hosea, whose heart recoils within him, whose compassion grows warm and tender (Hos. 11:8). This is the God who would one day be so moved by our misery that he gave his only Son, whose mercy triumphs over the judgment his justice demands. The LORD could not bear our wretchedness; so he came down and bore it himself. (cf. Hos. 11:8; James 2:13)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–18 — The Crisis That Sets the Stage
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Ammonites encamp for war and Israel musters at Mizpah, but they have no leader. The people and princes of Gilead ask, 'Who is the man who will begin to fight the Ammonites? He shall be head over all.' The stage is set for Jephthah.
verseByVerse.theology: God prepares deliverance even before the deliverer appears. The leaderless crisis sets the scene for the outcast Jephthah's rise.
verseByVerse.examples: God often allows a vacuum of leadership and a moment of crisis to prepare the way for the unlikely servant he intends to use.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Ammonites were called to arms, and they encamped in Gilead. And the people of Israel came together, and they encamped at Mizpah. And the people, the leaders of Gilead, said one to another, "Who is the man who will begin to fight against the Ammonites? He shall be head over all the inhabitants of Gilead."
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter ends by setting the stage for what follows. The Ammonites mass for war in Gilead, and Israel gathers at Mizpah — but with a glaring deficiency: they have no leader. The princes of Gilead can only ask one another, 'Who is the man who will begin to fight against the Ammonites? He shall be head over all the inhabitants of Gilead.' It is a question hanging in the air, a vacancy crying to be filled. Davis notes the literary artistry: the narrator leaves us with an unanswered question and an empty office, and the reader leans forward, wondering who will rise. The answer, scandalously, will be Jephthah — the outcast son of a prostitute, driven from his family, living among worthless men in the land of Tob. The very crisis described here, the leaderless desperation of Gilead, is what will force them to send for the man they had rejected. This is how God so often works. He allows the vacuum, the moment when no obvious deliverer stands forward, precisely to prepare the way for the unlikely servant he has chosen — often the very one society had cast aside. The stone the builders rejected becomes the cornerstone (Ps. 118:22). Gilead's anxious question, 'Who is the man?', is the question of every age that has forgotten God and finds itself leaderless in the hour of crisis. The answer, then and now, comes from where we least expect it. (cf. Ps. 118:22; 1 Cor. 1:28)

10.theology:
The Grieved Heart of God. The summit of the chapter: God declared 'I will save you no more,' yet 'became impatient over the misery of Israel' (v. 16). His love is rooted not in their worthiness but in his own covenant heart, moved even by self-inflicted suffering — the God of Hosea whose compassion grows warm (Hos. 11:8).

Repentance That Removes the Idol. Unlike the empty tears of Bochim, Israel here 'put away the foreign gods... and served the LORD' (v. 16). True repentance is shown not in remorse alone but in casting out the idol and turning to the living God (1 Thess. 1:9).

The Severe Mercy of Withheld Rescue. God's holy sarcasm — 'cry out to the gods whom you have chosen' (v. 14) — exposes the emptiness of idols. Sometimes the kindest providence is the rescue delayed, until we despair of false saviors and turn wholly to him.
10.examples:
Then: After the quiet years of Tola and Jair, Israel collected the gods of seven nations, was crushed by Ammon and Philistia, and heard God refuse to save — until they finally put away their idols and served him, and his soul could bear their misery no longer.

Now: Let your repentance go beyond regret to the actual removal of the idol. And when God seems to withhold rescue, do not despair — he may be exposing the emptiness of the false saviors you have trusted, to draw you wholly to himself. Above all, marvel at a God whose heart is grieved by your misery even when you brought it on yourself, a God so moved by our wretchedness that he gave his Son to bear it.

11.title: Jephthah
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty warrior, but he was the son of a prostitute. Gilead was the father of Jephthah.<sup>2</sup>And Gilead's wife also bore him sons. And when his wife's sons grew up, they drove Jephthah out and said to him, "You shall not have an inheritance in our father's house, for you are the son of another woman."<sup>3</sup>Then Jephthah fled from his brothers and lived in the land of Tob, and worthless fellows collected around Jephthah and went out with him.<sup>4</sup>After a time the Ammonites made war against Israel.<sup>5</sup>And when the Ammonites made war against Israel, the elders of Gilead went to bring Jephthah from the land of Tob.<sup>6</sup>And they said to Jephthah, "Come and be our leader, that we may fight against the Ammonites."<sup>7</sup>But Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, "Did you not hate me and drive me out of my father's house? Why have you come to me now when you are in distress?"<sup>8</sup>And the elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "That is why we have turned to you now, that you may go with us and fight against the Ammonites and be our head over all the inhabitants of Gilead."<sup>9</sup>Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, "If you bring me home again to fight against the Ammonites, and the LORD gives them over to me, I will be your head."<sup>10</sup>And the elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "The LORD will be witness between us, if we do not do as you say."<sup>11</sup>So Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, and the people made him head and leader over them. And Jephthah spoke all his words before the LORD at Mizpah.<sup>12</sup>Then Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites and said, "What do you have against me, that you have come to me to fight against my land?"<sup>13</sup>And the king of the Ammonites answered the messengers of Jephthah, "Because Israel on coming up from Egypt took away my land, from the Arnon to the Jabbok and to the Jordan; now therefore restore it peaceably."<sup>14</sup>Jephthah again sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites<sup>15</sup>and said to him, "Thus says Jephthah: Israel did not take away the land of Moab or the land of the Ammonites,<sup>16</sup>but when they came up from Egypt, Israel went through the wilderness to the Red Sea and came to Kadesh.<sup>17</sup>Israel then sent messengers to the king of Edom, saying, 'Please let us pass through your land,' but the king of Edom would not listen. And they sent also to the king of Moab, but he would not consent. So Israel remained at Kadesh.<sup>18</sup>"Then they journeyed through the wilderness and went around the land of Edom and the land of Moab and arrived on the east side of the land of Moab and camped on the other side of the Arnon. But they did not enter the territory of Moab, for the Arnon was the boundary of Moab.<sup>19</sup>Israel then sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, king of Heshbon, and Israel said to him, 'Please let us pass through your land to our country,'<sup>20</sup>but Sihon did not trust Israel to pass through his territory, so Sihon gathered all his people together and encamped at Jahaz and fought with Israel.<sup>21</sup>And the LORD, the God of Israel, gave Sihon and all his people into the hand of Israel, and they defeated them. So Israel took possession of all the land of the Amorites, who inhabited that country.<sup>22</sup>And they took possession of all the territory of the Amorites from the Arnon to the Jabbok and from the wilderness to the Jordan.<sup>23</sup>So then the LORD, the God of Israel, dispossessed the Amorites from before his people Israel; and are you to take possession of them?<sup>24</sup>Will you not possess what Chemosh your god gives you to possess? And all that the LORD our God has dispossessed before us, we will possess.<sup>25</sup>Now are you any better than Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he ever contend against Israel, or did he ever go to war with them?<sup>26</sup>While Israel lived in Heshbon and its villages, and in Aroer and its villages, and in all the cities that are on the banks of the Arnon, 300 years, why did you not deliver them within that time?<sup>27</sup>I therefore have not sinned against you, and you do me wrong by making war on me. The LORD, the Judge, decide this day between the people of Israel and the people of Ammon."<sup>28</sup>But the king of the Ammonites did not listen to the words of Jephthah that he sent to him.<sup>29</sup>Then the Spirit of the LORD was upon Jephthah, and he passed through Gilead and Manasseh and passed on to Mizpah of Gilead, and from Mizpah of Gilead he passed on to the Ammonites.<sup>30</sup>And Jephthah made a vow to the LORD and said, "If you will give the Ammonites into my hand,<sup>31</sup>then whatever comes out from the doors of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the Ammonites shall be the LORD's, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering."<sup>32</sup>So Jephthah crossed over to the Ammonites to fight against them, and the LORD gave them into his hand.<sup>33</sup>And he struck them from Aroer to the neighborhood of Minnith, twenty cities, and as far as Abel-keramim, with a great blow. So the Ammonites were subdued before the people of Israel.<sup>34</sup>Then Jephthah came to his home at Mizpah. And behold, his daughter came out to meet him with tambourines and with dances. She was his only child; besides her he had neither son nor daughter.<sup>35</sup>And as soon as he saw her, he tore his clothes and said, "Alas, my daughter! You have brought me very low, and you have become the cause of great trouble to me. For I have opened my mouth to the LORD, and I cannot take back my vow."<sup>36</sup>And she said to him, "My father, you have opened your mouth to the LORD; do to me according to what has gone out of your mouth, now that the LORD has avenged you on your enemies, on the Ammonites."<sup>37</sup>So she said to her father, "Let this thing be done for me: leave me alone two months, that I may go up and down on the mountains and weep for my virginity, I and my companions."<sup>38</sup>So he said, "Go." Then he sent her away for two months, and she departed, she and her companions, and wept for her virginity on the mountains.<sup>39</sup>And at the end of two months, she returned to her father, who did with her according to his vow that he had made. She had never known a man, and it became a custom in Israel<sup>40</sup>that the daughters of Israel went year by year to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite four days in the year.
11.overview:
Jephthah is the most theologically complex of the judges — a man of real faith and real tragedy bound together. He is the outcast son of Gilead by a prostitute, driven from his father's house by his half-brothers and disinherited. He flees to the land of Tob and gathers around him a band of 'worthless fellows.' He is, by every social measure, the rejected man, the dregs.

Yet when the Ammonites threaten, the very elders of Gilead who had cast him out come crawling back, begging him to lead them. Jephthah negotiates, extracts their commitment before the LORD at Mizpah, and becomes their head. He then sends a remarkable diplomatic message to the Ammonite king — a sustained theological and historical argument for Israel's right to the land, rooted in what the LORD their God had given them. Jephthah knows his Scripture and reasons from covenant history; he is no mere brigand but a man who thinks in terms of God's providence.

Then the Spirit of the LORD comes upon him, and on the eve of battle he makes the rash vow that has haunted readers for millennia: 'Whatever comes out from the doors of my house to meet me... shall be the LORD's, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering.' He wins a great victory — and returns to find his only child, his daughter, coming out to meet him with tambourines and dancing. The triumph turns to ashes in his mouth.

The vow is a window into the syncretism of the age: Jephthah, for all his theological argument, has absorbed the pagan notion that God can be bargained with by extravagant promises, even human sacrifice — a thing the LORD explicitly abhorred (Deut. 12:31). Faith and folly, devotion and darkness, dwell together in this one man. And yet Hebrews 11:32 lists Jephthah among the heroes of faith. Here is the staggering grace of God: that he uses, and even commends, deeply flawed men. Jephthah reminds us that the heroes of Scripture are not the heroes of legend; they are sinners saved and used by grace, pointing always to the one flawless Deliverer who offered not another but himself.

sections.title: The Outcast Son Recalled to Lead
sections.commentary:
Jephthah is introduced with a painful double identity: 'a mighty warrior, but he was the son of a prostitute.' The 'but' carries the weight of his whole life. Gifted and capable, yet stained by the circumstances of his birth, he is driven out by his legitimate half-brothers — 'You shall not have an inheritance in our father's house, for you are the son of another woman.' Rejected by his family, he flees to the land of Tob and becomes the leader of a band of 'worthless fellows,' a frontier outlaw. Davis observes the bitter injustice: Jephthah is punished all his life for a sin that was not his own, cast out for his father's transgression. He is the rejected stone, the despised outsider.

Then the wheel of providence turns. When Ammon attacks, the elders of Gilead — the very establishment that had tolerated his expulsion — come to Tob begging him to be their commander. The irony is exquisite and pointed: they need the man they threw away. Jephthah, understandably wary, confronts them: 'Did you not hate me and drive me out of my father's house? Why have you come to me now when you are in distress?' But he agrees, on terms sworn 'before the LORD at Mizpah.' Ferguson notes how the rejected one becomes the deliverer, a recurring biblical pattern. The stone the builders rejected becomes the cornerstone (Ps. 118:22); Joseph, sold by his brothers, becomes their savior; David, despised by his family, becomes king. And supremely, the One 'despised and rejected by men' becomes the only Savior of the very people who cast him out. Jephthah's restoration from outcast to head whispers the gospel of the rejected Redeemer. (cf. Ps. 118:22; Isa. 53:3)

sections.title: Jephthah's Theological Argument to Ammon
sections.commentary:
Before drawing his sword, Jephthah engages in diplomacy, sending messengers to the king of Ammon with a question: 'What do you have against me, that you have come to fight against my land?' The king claims Israel stole his territory in the days of the conquest. Jephthah's reply is a masterclass in covenant theology and history — a sustained argument that reveals he is no mere warlord but a man steeped in the story of God's dealings with Israel.

He rehearses the wilderness journey accurately: Israel did not seize Moabite or Ammonite land but took the territory of Sihon king of the Amorites, who attacked Israel first and was defeated by the LORD. The land in dispute was won from the Amorites, not from Ammon. Then comes the theological heart of his argument: 'The LORD, the God of Israel, dispossessed the Amorites... and are you to take possession of them?' And strikingly, he reasons by analogy: 'Will you not possess what Chemosh your god gives you to possess? And all that the LORD our God has dispossessed before us, we will possess.' Davis notes that Jephthah grounds Israel's claim not in might but in the gift of God — the land is theirs because the LORD gave it. He thinks providentially; he reads history as the outworking of God's sovereign disposing of nations.

This is the admirable side of Jephthah, the faith that Hebrews would later commend. He knows the Scriptures, reasons from God's redemptive acts, and trusts that the LORD is the true arbiter: 'The LORD, the Judge, decide this day between the people of Israel and the people of Ammon.' He appeals from human dispute to the divine Judge — the very title of the book. Here is a man who genuinely believes that history is God's courtroom and that the LORD will vindicate his people's right. The Ammonite king will not listen, but the reader has seen that Jephthah's deliverance rests on a real conviction about the God who gives and takes away nations and lands. The tragedy of the next section is all the sharper because the faith here is so genuine. (cf. Deut. 2:24–37; Acts 17:26)

sections.title: The Spirit, the Vow, and the Victory
sections.commentary:
'Then the Spirit of the LORD was upon Jephthah.' As with Othniel and Gideon, the divine empowering marks the true deliverer; the Spirit comes, and Jephthah advances against Ammon. And here, at the very moment of Spirit-anointing, Jephthah does the inexplicable: he makes a vow. 'If you will give the Ammonites into my hand, then whatever comes out from the doors of my house to meet me when I return in peace... shall be the LORD's, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering.'

The vow is tragic on every level. First, it is unnecessary — the Spirit of the LORD is already upon him; the victory is already as good as won. Jephthah, like the doubting Gideon, feels he must secure God's favor with an extravagant bargain. Second, it reveals the syncretism poisoning even Israel's better men. Davis and others stress that the very notion of buying victory by promising a burnt offering — and in context almost certainly a human one, given the phrase 'whatever comes out... to meet me' from the doors of a house — betrays a pagan conception of deity. The LORD does not bargain; he gives by grace, and he abhors human sacrifice as the detestable practice of the nations (Deut. 12:31; Jer. 7:31). Jephthah's theology, so sound in his argument to Ammon, is shot through with pagan instinct when it comes to securing God's blessing. He thinks he can leverage God.

The victory comes — 'the LORD gave them into his hand' — and it is crushing and complete; twenty cities subdued, Ammon humbled. The deliverance is real, the work of God genuine. But the vow now hangs over the homecoming like a thundercloud. The reader, knowing the words spoken, dreads the door of Jephthah's house. Here the book exposes a terrible truth: a man may be genuinely used by God, genuinely Spirit-empowered, and still carry within him a darkness that will devour his own joy. Faith and folly were never further intertwined than in the hour of Jephthah's triumph. (cf. Deut. 12:31; Eccl. 5:4–5)

sections.title: The Daughter at the Door
sections.commentary:
The homecoming is the most heartrending scene of the chapter. Jephthah returns to Mizpah in triumph, 'and behold, his daughter came out to meet him with tambourines and with dances.' She is celebrating his victory, leading the women in joyful welcome, exactly as Miriam celebrated the Red Sea — and the narrator drives the knife in deeper: 'She was his only child; besides her he had neither son nor daughter.' His whole future, his entire line, comes dancing out the door. And Jephthah tears his clothes: 'Alas, my daughter! You have brought me very low... for I have opened my mouth to the LORD, and I cannot take back my vow.'

The text is deliberately restrained about what follows, and interpreters have long debated whether Jephthah actually sacrificed her or devoted her to perpetual virginity. The plain sense of the language — a burnt offering, the daughter bewailing not her death but 'her virginity,' and the annual lament of the Israelite women — points most readers, with Davis, to the horror that Jephthah carried out the vow. Either way, the tragedy stands: a rash word spoken to manipulate God destroys the one he loved most. The daughter's response is remarkable — she submits, asking only two months to mourn 'her virginity' upon the mountains. Her dignity and faith shine even brighter than her father's.

The chapter is a sustained warning about the danger of foolish vows and the poison of treating God as one to be bargained with. 'It is a snare to say rashly, It is holy, and to reflect only after making vows' (Prov. 20:25). Jephthah imagined he was honoring God; in truth he was importing a pagan god's appetite into the worship of the LORD, and an innocent paid the price. Yet here too the gospel casts its shadow backward. Jephthah's vow demanded a substitute he could not provide without horror — the offering of his only beloved child. How differently the true and living God acted. He did not demand our child but gave his own — the only beloved Son, who came out to meet us not in unwitting tragedy but in willing love, and who offered up himself as the burnt offering that no human vow could ever supply (Heb. 10:5–10). Jephthah's grief at the door of his house points us to the Father's gift at the door of the tomb. (cf. Prov. 20:25; Gen. 22:12)

11.theology:
The Grace of God Toward Flawed Servants. Jephthah, the outcast son of a prostitute, a Spirit-empowered deliverer ruined by a rash and pagan-tinged vow, is nonetheless enrolled among the heroes of faith (Heb. 11:32). God uses and even commends deeply flawed men — sinners saved by grace, not legends of virtue.

The Rejected Becomes the Deliverer. The brothers who cast Jephthah out come begging him to lead them; the despised stone becomes the head. This pattern runs through Joseph, David, and supremely the One 'despised and rejected,' who saves the very people who cast him out (Isa. 53:3; Ps. 118:22).

The Folly of Bargaining with God. Jephthah's vow betrays the syncretism of the age — the pagan notion that God can be leveraged by extravagant promises, even human sacrifice, which the LORD abhors (Deut. 12:31). God gives by grace; he is not bought.
11.examples:
Then: The disinherited son of a prostitute became Israel's deliverer, argued Israel's cause from covenant history, was clothed with the Spirit, won a great victory — and destroyed his own beloved daughter through a rash vow born of pagan bargaining with God.

Now: Take heart that God uses the rejected and the flawed; your background and your failures do not disqualify you from his service. But beware rash vows and every attempt to leverage God by extravagant promises — he gives by grace, not barter. And marvel that the Father, unlike Jephthah, did not demand our child but freely offered his own as the sacrifice no human vow could supply.

12.title: Jephthah's Conflict and the Minor Judges
12.text: <sup>1</sup>The men of Ephraim were called to arms, and they crossed to Zaphon and said to Jephthah, "Why did you cross over to fight against the Ammonites and did not call us to go with you? We will burn your house over you with fire."<sup>2</sup>And Jephthah said to them, "I and my people had a great dispute with the Ammonites, and when I called you, you did not save me from their hand.<sup>3</sup>And when I saw that you would not save me, I took my life in my hand and crossed over against the Ammonites, and the LORD gave them into my hand. Why then have you come up to me this day to fight against me?"<sup>4</sup>Then Jephthah gathered all the men of Gilead and fought with Ephraim. And the men of Gilead struck Ephraim, because they said, "You are fugitives of Ephraim, you Gileadites, in the midst of Ephraim and Manasseh."<sup>5</sup>And the Gileadites captured the fords of the Jordan against the Ephraimites. And when any of the fugitives of Ephraim said, "Let me go over," the men of Gilead said to him, "Are you an Ephraimite?" When he said, "No,"<sup>6</sup>they said to him, "Then say Shibboleth," and he said, "Sibboleth," for he could not pronounce it right. Then they seized him and slaughtered him at the fords of the Jordan. At that time 42,000 of the Ephraimites fell.<sup>7</sup>Jephthah judged Israel six years. Then Jephthah the Gileadite died and was buried in his city in Gilead.<sup>8</sup>After him Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel.<sup>9</sup>He had thirty sons, and thirty daughters he gave in marriage outside his clan, and thirty daughters he brought in from outside for his sons. And he judged Israel seven years.<sup>10</sup>Then Ibzan died and was buried at Bethlehem.<sup>11</sup>After him Elon the Zebulunite judged Israel, and he judged Israel ten years.<sup>12</sup>Then Elon the Zebulunite died and was buried at Aijalon in the land of Zebulun.<sup>13</sup>After him Abdon the son of Hillel the Pirathonite judged Israel.<sup>14</sup>He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, who rode on seventy donkeys, and he judged Israel eight years.<sup>15</sup>Then Abdon the son of Hillel the Pirathonite died and was buried at Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites.
12.overview:
Chapter 12 opens with a grim sequel to Jephthah's victory: a civil war among Israelites themselves. The proud Ephraimites, exactly as they had done to Gideon, complain that they were not called to share in the glory of the Ammonite war — and this time they go further, threatening to burn Jephthah's house over him. But where Gideon had defused Ephraim with a soft answer, Jephthah, the hardened frontier warrior, answers with the sword.

The conflict escalates into open battle between Gilead and Ephraim. Jephthah's men seize the fords of the Jordan and devise a brutal test to identify fleeing Ephraimites: they make each fugitive say 'Shibboleth.' The Ephraimite dialect could not manage the 'sh' sound and produced 'Sibboleth' — and on that single mispronounced syllable, forty-two thousand men were slaughtered. It is one of the most chilling pictures in the book of Israel turning its weapons on itself.

The chapter closes with three more 'minor' judges — Ibzan of Bethlehem, Elon the Zebulunite, and Abdon — noted briefly for their years, their families, and their burial. Like Tola and Jair, they pass quietly across the page, marking the long stretches between crises.

The theology of the chapter is the tragedy of a people consuming itself. Israel, called to be one nation under one God, fractures along tribal lines and sheds its own blood over wounded pride. The Shibboleth test, dividing brother from brother by an accent, is a parable of how the people of God can turn the markers of belonging into instruments of death. It anticipates the disastrous civil war of chapters 19–21 and cries out for the King who would gather his scattered, warring people into one — the Prince of Peace who breaks down the dividing wall and makes the two one (Eph. 2:14).

sections.title: Ephraim's Pride and the Threat to Jephthah
sections.commentary:
The Ephraimites cross the Jordan and confront Jephthah with the same wounded vanity they had shown Gideon: 'Why did you cross over to fight against the Ammonites and did not call us to go with you?' But they raise the stakes far higher, adding a savage threat: 'We will burn your house over you with fire.' This is no mere complaint about being left out of the glory; it is a death threat from one tribe of Israel against the deliverer of another. Davis notes how Ephraim's chronic pride has curdled into open aggression; the tribe that should have rejoiced in Israel's deliverance instead seethes that it missed the honor.

Jephthah's reply is firm and, unlike Gideon's flattery, accusatory: 'I and my people had a great dispute with the Ammonites, and when I called you, you did not save me from their hand.' He claims he did summon them and they failed to come; now they show up only to fight their own brothers, not the enemy. There is a bitter truth here about misplaced zeal. Ephraim had no stomach for the hard battle against Ammon when it mattered, but plenty of appetite for a quarrel with a fellow Israelite afterward. How often the energy people will not spend on the real enemy they pour into conflict with their own. The craving for recognition, the refusal to celebrate another's success, the readiness to fight where no fighting is needed — these are the works of the flesh tearing at the body of God's people. Ephraim would not help save Israel, but it would gladly burn the house of the man who did. (cf. Phil. 2:3–4; Gal. 5:15)

sections.title: The Slaughter at the Fords: Shibboleth
sections.commentary:
The quarrel erupts into civil war. Jephthah gathers the men of Gilead and fights Ephraim, and the battle goes against Ephraim. Then Gilead seizes the fords of the Jordan, the crossing points the fleeing Ephraimites must use to get home, and there they devise their lethal test. When a fugitive tries to cross, the Gileadites ask, 'Are you an Ephraimite?' If he says no, they command, 'Say now, Shibboleth.' The Ephraimite dialect could not produce the 'sh' sound and came out 'Sibboleth' — and on that single syllable, life or death hung. 'Then they seized him and slaughtered him at the fords of the Jordan. At that time 42,000 of the Ephraimites fell.'

The number is staggering — forty-two thousand Israelites killed by other Israelites, far more than fell in the war against Ammon. The enemy without cost Israel less than the enemy within. Davis underscores the horror: this is God's covenant people, called to be one, slaughtering one another over tribal pride, betrayed by an accent. The Shibboleth test is one of Scripture's most haunting images, the moment a marker of identity — a way of speaking — becomes an instrument of mass execution. There is a sobering parable in it for the church. How easily the people of God turn the shibboleths of their tribe — their vocabulary, their secondary distinctives, their cultural accents — into tests by which they slaughter their own. Brothers who confess the same Lord can divide and destroy one another over the pronunciation of a word, the precise shade of a phrase. The fords of the Jordan ran red not with Canaanite blood but with Israelite. This is the fruit of a nation with no king, doing what is right in its own eyes, fracturing along every fault line.

Jephthah judged Israel six years, then died and was buried in Gilead. His story ends in blood among brothers, a fitting and sorrowful close to a life shaped by rejection and tragedy. The deliverer from Ammon could not deliver Israel from itself. Only the King who is our peace can take the warring tribes, Gilead and Ephraim, Jew and Gentile, and make of the two one new humanity, killing the hostility in his own body (Eph. 2:14–16). Until he reigns, the people of God are forever in danger of the fords of the Jordan. (cf. Eph. 2:14–16; 1 Cor. 1:10)

sections.title: Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon
sections.commentary:
The chapter closes, as chapter 10 began, with brief notices of 'minor' judges — Ibzan of Bethlehem, Elon the Zebulunite, and Abdon the Pirathonite. As with Tola and Jair, no battles or deliverances are recorded, only their years of judging, the size of their families, and their burial places. Ibzan had thirty sons and thirty daughters, marrying them strategically outside his clan; Abdon had forty sons and thirty grandsons who rode on seventy donkeys — marks of wealth, status, and dynastic ambition.

These quiet notices serve several purposes. They mark the passage of time, the long ordinary stretches between the dramatic crises that dominate the book. They remind us that most of God's providential care for his people runs through unremarkable leadership rather than spectacular deliverance. And, more subtly, Davis notes the recurring emphasis on large families, many wives, and herds of donkeys — the trappings of petty royalty. The minor judges increasingly resemble the kings Israel does not yet have, accumulating households and prestige. The drift toward monarchy is in the air; the people are restless for a king, and even these obscure judges live like minor princes.

There is dignity in the obscure faithfulness these men represent, the long labor of holding a society together that fills no exciting chapter. But there is also a quiet ache. None of these judges addresses the deepest problem — the idolatry and fragmentation of the heart. They govern; they do not transform. They leave behind sons and donkeys and tombs, but not a changed people. The book is building its case relentlessly: judge after judge, major and minor, faithful and flawed, comes and goes, and Israel remains what it was. The cycle grinds on. What Israel needs is not another judge who lives like a princeling and dies leaving a family, but a King who lives forever and leaves behind a transformed, Spirit-indwelt people. The minor judges fill the years; only Christ fills the need. (cf. 1 Cor. 4:2; Heb. 7:23–25)

12.theology:
The Tragedy of a People Consuming Itself. Israel, called to be one nation under one God, fractures over tribal pride and slaughters 42,000 of its own at the fords. The enemy within cost more than the enemy without. This cries out for the King who makes warring brothers one (Eph. 2:14).

The Peril of Shibboleths. A marker of belonging — an accent — became an instrument of mass execution. The people of God still turn their tribal distinctives, vocabulary, and secondary issues into tests by which they destroy their own. Christ calls his people to be one (1 Cor. 1:10).

Obscure Faithfulness and the Drift Toward Kingship. The minor judges mark the quiet years, yet increasingly live like petty kings with many wives and donkeys. They govern but do not transform; the cycle grinds on, exposing the need for a King who changes the heart, not merely the times.
12.examples:
Then: Ephraim's wounded pride sparked a civil war in which 42,000 Israelites died at the fords of the Jordan, betrayed by their inability to say 'Shibboleth' — God's people slaughtering their own over an accent and a grievance.

Now: Guard against the shibboleths by which we wound and divide fellow believers — the secondary distinctives, the cultural accents, the grievances over recognition that turn brothers into enemies. Pour your zeal into the real battle, not into quarrels with your own. And long for the day when the Prince of Peace gathers every warring tribe into one new people, the hostility forever killed in his body.

13.title: Samson's Birth
13.text: <sup>1</sup>And the people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, so the LORD gave them into the hand of the Philistines for forty years.<sup>2</sup>There was a certain man of Zorah, of the tribe of the Danites, whose name was Manoah. And his wife was barren and had no children.<sup>3</sup>And the angel of the LORD appeared to the woman and said to her, "Behold, you are barren and have not borne children, but you shall conceive and bear a son.<sup>4</sup>Therefore be careful and drink no wine or strong drink, and eat nothing unclean,<sup>5</sup>for behold, you shall conceive and bear a son. No razor shall come upon his head, for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb, and he shall begin to save Israel from the hand of the Philistines."<sup>6</sup>Then the woman came and told her husband, "A man of God came to me, and his appearance was like the appearance of the angel of God, very awesome. I did not ask him where he was from, and he did not tell me his name,<sup>7</sup>but he said to me, 'Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son. So then drink no wine or strong drink, and eat nothing unclean, for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb to the day of his death.'"<sup>8</sup>Then Manoah prayed to the LORD and said, "O Lord, please let the man of God whom you sent come again to us and teach us what we are to do with the child who will be born."<sup>9</sup>And God listened to the voice of Manoah, and the angel of God came again to the woman as she sat in the field. But Manoah her husband was not with her.<sup>10</sup>So the woman ran quickly and told her husband, "Behold, the man who came to me the other day has appeared to me."<sup>11</sup>And Manoah arose and went after his wife and came to the man and said to him, "Are you the man who spoke to this woman?" And he said, "I am."<sup>12</sup>And Manoah said, "Now when your words come true, what is to be the child's manner of life, and what is his mission?"<sup>13</sup>And the angel of the LORD said to Manoah, "Of all that I said to the woman let her be careful.<sup>14</sup>She may not eat of anything that comes from the vine, neither let her drink wine or strong drink, or eat any unclean thing. All that I commanded her let her observe."<sup>15</sup>Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, "Please let us detain you and prepare a young goat for you."<sup>16</sup>And the angel of the LORD said to Manoah, "If you detain me, I will not eat of your food. But if you prepare a burnt offering, then offer it to the LORD." (For Manoah did not know that he was the angel of the LORD.)<sup>17</sup>And Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, "What is your name, so that, when your words come true, we may honor you?"<sup>18</sup>And the angel of the LORD said to him, "Why do you ask my name, seeing it is wonderful?"<sup>19</sup>So Manoah took the young goat with the grain offering, and offered it on the rock to the LORD, to the one who works wonders, and Manoah and his wife were watching.<sup>20</sup>And when the flame went up toward heaven from the altar, the angel of the LORD went up in the flame of the altar. Now Manoah and his wife were watching, and they fell on their faces to the ground.<sup>21</sup>The angel of the LORD appeared no more to Manoah and to his wife. Then Manoah knew that he was the angel of the LORD.<sup>22</sup>And Manoah said to his wife, "We shall surely die, for we have seen God."<sup>23</sup>But his wife said to him, "If the LORD had meant to kill us, he would not have accepted a burnt offering and a grain offering at our hands, or shown us all these things, or now announced to us such things as these."<sup>24</sup>And the woman bore a son and called his name Samson. And the young man grew, and the LORD blessed him.<sup>25</sup>And the Spirit of the LORD began to stir him in Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.
13.overview:
With Samson the book reaches its final and most paradoxical judge, and his story begins not with a battle but with a birth — and not just any birth, but the miraculous gift of a son to a barren woman. The pattern is one of Scripture's great signposts of grace: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah, and the mother of Samson all conceive by divine intervention after long barrenness, and each son is marked for God's purposes. The barren womb opened by God is a recurring overture to redemption, climaxing in the virgin's womb at Bethlehem.

The angel of the LORD appears to the unnamed wife of Manoah of the tribe of Dan, announcing that she will bear a son who is to be a Nazirite from the womb — set apart to God, never to cut his hair, drink wine, or touch a corpse. And the commission is remarkable in its limitation: 'he shall begin to save Israel from the hand of the Philistines.' Not save — begin to save. Even before he is born, Samson is announced as an incomplete deliverer, a down payment rather than the full price.

Manoah, anxious and a little obtuse, asks for the angel to return and instruct them how to raise the boy. The angel comes again, and in a scene of mounting wonder, ascends to heaven in the flame of the altar sacrifice as Manoah and his wife fall on their faces. They realize they have seen God and fear death; the wife, the clearer-headed of the two, reasons that the LORD would not have accepted their offering if he meant to kill them.
