The chapter establishes the towering hope and the built-in tragedy of Samson. Here is a child of promise, Spirit-stirred, set apart from the womb, a Nazirite consecrated to God — every advantage of grace lavished on him before he draws breath. And yet the seeds of failure are sown in the very word 'begin,' and in a tribe (Dan) already marked for apostasy. Samson's birth narrative shines with the grace of God who opens barren wombs and consecrates deliverers; his life will show how thoroughly a man can squander such grace. The annunciation points forward to the greater Annunciation, when another son would be set apart from the womb — not to begin salvation, but to finish it. (cf. Luke 1)

sections.title: The Barren Womb and the Angel's Announcement
sections.commentary:
The cycle turns once more, and this time the oppression is described with an ominous brevity: Israel did evil, 'so the LORD gave them into the hand of the Philistines for forty years.' Notably, there is no mention of Israel crying out. The people have sunk so deep into accommodation with their oppressors that they no longer even groan for deliverance. Davis observes that this silence marks how far the spiral has descended; by Samson's day, Israel is content in its bondage, intermarrying and coexisting with the Philistines rather than longing to be free. God will have to raise up a deliverer for a people who are not even asking.

And so the deliverance begins, as it so often does, with a barren woman. The angel of the LORD appears to Manoah's unnamed wife with the great announcement: 'Behold, you are barren and have not borne children, but you shall conceive and bear a son.' This is the signature of grace running through Scripture — Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah, Elizabeth — the closed womb opened by God to bring forth a child of promise. The barrenness underscores that the deliverer is entirely God's gift, not the product of human strength. The son is to be a Nazirite from the womb: no razor on his head, no wine, set apart to God. And the commission carries its fateful qualification: 'he shall begin to save Israel.' Ferguson highlights the deliberate incompleteness. Samson is a partial deliverer by divine design, a beginning that awaits a completion. The grace lavished on him is immense — chosen, consecrated, Spirit-destined before birth. The barren womb opened for Samson is a small Bethlehem, pointing to the womb where God would one day bring forth not a beginner but the Finisher of salvation. (cf. 1 Sam. 1:5–20; Luke 1:7)

sections.title: Manoah's Prayer and the Angel's Return
sections.commentary:
Manoah, the husband, responds to his wife's report with a prayer that is both earnest and slightly comic: 'O Lord, please let the man of God whom you sent come again to us and teach us what we are to do with the child who will be born.' His concern for godly parenting is commendable — he wants to raise the boy rightly — but there is also a hint that Manoah cannot quite trust his wife's account and needs the message repeated to him directly. Davis gently notes the irony that runs through the chapter: throughout, Manoah's wife is the more spiritually perceptive of the two, while Manoah fumbles and frets.

God graciously answers the prayer; the angel returns, again first to the woman, who runs to fetch her husband. Manoah's questions are practical and a touch anxious — 'What is to be the child's manner of life, and what is his mission?' — and the angel essentially repeats the instructions already given to the wife, emphasizing again the Nazirite restrictions she is to observe even during pregnancy. There is tender pastoral instruction in God's patience here. He does not rebuke Manoah for needing reassurance; he sends the messenger again, repeats the word, and accommodates the anxious parents. The God who bore with Gideon's fleeces bears with Manoah's questions. He meets sincere if fumbling faith with fresh grace. And the repeated stress on consecration — the whole household ordered around the child's setting-apart to God — reminds us that the deliverer's life was meant to be marked, from the womb, by holiness. The tragedy of Samson is measured precisely against this lavish consecration he would so casually betray. (cf. Prov. 22:6; Deut. 6:6–7)

sections.title: The Flame of the Altar and the Fear of Death
sections.commentary:
Manoah, still not fully grasping who his visitor is, offers to prepare a young goat as a meal. The angel declines the food but directs that any offering be made to the LORD, and when Manoah asks his name 'so that we may honor you,' the angel replies, 'Why do you ask my name, seeing it is wonderful?' That word 'wonderful' is the same root Isaiah will use for the coming child: 'his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor' (Isa. 9:6). Many Reformed interpreters, with Calvin, see here a pre-incarnate appearance of the Son, the Angel of the LORD whose name is beyond telling.

Then comes the moment of revelation. As Manoah offers the sacrifice on the rock, 'the angel of the LORD went up in the flame of the altar. And Manoah and his wife... fell on their faces to the ground.' The visitor ascends in the fire of the offering and vanishes. Now Manoah understands, and his understanding terrifies him: 'We shall surely die, for we have seen God.' His fear is the right instinct of sinful humanity before the holy God. But his wife, clear-headed as ever, answers with beautiful gospel logic: 'If the LORD had meant to kill us, he would not have accepted a burnt offering and a grain offering at our hands.' Her reasoning is profound — the accepted sacrifice is the proof of peace. Davis savors her theology: the God who receives the offering does not destroy the offerer. This is the very assurance of the gospel. The flame that consumed the sacrifice is the sign that judgment has fallen on the substitute, not the sinner; the accepted offering means peace with God. The chapter ends with the birth of Samson and the first stirrings of the Spirit, the great hope and great tragedy of Israel now drawing his first breath. The God who ascended in the altar flame would one day descend into the flame of judgment himself, the Wonderful one offered up so that those who have seen God might not die but live. (cf. Isa. 9:6; Heb. 10:10)

13.theology:
The Grace of the Opened Womb. Samson, like Isaac, Samuel, and John the Baptist, is born to a barren woman by divine gift — the signpost of grace running through Scripture, marking the deliverer as entirely God's provision, not human achievement. It points to the womb of Bethlehem.

Set Apart from the Womb — Yet Only to Begin. Samson is consecrated a Nazirite before birth, lavished with grace, yet commissioned only to 'begin to save Israel' (v. 5). The built-in incompleteness exposes the need for a Deliverer who would not begin but finish salvation.

The Accepted Sacrifice Means Peace. Manoah feared death for seeing God, but his wife reasoned that the accepted offering proved God's favor. The flame that consumes the substitute is the sign that judgment falls not on the sinner — the very logic of the cross (Heb. 10:10).
13.examples:
Then: To a barren woman and an anxious husband in apostate Israel, God announced and gave a son set apart from the womb, appearing as the Angel of the LORD who ascended in the altar flame — lavishing grace on a deliverer who would only begin the work of salvation.

Now: Marvel that God brings forth his deliverance from barren wombs and hopeless situations, that salvation is always his gift and never our achievement. Rest, as Manoah's wife did, in the logic of the accepted sacrifice: the God who received the offering of his Son will never destroy those for whom that offering was made. The flame fell on the substitute, that you might live.

14.title: Samson's Marriage
14.text: <sup>1</sup>Samson went down to Timnah, and at Timnah he saw one of the daughters of the Philistines.<sup>2</sup>Then he came up and told his father and mother, "I saw one of the daughters of the Philistines at Timnah. Now get her for me as my wife."<sup>3</sup>But his father and mother said to him, "Is there not a woman among the daughters of your relatives, or among all our people, that you must go to take a wife from the uncircumcised Philistines?" But Samson said to his father, "Get her for me, for she is right in my eyes."<sup>4</sup>His father and mother did not know that it was from the LORD, for he was seeking an opportunity against the Philistines. At that time the Philistines ruled over Israel.<sup>5</sup>Then Samson went down with his father and mother to Timnah, and they came to the vineyards of Timnah. And behold, a young lion came toward him roaring.<sup>6</sup>Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and although he had nothing in his hand, he tore the lion in pieces as one tears a young goat. But he did not tell his father or his mother what he had done.<sup>7</sup>Then he went down and talked with the woman, and she was right in Samson's eyes.<sup>8</sup>After some days he returned to take her. And he turned aside to see the carcass of the lion, and behold, there was a swarm of bees in the body of the lion, and honey.<sup>9</sup>He scraped it out into his hands and went on, eating as he went. And he came to his father and mother and gave some to them, and they ate. But he did not tell them that he had scraped the honey from the carcass of the lion.<sup>10</sup>His father went down to the woman, and Samson prepared a feast there, for so the young men used to do.<sup>11</sup>As soon as the people saw him, they brought thirty companions to be with him.<sup>12</sup>And Samson said to them, "Let me now put a riddle to you. If you can tell me what it is, within the seven days of the feast, and find it out, then I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes,<sup>13</sup>but if you cannot tell me what it is, then you shall give me thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes." And they said to him, "Put your riddle, that we may hear it."<sup>14</sup>And he said to them, "Out of the eater came something to eat. Out of the strong came something sweet." And in three days they could not solve the riddle.<sup>15</sup>On the fourth day they said to Samson's wife, "Entice your husband to tell us what the riddle is, lest we burn you and your father's house with fire. Have you invited us here to impoverish us?"<sup>16</sup>And Samson's wife wept over him and said, "You only hate me; you do not love me. You have put a riddle to my people, and you have not told me what it is." And he said to her, "Behold, I have not told my father nor my mother, and shall I tell you?"<sup>17</sup>She wept before him the seven days that their feast lasted, and on the seventh day he told her, because she pressed him hard. Then she told the riddle to her people.<sup>18</sup>And the men of the city said to him on the seventh day before the sun went down, "What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?" And he said to them, "If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have found out my riddle."<sup>19</sup>And the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and he went down to Ashkelon and struck down thirty men of the town and took their spoil and gave the garments to those who had told the riddle. In hot anger he went back to his father's house.<sup>20</sup>And Samson's wife was given to his companion, who had been his best man.
14.overview:
If chapter 13 was all grace, chapter 14 introduces all the willfulness that will define Samson's life. The consecrated Nazirite, the child of promise, makes his first recorded act the demand for a pagan Philistine wife: 'Get her for me, for she is right in my eyes.' That phrase — 'right in my eyes' — is the book's own diagnosis of the age (17:6; 21:25), and now it falls from the lips of the deliverer himself. Samson is not the antidote to Israel's disease; he is its most vivid symptom.

His parents object — she is an uncircumcised Philistine — but Samson insists, and the narrator slips in a sovereign aside: 'his father and mother did not know that it was from the LORD, for he was seeking an opportunity against the Philistines.' Even Samson's carnal appetite is woven into God's purposes. On the way to Timnah a young lion attacks, and the Spirit of the LORD rushes upon Samson; he tears it apart bare-handed. Later he finds bees and honey in the carcass and eats — a Nazirite touching the dead, breaking his vow for the sweetness of a moment.

From the dead lion and its honey Samson spins a riddle at his wedding feast, wagering thirty garments against the Philistine guests. They cannot solve it, so they threaten his bride, who weeps and wheedles until he tells her, and she betrays him to her people. Enraged, Samson, again Spirit-empowered, strikes down thirty men of Ashkelon to pay the wager, and storms home in fury, his bride given to another.

The chapter is a study in a man of immense God-given power and zero self-control. The Spirit rushes on him with superhuman strength, yet he cannot govern his own appetites. He breaks his vows for honey and a woman; he is ruled by his eyes and his temper. And yet God is sovereignly at work even through Samson's sins, advancing the deliverance of Israel through the deliverer's very disobedience. Here is the mystery of providence: God weaves even our willful folly into his redemptive purpose. But the warning is severe — gifting is not godliness, and the Spirit's power on a life is no substitute for the Spirit's fruit in a heart. (cf. Gal. 5:22–23)

sections.title: She Is Right in My Eyes
sections.commentary:
Samson's very first recorded act sets the tragic key of his whole life. He goes down to Timnah, sees a Philistine woman, and returns with a demand: 'Get her for me, for she is right in my eyes.' The consecrated Nazirite, the child of promise, is governed not by the law of God or the welfare of Israel but by his own appetite — what is right in his eyes. Davis catches the devastating significance: the phrase is the refrain of the entire book ('everyone did what was right in his own eyes'), and here it issues from the mouth of the deliverer himself. Samson embodies the disease he is sent to cure. His parents protest — should he not take a wife from his own people rather than the uncircumcised Philistines? — for intermarriage with the pagan oppressor was both forbidden and spiritually ruinous. But Samson will not hear it; his eyes have decided.

And then the narrator drops a startling sovereign aside: 'His father and mother did not know that it was from the LORD, for he was seeking an opportunity against the Philistines.' Here is the mystery of providence at full stretch. Samson's desire is sinful — he is doing what is right in his own eyes — and yet God is weaving even this carnal impulse into his redemptive plan to confront the Philistines. Sproul cautions that we must hold both truths without collapsing either: Samson is fully responsible for his disobedience, and God is fully sovereign over its outcome. God does not author Samson's lust, but he governs it, bending even the deliverer's rebellion toward Israel's deliverance. This is the same sovereignty that turned Joseph's betrayal and the cross itself into salvation: what man means for evil, God means for good (Gen. 50:20). Yet the comfort of providence is no license for sin; Samson's life will prove that doing what is right in our own eyes, even when God overrules it for good, brings ruin on the one who does it. (cf. Gen. 50:20; Judg. 21:25)

sections.title: The Lion, the Honey, and the Broken Vow
sections.commentary:
On the road to Timnah, a young lion roars against Samson, and 'the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and although he had nothing in his hand, he tore the lion in pieces as one tears a young goat.' The verb 'rushed' is violent and sudden; the Spirit comes upon Samson with explosive, superhuman force. This is the great paradox of the man: he is genuinely Spirit-empowered, the strongest of all the judges, and yet the least self-governed. The same Spirit who clothed Gideon and stirred Othniel rushes on Samson — but where they were empowered for deliverance, Samson's power so often serves his own impulses. Davis notes the discomfiting truth that the Spirit's empowering for a task is not the same as the Spirit's sanctifying of a soul.

Returning later, Samson turns aside to look at the lion's carcass and finds that bees have made honey in it. He scrapes out the honey, eats it as he walks, and even gives some to his parents — telling them nothing of its source. The detail is loaded. A Nazirite was forbidden to touch any dead body (Num. 6:6); Samson not only touches the carcass but eats from it, breaking his consecration for the sweetness of a moment, and then conceals the violation. Davis observes how casually Samson treats his sacred vows — the honey is sweet, so the corpse-ban is forgotten. Here is the pattern of his ruin in miniature: immediate appetite overriding solemn consecration. The sweetness in his mouth costs him his set-apartness, and he does not even seem to notice. How often sin offers honey from the carcass — real pleasure, genuine sweetness — at the price of holiness we barely pause to count. Samson eats and walks on, his vow quietly broken, his conscience untroubled. The strongest man in Israel cannot say no to a handful of honey. (cf. Num. 6:6–7; Heb. 12:16)

sections.title: The Riddle and the Wager
sections.commentary:
At the seven-day wedding feast, Samson poses a riddle to the thirty Philistine companions, wagering thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes: 'Out of the eater came something to eat. Out of the strong came something sweet.' It is drawn from his secret experience with the lion and the honey — a private joke that no one could possibly solve, which is rather the point; Samson is showing off and rigging the game. For three days the Philistines are stumped. Then they turn to Samson's bride with a threat chillingly like the one her people will use again later: 'Entice your husband to tell us... lest we burn you and your father's house with fire.'

The bride does what the Philistine women in Samson's life always do — she weeps, presses, accuses him of not loving her, and wears him down. 'She wept before him the seven days... and on the seventh day he told her, because she pressed him hard.' She immediately betrays the answer to her people, who deliver the solution to Samson just before the deadline: 'What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?' Davis points out that this episode is a dress rehearsal for Delilah; Samson's fatal weakness — his inability to resist the tears and pressure of a Philistine woman — is on full display, and he learns nothing from it. He recognizes the betrayal at once, his bitter retort confirming it: 'If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have found out my riddle.' The strongest man in Israel, who tore a lion bare-handed, is helpless before a weeping woman. His strength is in his arms; his weakness is in his heart, and his enemies have already found the door. (cf. Prov. 7:21–23; Judg. 16:16)

sections.title: Vengeance at Ashkelon
sections.commentary:
Defeated at his own rigged game and owing thirty sets of clothes, Samson responds with violence: 'the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and he went down to Ashkelon and struck down thirty men of the town and took their spoil and gave the garments to those who had told the riddle.' Once again the Spirit of the LORD empowers him — and once again the power serves Samson's personal grievance. He pays his gambling debt with the lives and clothes of thirty murdered strangers, then storms home 'in hot anger' to his father's house. His bride, abandoned in his fury, is given to his best man.

The episode crystallizes the troubling enigma of Samson. The Spirit genuinely comes upon him; God genuinely uses these acts to begin striking the Philistines, advancing Israel's deliverance through Samson's volatile rage. And yet Samson himself is acting out of wounded pride and hot temper, not zeal for God or love for his people. Davis presses the uncomfortable lesson: God can accomplish his sovereign purposes through a man's sin without endorsing the sin, and the man remains fully accountable. Samson's anger 'works' for God's plan, but it is still anger; the killing at Ashkelon advances deliverance, but it springs from a heart ungoverned by grace. Here is the great warning of Samson's life: immense gifting without holiness, power without self-control, the Spirit's might without the Spirit's fruit. He has the strength to tear lions and slay armies, but not the strength to master his own temper or keep his own vows. Gifting is not godliness. The man James describes — slow to anger, bridling his tongue and his passions — is stronger than the man who takes a city, for 'whoever rules his spirit is greater than he who takes a city' (Prov. 16:32). Samson took cities; he never ruled his spirit. (cf. Prov. 16:32; Gal. 5:22–23)

14.theology:
Right in My Own Eyes. Samson's defining demand — 'she is right in my eyes' (v. 3) — is the book's diagnosis of the whole age now falling from the deliverer's own lips. He embodies Israel's disease rather than curing it: a man ruled by appetite rather than the word of God.

Sovereignty Over Sin. 'His parents did not know that it was from the LORD' (v. 4). God weaves even Samson's carnal choices into his plan to confront the Philistines, without authoring the sin. What man means for self, God means for deliverance — yet the sinner remains fully responsible (Gen. 50:20).

Gifting Is Not Godliness. The Spirit rushes on Samson with superhuman power, yet he cannot govern his appetites, his temper, or his vows. The Spirit's empowering for a task is not the Spirit's sanctifying of the soul. Power without self-control is ruin (Prov. 16:32).
14.examples:
Then: The consecrated Nazirite demanded a pagan wife because she was 'right in his eyes,' broke his vow for honey from a carcass, rigged a riddle, was betrayed by a weeping woman, and paid his debt with thirty murdered men — Spirit-empowered yet utterly self-indulgent.

Now: Beware living by what is 'right in your own eyes' rather than the word of God. Beware the honey from the carcass — real pleasure bought at the price of holiness barely counted. And never mistake gifting for godliness: the Spirit's power to do great things is no substitute for the Spirit's fruit of self-control. Whoever rules his spirit is greater than he who takes a city.

15.title: Samson's Vengeance
15.text: <sup>1</sup>After some days, at the time of wheat harvest, Samson went to visit his wife with a young goat. And he said, "I will go in to my wife in the chamber." But her father would not allow him to go in.<sup>2</sup>And her father said, "I really thought that you utterly hated her, so I gave her to your companion. Is not her younger sister more beautiful than she? Please take her instead."<sup>3</sup>And Samson said to them, "This time I shall be innocent in regard to the Philistines, when I do them harm."<sup>4</sup>So Samson went and caught 300 foxes and took torches. And he turned them tail to tail and put a torch between each pair of tails.<sup>5</sup>And when he had set fire to the torches, he let the foxes go into the standing grain of the Philistines and set fire to the stacked grain and the standing grain, as well as the olive orchards.<sup>6</sup>Then the Philistines said, "Who has done this?" And they said, "Samson, the son-in-law of the Timnite, because he has taken his wife and given her to his companion." And the Philistines came up and burned her and her father with fire.<sup>7</sup>And Samson said to them, "If this is what you do, I swear I will be avenged on you, and after that I will quit."<sup>8</sup>And he struck them hip and thigh with a great blow, and he went down and stayed in the cleft of the rock of Etam.<sup>9</sup>Then the Philistines came up and encamped in Judah and made a raid on Lehi.<sup>10</sup>And the men of Judah said, "Why have you come up against us?" They said, "We have come up to bind Samson, to do to him as he did to us."<sup>11</sup>Then 3,000 men of Judah went down to the cleft of the rock of Etam, and said to Samson, "Do you not know that the Philistines are rulers over us? What then is this that you have done to us?" And he said to them, "As they did to me, so have I done to them."<sup>12</sup>And they said to him, "We have come down to bind you, that we may give you into the hands of the Philistines." And Samson said to them, "Swear to me that you will not attack me yourselves."<sup>13</sup>They said to him, "No; we will only bind you and give you into their hands. We will surely not kill you." So they bound him with two new ropes and brought him up from the rock.<sup>14</sup>When he came to Lehi, the Philistines came shouting to meet him. Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and the ropes that were on his arms became as flax that has caught fire, and his bonds melted off his hands.<sup>15</sup>And he found a fresh jawbone of a donkey, and put out his hand and took it, and with it he struck 1,000 men.<sup>16</sup>And Samson said, "With the jawbone of a donkey, heaps upon heaps, with the jawbone of a donkey have I struck down a thousand men."<sup>17</sup>As soon as he had finished speaking, he threw away the jawbone out of his hand. And that place was called Ramath-lehi.<sup>18</sup>And he was very thirsty, and he called upon the LORD and said, "You have granted this great salvation by the hand of your servant, and shall I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?"<sup>19</sup>And God split open the hollow place that is at Lehi, and water came out from it. And when he drank, his spirit returned, and he revived. Therefore the name of it was called En-hakkore; it is at Lehi to this day.<sup>20</sup>And he judged Israel in the days of the Philistines twenty years.
15.overview:
Chapter 15 is a chronicle of escalating vengeance, a cycle of retaliation between Samson and the Philistines that spirals upward in violence. It opens with Samson returning to claim his estranged wife, only to learn her father has given her to another. His response is spectacular and destructive: he catches three hundred foxes, ties them tail to tail with torches between them, and sends them blazing through the Philistine grain fields, vineyards, and olive groves, destroying their entire harvest.

The Philistines retaliate by burning Samson's wife and her father — the very fate she had betrayed him to avoid, a bitter irony. Samson avenges them with great slaughter, then retreats to a rock. The Philistines invade Judah to capture him, and here the depth of Israel's degradation appears: three thousand men of Judah come not to fight the Philistines but to bind their own deliverer and hand him over. They would rather serve their oppressors than be freed by God's man. Samson allows himself to be bound, then, when the Spirit rushes upon him, snaps the ropes and seizes a fresh donkey's jawbone, striking down a thousand Philistines.

His victory song revels in the absurdity of the weapon: 'With the jawbone of a donkey, heaps upon heaps... I have struck down a thousand men.' Then, exhausted and parched, he cries out to the LORD in his first recorded prayer, complaining that he will die of thirst. God graciously splits open a hollow place and brings forth water, and Samson drinks and revives. He judges Israel twenty years.

The chapter displays both the comedy and tragedy of Samson. He is a one-man wrecking crew, used by God to harass the Philistines and begin Israel's deliverance. Yet his deliverance is solo, reactive, and personal — driven by private vendetta rather than any vision for Israel. And the spectacle of Judah binding its own savior is a devastating indictment: a people so comfortable in bondage that they resent the one sent to free them. It anticipates the supreme tragedy of the gospel, when the people of God would bind their true Deliverer and hand him over to the Gentiles. Yet even in Samson's weakness — crying out in thirst — we glimpse the dependence that should mark every servant of God. (cf. John 18:30; 2 Cor. 12:9)

sections.title: The Foxes and the Burning Fields
sections.commentary:
Samson returns to Timnah to reclaim his wife, bearing a young goat as a peace-gift, only to be told by her father that he gave her to Samson's best man, assuming Samson had rejected her in his fury. The father even offers the younger sister as a substitute. Samson, enraged, declares himself justified in whatever harm he now does the Philistines and unleashes one of the most bizarre acts of sabotage in Scripture: he catches three hundred foxes (or jackals), ties them tail to tail with torches between each pair, and turns them loose into the standing grain, the vineyards, and the olive groves at harvest time. The Philistines' entire agricultural economy goes up in flames.

The Philistines respond by burning Samson's wife and her father to death — the exact fate she had betrayed his riddle to escape (14:15). Davis notes the dark irony: her treachery to save herself from fire delivered her into it after all. Samson then avenges them, striking the Philistines 'hip and thigh with a great blow,' and withdraws to a rock. The cycle of vengeance escalates with each turn — burned fields, burned family, slaughter, retreat — each side raising the stakes. There is a sober lesson in this spiral. Vengeance, once started, feeds on itself and consumes everyone in reach; it has no natural stopping point, only an ever-rising body count. Samson's private war is real, and God genuinely uses it to begin afflicting the Philistines, but it is driven entirely by personal grievance, not by any love for God or Israel. This is what deliverance looks like when the deliverer is governed by his passions rather than by God: destructive, reactive, and ultimately self-consuming. The Lord who says 'Vengeance is mine' alone can break such cycles, absorbing the wrong rather than escalating it. (cf. Rom. 12:19; Matt. 5:38–39)

sections.title: Judah Binds Its Own Deliverer
sections.commentary:
The Philistines invade Judah to capture Samson, and here the chapter exposes the deepest degradation of Israel's condition. The men of Judah ask the Philistines, 'Why have you come up against us?' and on learning it is to seize Samson, three thousand men of Judah go down — not to fight the Philistines, but to bind their own deliverer. 'Do you not know that the Philistines are rulers over us?' they say to Samson, in a sentence that lays bare how thoroughly they have accepted their slavery. They are not groaning for freedom; they are angry at the one disturbing their comfortable bondage.

Davis underscores the staggering tragedy: God sends a deliverer, and the people of God arrest him and hand him over to the enemy. They would rather preserve their peace with the oppressor than be liberated by God's man. The very tribe of Judah — the royal, messianic tribe that opened the book leading the conquest — now leads the betrayal of its savior. Samson, remarkably, submits to being bound, extracting only their promise not to kill him themselves. He lets his own people deliver him into enemy hands. The scene is a haunting foreshadow of the gospel. Here is Israel's deliverer, bound by his own people and handed over to the Gentiles because they preferred their accommodation with the world to the freedom he offered. So one day the true Deliverer would come to his own, and his own would not receive him (John 1:11); the leaders of Israel would bind him and hand him to Rome, saying in effect, 'We have no king but Caesar' — we prefer our bondage to your salvation. A people content in slavery will always resent the one who comes to set them free. The cross casts its shadow over the rock of Etam. (cf. John 1:11; John 19:15)

sections.title: The Jawbone and the Thousand
sections.commentary:
Bound and delivered to the Philistines, who shout in triumph at the sight, Samson is suddenly transformed: 'the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and the ropes that were on his arms became as flax that has caught fire, and his bonds melted off his hands.' The cords burn away like burning thread; the deliverer is loosed by the power of God. He seizes the nearest weapon — 'a fresh jawbone of a donkey' — and strikes down a thousand Philistines. The weapon is deliberately absurd and unclean: the jawbone of a dead animal, a thing a Nazirite should not even touch, becomes the instrument of slaughter. Once more God saves through the humblest and most unlikely means, as he did with Shamgar's oxgoad and Jael's tent peg.

Samson celebrates with a triumphant pun: 'With the jawbone of a donkey, heaps upon heaps, with the jawbone of a donkey have I struck down a thousand men.' The Hebrew plays on the similarity between the words for 'donkey' and 'heap,' a swaggering bit of wordplay over the piled corpses. Davis notes the bravado: Samson's victory songs always celebrate Samson. There is no 'the LORD has given' as in Gideon's and Deborah's praise; the focus is on his own exploit, his own jawbone, his own heaps. Yet the deliverance is real, and God is genuinely at work, loosing the cords and empowering the blow. Here is the persistent paradox of the man — God's power flowing through a self-absorbed vessel. The same grace that melts the ropes is wasted on a heart that takes the credit. The donkey's jawbone preaches that salvation belongs to the LORD and uses the lowliest means; Samson's song nearly drowns out the sermon. (cf. 1 Cor. 1:27–29; Judg. 7:2)

sections.title: The Cry of Thirst and the Water from the Rock
sections.commentary:
The chapter ends on a surprisingly tender note. After the slaughter, Samson is 'very thirsty,' and for the first time in the narrative he prays: 'You have granted this great salvation by the hand of your servant, and shall I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?' It is a flawed prayer — self-pitying, even a little petulant, and notably he now acknowledges the victory as God's 'great salvation,' though only when he wants something. Yet it is a prayer; the swaggering strongman, brought low by simple thirst, finally turns to God in dependence. Davis observes that it takes a parched throat to make Samson pray — that God sometimes uses our weakness, our limits, our bodily frailty to drive us at last to call on him.

And God answers with grace far exceeding the quality of the prayer. He splits open the hollow place at Lehi, and water gushes out; Samson drinks, his spirit revives, and the spring is named En-hakkore, 'the spring of him who called.' The echoes of the wilderness are deliberate — water from the rock for a thirsty, complaining servant, as God gave Israel water from the rock at Massah and Meribah. And Paul tells us that Rock was Christ (1 Cor. 10:4). The God who brought water from the rock for grumbling Israel and parched Samson is the God who, on the cross, was himself struck so that living water might flow to all who thirst. Samson, the mighty deliverer reduced to begging for a drink, is a picture of every servant of God: our strength is borrowed, our life dependent, and the moment we forget it, thirst will remind us. He judged Israel twenty years — a real but partial deliverance, the work merely begun, awaiting the One who would cry 'I thirst' that we might drink forever. (cf. 1 Cor. 10:4; John 19:28)

15.theology:
The Spiral of Vengeance. Samson and the Philistines escalate retaliation upon retaliation — burned fields, burned family, slaughter upon slaughter. Private vengeance has no stopping point; it consumes all in reach. Only the Lord, who absorbs wrong rather than escalating it, can break the cycle (Rom. 12:19).

A People Content in Bondage. Judah binds its own deliverer and hands him to the enemy, preferring slavery to freedom. This haunting scene foreshadows the gospel: the Deliverer came to his own, and his own bound him and handed him over (John 1:11; 19:15).

Strength Brought Low to Dependence. The mighty Samson, undone by simple thirst, finally prays, and God gives water from the rock. Our strength is borrowed; weakness drives us to the God who struck the true Rock that living water might flow (1 Cor. 10:4).
15.examples:
Then: Samson torched the Philistine harvest with foxes, was bound by his own countrymen of Judah who preferred bondage to freedom, broke loose by the Spirit and slew a thousand with a donkey's jawbone, then was humbled by thirst into his first prayer and given water from the rock.

Now: Refuse the spiral of vengeance that consumes everyone it touches; leave repayment to God. Beware the comfortable slavery that resents its own rescue, preferring peace with the world to the freedom Christ offers. And let your weaknesses — even bodily ones — drive you to prayer and dependence, for our strength is borrowed and our life flows from the smitten Rock.

16.title: Samson and Delilah
16.text: <sup>1</sup>Samson went to Gaza, and there he saw a prostitute, and he went in to her.<sup>2</sup>The Gazites were told, "Samson has come here." And they surrounded the place and set an ambush for him all night at the gate of the city. They kept quiet all night, saying, "Let us wait till the light of the morning; then we will kill him."<sup>3</sup>But Samson lay till midnight, and at midnight he arose and took hold of the doors of the gate of the city and the two posts, and pulled them up, bar and all, and put them on his shoulders and carried them to the top of the hill that is in front of Hebron.<sup>4</sup>After this he loved a woman in the Valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah.<sup>5</sup>And the lords of the Philistines came up to her and said to her, "Seduce him, and see where his great strength lies, and by what means we may overpower him, that we may bind him to humble him. And we will each give you 1,100 pieces of silver."<sup>6</sup>So Delilah said to Samson, "Please tell me where your great strength lies, and how you might be bound, that one could subdue you."<sup>7</sup>Samson said to her, "If they bind me with seven fresh bowstrings that have not been dried, then I shall become weak and be like any other man."<sup>8</sup>Then the lords of the Philistines brought up to her seven fresh bowstrings that had not been dried, and she bound him with them.<sup>9</sup>Now she had men lying in ambush in an inner chamber. And she said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" But he snapped the bowstrings, as a thread of flax snaps when it touches the fire. So the secret of his strength was not known.<sup>10</sup>Then Delilah said to Samson, "Behold, you have mocked me and told me lies. Please tell me how you might be bound."<sup>11</sup>And he said to her, "If they bind me with new ropes that have not been used, then I shall become weak and be like any other man."<sup>12</sup>So Delilah took new ropes and bound him with them and said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" And the men lying in ambush were in an inner chamber. But he snapped the ropes off his arms like a thread.<sup>13</sup>Then Delilah said to Samson, "Until now you have mocked me and told me lies. Tell me how you might be bound." And he said to her, "If you weave the seven locks of my head with the web and fasten it tight with the pin, then I shall become weak and be like any other man."<sup>14</sup>So while he slept, Delilah took the seven locks of his head and wove them into the web. And she made them tight with the pin and said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" But he awoke from his sleep and pulled away the pin, the loom, and the web.<sup>15</sup>And she said to him, "How can you say, 'I love you,' when your heart is not with me? You have mocked me these three times, and you have not told me where your great strength lies."<sup>16</sup>And when she pressed him hard with her words day after day, and urged him, his soul was vexed to death.<sup>17</sup>And he told her all his heart, and said to her, "A razor has never come upon my head, for I have been a Nazirite to God from my mother's womb. If my head is shaved, then my strength will leave me, and I shall become weak and be like any other man."<sup>18</sup>When Delilah saw that he had told her all his heart, she sent and called the lords of the Philistines, saying, "Come up again, for he has told me all his heart." Then the lords of the Philistines came up to her and brought the money in their hands.<sup>19</sup>She made him sleep on her knees. And she called a man and had him shave off the seven locks of his head. Then she began to torment him, and his strength left him.<sup>20</sup>And she said, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" And he awoke from his sleep and said, "I will go out as at other times and shake myself free." But he did not know that the LORD had left him.<sup>21</sup>And the Philistines seized him and gouged out his eyes and brought him down to Gaza and bound him with bronze shackles. And he ground at the mill in the prison.<sup>22</sup>But the hair of his head began to grow again after it had been shaved.<sup>23</sup>Now the lords of the Philistines gathered to offer a great sacrifice to Dagon their god and to rejoice, and they said, "Our god has given Samson our enemy into our hand."<sup>24</sup>And when the people saw him, they praised their god. For they said, "Our god has given our enemy into our hand, the ravager of our country, who has killed many of us."<sup>25</sup>And when their hearts were merry, they said, "Call Samson, that he may entertain us." So they called Samson out of the prison, and he entertained them. They made him stand between the pillars.<sup>26</sup>And Samson said to the young man who held him by the hand, "Let me feel the pillars on which the house rests, that I may lean against them."<sup>27</sup>Now the house was full of men and women. All the lords of the Philistines were there, and on the roof there were about 3,000 men and women, who looked on while Samson entertained.<sup>28</sup>Then Samson called to the LORD and said, "O Lord GOD, please remember me and please strengthen me only this once, O God, that I may be avenged on the Philistines for my two eyes."<sup>29</sup>And Samson grasped the two middle pillars on which the house rested, and he leaned his weight against them, his right hand on the one and his left hand on the other.<sup>30</sup>And Samson said, "Let me die with the Philistines." Then he bowed with all his strength, and the house fell upon the lords and upon all the people who were in it. So the dead whom he killed at his death were more than those whom he had killed during his life.<sup>31</sup>Then his brothers and all his family came down and took him and brought him up and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of Manoah his father. He had judged Israel twenty years.
16.overview:
Chapter 16 is the climax and the catastrophe of Samson's life — the slow, willful self-destruction of the strongest man in Israel, and then, out of the ruin, a final act of deliverance that achieves in death what his life never did. It is one of the most tragic and most gospel-shadowed chapters in the Old Testament.

It opens with Samson at Gaza visiting a prostitute, then tearing the city gates from their posts and carrying them up a hill — a display of titanic strength wasted on a night of lust. Then comes Delilah. The Philistine lords bribe her to discover the secret of his strength, and the narrative builds with agonizing repetition: three times she asks, three times he toys with her with false answers, three times the Philistines spring their trap, and three times he escapes. He is playing a deadly game, flirting with his own ruin, treating the secret of his consecration as a joke.

Delilah does what the Philistine women always do — she weeps, presses, accuses him daily until 'his soul was vexed to death,' and at last 'he told her all his heart.' The razor comes, his hair is shaved, his strength departs. And then the most chilling sentence in the book: 'He did not know that the LORD had left him.' He rises to shake himself free as before, but the Spirit is gone, and he does not even realize it. The Philistines seize him, gouge out his eyes, and set him grinding grain like an animal in the prison of Gaza.

But the narrator slips in a clause heavy with hope: 'the hair of his head began to grow again.' At the Philistine festival to Dagon, the blind, broken Samson is brought out to entertain his captors, and he prays his second and final prayer: 'O Lord GOD, please remember me and strengthen me only this once.' He grasps the temple pillars and pulls the house down on himself and three thousand Philistines. 'The dead whom he killed at his death were more than those he had killed during his life.' Here is the deepest Christological shadow in the book: a deliverer who accomplishes more in his death than in his living, who triumphs through being broken — pointing to the One whose death, far from defeat, was the very victory that saved the world. (cf. Heb. 11:32–34; Col. 2:15)

sections.title: The Gates of Gaza
sections.commentary:
The chapter opens with Samson at Gaza, in the bed of a prostitute — the consecrated Nazirite, the deliverer of Israel, spending his strength on a night of lust in the heart of enemy territory. The Philistines surround the city, planning to kill him at dawn. But at midnight Samson rises, seizes the massive city gates — doors, posts, bar, and all — hoists them onto his shoulders, and carries them to the top of a hill near Hebron, miles away. It is a feat of staggering, almost comic strength.

And yet Davis points to the tragedy beneath the spectacle: this colossal power, given by God to deliver Israel, is being squandered on a lustful escapade and a show of bravado. Samson uses his strength to extract himself from the consequences of his own sin, not to free his people. He is utterly heedless of danger, presuming on his invincibility, walking into the enemy's stronghold for a prostitute. The man cannot govern his appetites, and his very impunity is hardening him. Each escape from disaster only deepens his recklessness, convincing him that nothing can touch him. This is the deadly logic of presumption — the belief, fed by repeated near-misses, that the rules do not apply to me, that I can sin and always shake myself free. Samson is being set up for the fall, not by any sudden ambush but by his own slow-growing conviction of invulnerability. The strongest man alive is the weakest of all where it matters most, and his string of escapes is not evidence of safety but the rope with which he is hanging himself. Pride and presumption go before the fall. (cf. 1 Cor. 10:12; Prov. 16:18)

sections.title: Delilah and the Deadly Game
sections.commentary:
Then Samson loves Delilah, and the Philistine lords seize their chance, bribing her with an enormous sum to discover the secret of his strength. What follows is told with deliberate, agonizing repetition. Delilah asks; Samson lies — bind me with fresh bowstrings, with new ropes, weave my hair into the loom; each time the Philistines lie in wait, each time she cries 'The Philistines are upon you, Samson!' and each time he snaps free. The pattern repeats three times, and the reader watches in mounting horror as Samson plays a deadly game on the very edge of the precipice.

The most damning detail is what Samson can plainly see and willfully ignores. Each time he reveals a 'secret,' the Philistines immediately try to use it against him. The evidence is undeniable: Delilah is betraying him, working for his enemies, edging ever closer to the truth. Any sane man would flee. But Samson stays, drawn back again and again to the very source of his danger. Davis names the deadly fascination — Samson is in love with his own destruction, mesmerized by the thing that will ruin him, unable to tear himself away even as the trap closes visibly around him. This is how sin so often works in the believer's life: not in one sudden plunge but in a series of knowing flirtations, each one revealing a little more, each one bringing the enemy a little closer, while we tell ourselves we can still shake free. The man who would not run from Delilah is every soul that lingers at the door of a sin it can clearly see is hunting it. He is playing with the secret of his consecration as if it were a parlor game, and the next round will cost him everything. (cf. Prov. 7:22–23; James 1:14–15)

sections.title: He Did Not Know That the LORD Had Left Him
sections.commentary:
Delilah deploys her final weapon, the same one that broke Samson with his first wife: relentless emotional pressure. 'How can you say, I love you, when your heart is not with me?' She presses him daily with her words until 'his soul was vexed to death,' and at last — worn down, not overpowered — 'he told her all his heart.' He surrenders the secret of his Nazirite consecration, the sign of his set-apartness to God, treating as a lover's confidence the very mark of his calling. She shaves his head as he sleeps on her knees, and his strength leaves him.

Then comes the most haunting and terrible sentence in the book: 'He awoke from his sleep and said, I will go out as at other times and shake myself free. But he did not know that the LORD had left him.' The horror is in the not knowing. Samson imagines nothing has changed; he reaches for the old power as if it were his own possession, a reflex, a personal endowment — and it is gone, and he cannot even feel the absence. Davis and Ferguson both linger here in dread: the most frightening thing about Samson's fall is that he was unaware of it. The presence of God had departed so gradually, through so many small compromises, that its final withdrawal went unnoticed. This is the most chilling possibility in the spiritual life — to go on through the motions, presuming on a power and a presence that have quietly slipped away, not knowing that the LORD has left. The Philistines seize him, gouge out his eyes, and bind him to grind grain in the prison, the mighty deliverer reduced to a blinded beast at the mill, mocked by the people he was sent to defeat. And yet — the narrator plants one seed of hope — 'the hair of his head began to grow again.' Grace is not finished with him. (cf. Eph. 4:30; Rev. 3:17)

sections.title: Let Me Die with the Philistines
sections.commentary:
The Philistines gather to celebrate in the temple of their god Dagon, attributing their triumph to him: 'Our god has given Samson our enemy into our hand.' At the height of the festivities, drunk with victory, they call for the blind Samson to be brought out to entertain them — the captured champion as the evening's amusement. Three thousand Philistines crowd the temple and its roof to watch. Samson asks the boy leading him to let him feel the central pillars on which the house rests.

And there, blind and broken, Samson prays the second and last prayer of his life: 'O Lord GOD, please remember me and strengthen me only this once, O God, that I may be avenged on the Philistines for my two eyes.' It is still, characteristically, a prayer about his own vengeance — Samson remains Samson to the end. Yet it is a prayer of genuine dependence, an acknowledgment that the strength was never his own but God's to give. Davis notes the bitter mercy of his blindness: only when he could no longer see did Samson finally look to God. He grasps the two central pillars, cries, 'Let me die with the Philistines,' and bows with all his might, and the temple crashes down. 'So the dead whom he killed at his death were more than those he had killed during his life.'

Here is the deepest Christological shadow in all of Judges. Samson, the deliverer, accomplishes more in his dying than in his living; his greatest victory comes through his death, achieved by being broken. Hebrews 11 enrolls him among the heroes of faith, for in that final act, by faith, he 'was made strong out of weakness' (Heb. 11:34). And the pattern points unmistakably forward. Samson stretched out his arms between two pillars and died to defeat the enemies of God's people — a flawed, dim foreshadowing of the true Deliverer who stretched out his arms on two beams of wood and, in dying, achieved the salvation his life had been moving toward all along. But the contrasts are as great as the likeness. Samson died praying for vengeance; Christ died praying, 'Father, forgive them.' Samson died with his enemies; Christ died for his enemies. Samson's death killed thousands; Christ's death saved an innumerable multitude. Samson was a deliverer ruined by sin who managed one last act of grace; Christ was the sinless Deliverer whose death was no ruin but the deliberate triumph of God, disarming the powers and making a public spectacle of them (Col. 2:15). Samson's broken life points, through all its tragedy, to the One whose death achieved what no living judge ever could. (cf. Heb. 11:32–34; Luke 23:34)

16.theology:
The Slow Departure of God's Presence. 'He did not know that the LORD had left him' (v. 20) is the most chilling line in the book. The Spirit's presence withdrew so gradually, through so many small compromises, that its final absence went unnoticed. The terror of presuming on grace that has quietly slipped away.

Flirting with Destruction. Samson played a deadly game with Delilah, seeing the trap close and refusing to flee, in love with the thing that would ruin him. Sin works not by one plunge but by knowing flirtations, each bringing the enemy nearer (James 1:14–15).

The Death That Achieves More Than the Life. Samson killed more in his death than in his life, made strong out of weakness, arms stretched between the pillars (Heb. 11:34). A flawed shadow of the true Deliverer, who stretched his arms on the cross and triumphed through death — yet died for his enemies, praying forgiveness, saving a multitude (Col. 2:15).
16.examples:
Then: The strongest man alive wasted his power on lust and bravado, played a deadly game with Delilah until he surrendered the secret of his consecration, lost the Spirit without even knowing it, was blinded and enslaved — and in his dying, by one last prayer, pulled down more enemies than he had killed in all his life.

Now: Beware the gradual departure of God's presence through accumulated small compromises, lest you too presume on a grace that has quietly left. Flee the sin you can see hunting you rather than flirting with it. And look beyond every broken deliverer to the One whose death was no ruin but the deliberate triumph of God — who stretched out his arms not for vengeance but for forgiveness, and in dying saved his enemies.

17.title: Micah's Idol
17.text: <sup>1</sup>There was a man of the hill country of Ephraim, whose name was Micah.<sup>2</sup>And he said to his mother, "The 1,100 pieces of silver that were taken from you, about which you uttered a curse, and also spoke it in my ears, behold, the silver is with me; I took it." And his mother said, "Blessed be my son by the LORD."<sup>3</sup>And he restored the 1,100 pieces of silver to his mother. And his mother said, "I dedicate the silver to the LORD from my hand for my son, to make a carved image and a metal image. Now therefore I will restore it to you."<sup>4</sup>So when he restored the money to his mother, his mother took 200 pieces of silver and gave it to the silversmith, who made it into a carved image and a metal image. And it was in the house of Micah.<sup>5</sup>And the man Micah had a shrine, and he made an ephod and household gods, and ordained one of his sons, who became his priest.<sup>6</sup>In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.<sup>7</sup>Now there was a young man of Bethlehem in Judah, of the family of Judah, who was a Levite, and he sojourned there.<sup>8</sup>And the man departed from the town of Bethlehem in Judah to sojourn where he could find a place. And as he journeyed, he came to the hill country of Ephraim to the house of Micah.<sup>9</sup>And Micah said to him, "Where do you come from?" And he said to him, "I am a Levite of Bethlehem in Judah, and I am going to sojourn where I may find a place."<sup>10</sup>And Micah said to him, "Stay with me, and be to me a father and a priest, and I will give you ten pieces of silver a year and a suit of clothes and your living." And the Levite went in.<sup>11</sup>And the Levite was content to dwell with the man, and the young man became to him like one of his sons.<sup>12</sup>And Micah ordained the Levite, and the young man became his priest, and was in the house of Micah.<sup>13</sup>Then Micah said, "Now I know that the LORD will prosper me, because I have a Levite as priest."
17.overview:
With chapter 17 the book enters its final movement — the so-called appendix, two horrifying narratives (chs. 17–18 and 19–21) that are not part of the judge-cycles but function as case studies in what Israel had become 'in those days,' when 'there was no king in Israel' and 'everyone did what was right in his own eyes.' This fourfold refrain (17:6; 18:1; 19:1; 21:25) is the interpretive key. The appendix does not narrate deliverance; it narrates collapse — the rot at the heart of the nation, in its religion (chs. 17–18) and in its morality (chs. 19–21).

Chapter 17 introduces Micah, a man of the hill country of Ephraim, in a story that would be almost comic if it were not so spiritually disastrous. Micah steals eleven hundred pieces of silver from his own mother, then, frightened by her curse, confesses and returns it. The mother, delighted, consecrates the silver 'to the LORD' — and uses it to make a carved image and a metal idol. Micah sets up a private shrine in his house, complete with idol, ephod, and household gods, and installs one of his sons as priest. Then a wandering Levite arrives, and Micah hires him as his personal priest, concluding, 'Now I know that the LORD will prosper me, because I have a Levite as priest.'

The horror of the chapter is its syncretism — its blending of the worship of the LORD with idolatry, its use of God's name to sanctify thoroughly pagan practices. Micah is not an atheist; he is, in his own mind, devout. He wants the LORD's blessing, invokes the LORD's name, hires a Levite to make it all proper. But every element is a violation: graven images, a private shrine, a homemade priesthood, religion as a means to personal prosperity. He has fashioned a god he can keep in his house and a religion he can control for his own ends.

This is the deadliest form of false religion — not the open rejection of God but the domestication of God, using his name to bless what he forbids, making faith a tool for self-interest. Micah's confident 'Now I know the LORD will prosper me' is the voice of every age that treats God as a means to its own ends. And the absence of a king — the absence of any restraining authority, any submission to the revealed will of God — lets every man build his own religion in his own house, right in his own eyes. The chapter cries out for the true King who alone is worshiped rightly, and who cannot be domesticated, bargained with, or kept in a private shrine. (cf. Exod. 20:4; 2 Tim. 4:3)

sections.title: Stolen Silver and a Mother's Curse
sections.commentary:
The story opens in a single dysfunctional household and immediately signals moral confusion. Micah, a man of the Ephraimite hill country, has stolen eleven hundred pieces of silver from his own mother — a startling breach of the commandments to honor one's parents and not to steal, all within one family. When he overhears his mother uttering a curse on the thief, he is frightened enough to confess and return the silver. The mother's response is the first sign of the chapter's tangled piety: instead of rebuking the theft, she blesses her son 'by the LORD' and declares that she had dedicated the silver 'to the LORD' on his behalf.

Then comes the jarring twist. Her devotion 'to the LORD' takes the form of making 'a carved image and a metal image' — precisely what the second commandment forbids. She takes the recovered silver to a silversmith, who fashions an idol, and it is set up in Micah's house. Davis catches the breathtaking confusion: every religious instinct in this family points the right direction — toward the LORD, toward dedication and blessing — and every actual practice violates his explicit command. They invoke Yahweh's name while breaking Yahweh's law. This is the essence of syncretism, and it is more dangerous than open paganism precisely because it feels devout. The mother believes she is honoring God; she is in fact manufacturing an idol. How often religion goes wrong not by abandoning God's name but by attaching it to things God hates — sanctifying our preferences, our self-made worship, our cultural idols with a pious label. The household that begins with theft and a curse and ends with a homemade god has lost the very first principle: God will not be worshiped by images of our own devising, however sincere. (cf. Exod. 20:4–6; Deut. 12:8)

sections.title: Everyone Did What Was Right in His Own Eyes
sections.commentary:
Micah formalizes the family religion: he has 'a shrine,' he makes 'an ephod and household gods,' and he 'ordained one of his sons, who became his priest.' Every phrase is a violation of God's appointed order. Worship was to be centered at the tabernacle, not in private house-shrines; the priesthood belonged to Aaron's line, not to whichever son a man chose to ordain; images and household gods (teraphim) were forbidden outright. Micah has built a complete alternative religious system in his own home, self-designed and self-administered, a boutique faith tailored to his preferences.

And then the narrator gives the verse that unlocks the entire final section of the book: 'In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.' This is the diagnosis. With no king — no central authority, no submission to God's revealed will, no restraint on the autonomous self — every man becomes his own lawgiver, his own priest, his own god-maker. Davis and Ferguson both stress that the refrain is not primarily a political comment but a spiritual one. The deepest problem is not that Israel lacked a monarch but that Israel lacked submission to the King who already reigned, the LORD their God. 'Right in his own eyes' is the creed of human autonomy, the original sin of Eden replayed: I will decide good and evil for myself; I will worship as I see fit; I will be my own authority. It is the spirit of every age, including ours, that makes the self the final arbiter of truth and the personal preference the measure of religion. Micah's house-shrine is simply human autonomy applied to worship. And the only cure is the true King, before whom every knee bows and every private religion falls — the King who will not be made in our image but remakes us in his. (cf. Judg. 21:25; Gen. 3:5)

sections.title: The Hired Levite and Religion as Self-Interest
sections.commentary:
A young Levite from Bethlehem in Judah, wandering in search of a place to live, comes to Micah's house. Micah seizes the opportunity to upgrade his religious establishment: a real Levite is more impressive than his own son as priest. He offers the man wages, food, and clothing — 'Be to me a father and a priest' — and the Levite, content with the arrangement, settles in. Micah is delighted, and his delight reveals the whole rotten theology of the chapter: 'Now I know that the LORD will prosper me, because I have a Levite as priest.'

There it is — religion as a prosperity transaction. Micah treats the Levite like a good-luck charm, a guarantee of divine favor. He imagines he has secured God's blessing by acquiring the right religious credentials: a proper priest, a well-appointed shrine, the correct trappings. He has reduced the living God to a mechanism for personal prosperity, a system to be managed for his own benefit. Davis exposes the deadliness of it: Micah does not want to serve God; he wants God to serve him. The whole apparatus — the idol, the ephod, the hired Levite — exists to make Micah prosper. This is the syncretism of the human heart in every generation, the assumption that the right religious performance obligates God to bless, that faith is a transaction in which we supply the rituals and God supplies the rewards. It is precisely the prosperity instinct Paul warned of, 'imagining that godliness is a means of gain' (1 Tim. 6:5). And it is the polar opposite of true worship, which seeks not God's gifts but God himself, and bows to him as King rather than hiring him as a servant. Micah's confident 'Now I know the LORD will prosper me' will be exposed as hollow in the very next chapter, when the Danites simply walk off with his god and his priest, and Micah is left crying, 'You take my gods that I made... and what have I left?' A god you can make is a god they can steal. (cf. 1 Tim. 6:5; Judg. 18:24)

17.theology:
The Domestication of God. Micah's syncretism — invoking the LORD's name while making idols, building a private shrine, hiring a priest — is more dangerous than open paganism because it feels devout. The deadliest false religion does not reject God but tames him, using his name to bless what he forbids.

Right in His Own Eyes. The refrain (v. 6) diagnoses the whole age: with no submission to the King who reigns, every man becomes his own lawgiver and god-maker. It is the creed of human autonomy, Eden's sin replayed — making the self the final authority over truth and worship.

Religion as Self-Interest. 'Now I know that the LORD will prosper me, because I have a Levite' (v. 13). Micah wants God to serve him, not to serve God — godliness imagined as a means of gain (1 Tim. 6:5). A god you can make is a god they can steal.
17.examples:
Then: Micah stole from his mother, who dedicated the silver 'to the LORD' by making an idol; he built a private shrine, ordained his own son, then hired a wandering Levite, certain that the right religious credentials guaranteed God's blessing — devout in name, idolatrous in fact.

Now: Beware the domestication of God — the syncretism that attaches his name to what he forbids and sanctifies our self-made worship with a pious label. Beware treating faith as a transaction that obligates God to prosper us. The living God cannot be kept in a private shrine, hired like a servant, or made in our image; he is the King who remakes us in his.

18.title: The Danites Steal the Idol
18.text: <sup>1</sup>In those days there was no king in Israel. And in those days the tribe of the people of Dan was seeking for itself an inheritance to dwell in, for until then no inheritance among the tribes of Israel had fallen to them.<sup>2</sup>So the people of Dan sent five able men from the whole number of their tribe, from Zorah and from Eshtaol, to spy out the land and to explore it. And they said to them, "Go and explore the land." And they came to the hill country of Ephraim, to the house of Micah, and lodged there.<sup>3</sup>When they were by the house of Micah, they recognized the voice of the young Levite. And they turned aside and said to him, "Who brought you here? What are you doing in this place? What is your business here?"<sup>4</sup>And he said to them, "This is how Micah dealt with me: he has hired me, and I have become his priest."<sup>5</sup>And they said to him, "Inquire of God, please, that we may know whether the journey on which we are setting out will succeed."<sup>6</sup>And the priest said to them, "Go in peace. The journey on which you go is under the eye of the LORD."<sup>7</sup>Then the five men departed and came to Laish and saw the people who were there, how they lived in security, after the manner of the Sidonians, quiet and unsuspecting, lacking nothing that is in the earth and possessing wealth, and how they were far from the Sidonians and had no dealings with anyone.<sup>8</sup>And when they came to their brothers at Zorah and Eshtaol, their brothers said to them, "What do you report?"<sup>9</sup>They said, "Arise, and let us go up against them, for we have seen the land, and behold, it is very good. And will you do nothing? Do not be slow to go, to enter in and possess the land.<sup>10</sup>As soon as you go, you will come to an unsuspecting people. The land is spacious, for God has given it into your hands, a place where there is no lack of anything that is in the earth."<sup>11</sup>So 600 men of the tribe of Dan, armed with weapons of war, set out from Zorah and Eshtaol,<sup>12</sup>and went up and encamped at Kiriath-jearim in Judah. On this account that place is called Mahaneh-dan to this day; behold, it is west of Kiriath-jearim.<sup>13</sup>And they passed on from there to the hill country of Ephraim, and came to the house of Micah.<sup>14</sup>Then the five men who had gone to scout out the country of Laish said to their brothers, "Do you know that in these houses there are an ephod, household gods, a carved image, and a metal image? Now therefore consider what you will do."<sup>15</sup>And they turned aside there and came to the house of the young Levite, at the home of Micah, and asked him about his welfare.<sup>16</sup>Now the 600 men of the Danites, armed with their weapons of war, stood by the entrance of the gate.<sup>17</sup>And the five men who had gone to scout out the land went up and entered and took the carved image, the ephod, the household gods, and the metal image, while the priest stood by the entrance of the gate with the 600 men armed with weapons of war.<sup>18</sup>And when these went into Micah's house and took the carved image, the ephod, the household gods, and the metal image, the priest said to them, "What are you doing?"<sup>19</sup>And they said to him, "Keep quiet; put your hand on your mouth and come with us and be to us a father and a priest. Is it better for you to be priest to the house of one man, or to be priest to a tribe and clan in Israel?"<sup>20</sup>And the priest's heart was glad. He took the ephod and the household gods and the carved image and went along with the people.<sup>21</sup>So they turned and departed, putting the little ones and the livestock and the goods in front of them.<sup>22</sup>When they had gone a distance from the home of Micah, the men who were in the houses near Micah's house were called out, and they overtook the people of Dan.<sup>23</sup>And they shouted to the people of Dan, who turned around and said to Micah, "What is the matter with you, that you come with such a company?"<sup>24</sup>And he said, "You take my gods that I made and the priest, and go away, and what have I left? How then do you ask me, 'What is the matter with you?'"<sup>25</sup>And the people of Dan said to him, "Do not let your voice be heard among us, lest angry fellows fall upon you, and you lose your life with the lives of your household."<sup>26</sup>Then the people of Dan went their way. And when Micah saw that they were too strong for him, he turned and went back to his home.<sup>27</sup>But the people of Dan took what Micah had made, and the priest who belonged to him, and they came to Laish, to a people quiet and unsuspecting, and struck them with the edge of the sword and burned the city with fire.<sup>28</sup>And there was no deliverer because it was far from Sidon, and they had no dealings with anyone. It was in the valley that belongs to Beth-rehob. Then they rebuilt the city and lived in it.<sup>29</sup>And they named the city Dan, after the name of Dan their ancestor, who was born to Israel; but the name of the city was Laish at the first.<sup>30</sup>And the people of Dan set up the carved image for themselves, and Jonathan the son of Gershom, son of Moses, and his sons were priests to the tribe of the Danites until the day of the captivity of the land.<sup>31</sup>So they set up Micah's carved image that he made, as long as the house of God was at Shiloh.
18.overview:
Chapter 18 extends the religious collapse of chapter 17 from a single household to an entire tribe, showing how private idolatry becomes institutional apostasy. The tribe of Dan, having failed to secure its allotted territory (as far back as 1:34, where the Amorites pushed them into the hills), goes looking for new land to seize. They send five spies, who lodge at Micah's house and recognize the voice of his hired Levite.

The spies inquire of the Levite whether their mission will succeed, and he gives them a glib oracle of blessing. They scout out Laish, a quiet, unsuspecting, isolated city in the far north, and report back that it is ripe for conquest. The tribe musters six hundred armed men and sets out. On the way they stop at Micah's house — and simply steal his gods. The five spies take the carved image, the ephod, the household gods, and the metal idol, and persuade the Levite to come with them: 'Is it better for you to be priest to the house of one man, or... to a tribe and clan in Israel?' The hireling priest, delighted at the promotion, takes the idols and joins them.

Micah pursues, protesting the theft of 'my gods that I made,' but the Danites threaten him with violence, and he turns home, helpless. The pathos of his cry — 'You take my gods... and what have I left?' — exposes the absurdity of idolatry: a god that can be stolen, a deity that depends on its owner to protect it. The Danites press on, slaughter the peaceful people of Laish, burn the city, rebuild it as Dan, and set up the stolen idol there. And the narrator delivers the devastating conclusion: they established this idolatry, with a priesthood, 'until the day of the captivity of the land.'

The theology is the institutionalizing of sin. What began as one man's private shrine becomes a tribal cult center that will corrupt Israel for centuries — indeed, Dan would become one of the two sites of Jeroboam's golden calves (1 Kings 12:29). Apostasy, tolerated in the home, metastasizes into the nation. And it all unfolds, again, because 'there was no king in Israel' — no authority to restrain the strong from seizing land, gods, and priests by sheer force. The chapter is a sobering study in how unchecked sin, left to do what is right in its own eyes, builds enduring structures of corruption that outlast their founders. (cf. 1 Kings 12:28–30; Isa. 46:1–2)

sections.title: The Danites Seek Land and Consult the Levite
sections.commentary:
The chapter opens with the refrain that frames the whole appendix — 'In those days there was no king in Israel' — and introduces the tribe of Dan, still landless. This failure traces back to chapter 1, where the Amorites pressed Dan into the hill country and would not let them possess the plain (1:34); rather than trust God to give them their inheritance, the Danites now go looking to seize someone else's. They dispatch five spies, who lodge at Micah's house and recognize the accent or voice of the young Levite. They ask him to inquire of God whether their journey will prosper, and he obligingly delivers a smooth oracle: 'Go in peace. The journey on which you go is under the eye of the LORD.'

Davis notes the hollow professionalism of this hired priest. He produces religious assurance on demand, a blessing to order, with no apparent thought as to whether it reflects the actual will of God. He is a spiritual mercenary, dispensing comforting oracles to whoever employs him. The spies, reassured, scout Laish and find it ideal prey: a people 'quiet and unsuspecting,' isolated, prosperous, with no ally to deliver them. The spies' report drips with the language of conquest stripped of any reference to God's command — 'God has given it into your hands,' they say, baptizing naked aggression in pious words. Here is the danger of religion in the service of human ambition: a priest who blesses whatever we want to do, an oracle that always says yes, a 'word from the LORD' conveniently matching our desires. It is the original temptation of false prophecy — speaking peace and success to those whose plans God never sanctioned (Jer. 23:16–17). The Danites have found the perfect chaplain for their greed: one who will sanctify their seizure of Laish as the will of God. (cf. Jer. 23:16–17; 2 Tim. 4:3)

sections.title: The Theft of the Idol and the Priest
sections.commentary:
Six hundred armed Danites set out for Laish, and on the way they stop at Micah's house. While the warriors stand at the gate, the five spies go in and simply take everything — the carved image, the ephod, the household gods, the metal idol. When the Levite protests, 'What are you doing?', they make him an offer he is only too happy to accept: 'Is it better for you to be priest to the house of one man, or to be priest to a tribe and clan in Israel?' The hireling priest does the math instantly — a bigger congregation, more prestige, better prospects — and 'the priest's heart was glad. He took the ephod and the household gods and the carved image and went along with the people.' He steals away with the very idols he was paid to tend, betraying his employer for a promotion.

Davis exposes the mercenary heart laid bare: the priest serves not God but his own advancement, and his loyalty extends only as far as his self-interest. The man who would sell his services to Micah will abandon Micah the moment a better offer comes. This is the hireling Jesus described, who 'cares nothing for the sheep' and flees when his own comfort is threatened (John 10:12–13). When Micah and his neighbors pursue, the Danites turn with menace, warning him to be silent 'lest angry fellows fall upon you and you lose your life.' Might makes right; the strong simply take what they want, gods and priest and all, and threaten murder if the victim objects. Micah, outnumbered and helpless, sees that 'they were too strong for him' and turns home. The whole sordid transaction — the casual theft, the mercenary priest, the threats of violence — is a portrait of a society with no king, no law, no restraint, where the powerful do what is right in their own eyes and the weak have no recourse. Even the idols offer no protection; they are simply carried off by whoever is stronger. (cf. John 10:12–13; Mic. 2:1–2)

sections.title: What Have I Left? The Absurdity of Idolatry
sections.commentary:
The chapter's most piercing line is Micah's cry as the Danites march off with his religious establishment: 'You take my gods that I made... and what have I left?' In that single sentence the absurdity of all idolatry is laid bare. 'My gods that I made' — a god a man manufactures, a deity dependent on its maker, a thing that can be picked up and carried away by anyone strong enough to take it. What kind of god needs his worshiper to defend him? What kind of deity can be stolen? Davis and the prophets after him drive the point home: the idol cannot save itself, let alone its maker (Isa. 46:1–2). Micah's question answers itself. A god you can make is a god they can steal, and a man who trusts in such a god is left, in the end, with nothing.

The Danites press on to Laish and fall upon its quiet, defenseless people, putting them to the sword and burning the city. They rebuild it, name it Dan, and there 'set up the carved image' — Micah's stolen idol now installed as the cult center of an entire tribe. The narrator adds two devastating historical notes. The renegade Levite is named: Jonathan, a descendant of Moses himself — the line of the great lawgiver now leading idolatry. And the idolatry endured 'all the time that the house of God was at Shiloh,' indeed 'until the day of the captivity of the land.'
